INOTICE HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be .holden at the COURT NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 17th day of October next, at half- past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, When the Grand 'Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising Within the Hundreds of Bucklow. Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knots- ford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be In atten- dance at the Court House, Knutsford. at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 17th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will te Adjourned to the Castle of Chester. on TEUBSDAY, the 20th day of Ockiber next, at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. Countryman: "An' sure is it orphans that live there?" Fellow-passenger: "You've guessed it the first time." Countryman (after admiring buildings): "Well, it's a splendid thing to be born an orphan l" MAllir and many a time has the failure of one man to meet his obligations brought on the ruin of a score of others, just as the toppling down in tine of bricks of the master brick causes the fall of all the rest. Thousands remain poor all their lives who, if they were more faithful of their word, would secure a large run of custom, and so make their fortunes. Be punctual if you would succeed.

EVERYONE desires that his labour should com- mand respect, but few understand the way to bring it about. It will never be done by leaving one employment for another; the same character will shine through both. Instead of this, let each one put the very best and highest qualities he can command into the work he has on hand; let him throw his whole soul into it, becoming one with it, hoping, labouring, and, if need be, sacrificing for It, so that he makes it grow in excellence.

Nitzni.ns in early times were made of fish bone, bone, or ivoty, and their first form was probably that of a rude eyeless bedlan. Since the time of the discovery of bronze, however, metal needles have been in use in civilised communities. It is on record that needles of steel were made at Nurem- berg towards the end of the fourteenth century. For upwards of two hundred years the mann- fseure has been established in England; Red- dffols, in Worcestershire, with several other small towns in Warwickskire, being the centre of the indiustry, first planted there by Germans.

The Duke of Edinburgh came to town purposely to be present on Saturday night at the first per- formance of " Haddon Hall." The Duke is an old friend of Sir Arthur Sullivan, and in the prince's bachelor days the composer was one of his in- timates. The Duke of Edinburgh is also an occa- sional visitor at Sir Arthur's flat, and besides lead- ing the applause on Saturday night—for the Duke was very demonstrative in his approval of the work —he went behind to offer his congratulations per- sonally to the composer.

A scandalous outrage is reported by a pack of so- called sportsmen, which shows that a landlord's fnends can take pptshots at passengers with im- punity. It happened on the high road in the parish of Winkfield, mar Ascot, on Saturday. A party of the landlord's friends were opt partridge shooting, and one of them chose the high road AA his station. The birds were driven across the road, and he fired at them regardless of the danger to passers-by. A schoolboy received a shower of pellets in the head, and a cyclist was aisabled and brought down. The creature who committed this outrage slunk off across the fields, and the land- lord's law of trespass and the sacredness of pro- perty prevented anyone following him. The pollee 1-iould inquire into this case, and find out the name of the cowardly sportsman. ---------

PSir Gilbert Campbell, one of the devoted band of " littery gents," just convicted at the Old Bailey, is the third baronet of the line. His father distinguished himself as a major of cavalry in the East India service, and was for some time Ohargti d'Affaires at Teheran. For some services performed in that capacity he was, just sixty years ago, knighted, his father, the first baronet, being still . alive. The baronetcy dates back to 1831, and there. is every chance of its being perpetuated, Sir Gilbert having a son who has just attained his naajority. Sir Gilbert's sister is married to a Prebendary of Salisbury.

The system of o.°k-sharing in farming is found to work advantageously in South Carolina, and might be worth a trial in this country. The farms are from fifty to one hundred acres. The ,owner of the land and buildings gets the most likely man he can find to work the farm for a year on sharing terms. The latter must find the horses or mules and farm implements. The owner provides half the seed, and half, or sometimes or whole, of the artificial manures, where these are necessary. At the end of the season the owner and the farmer share the crops in equal proportions. If the result has been mutually satisfactory, the partnership is continured ; if not satisfactory, it is terminated, and the parties form new partnerships without much difficulty

It is not generally known that Prince George of Wales, concerning whose reported engagement so many statements are being made at the present time, is very fond of taking one of his sisters for a stroll in the morning when they are in London. They have often been seen looking at the shops in the Buckingham Palace-road, but very few persons recognise them, a fact which causes them much delight, as they are thus enabled to enjoy them- selves unmolested by the usual crowd.

The Misses Kenealy, who courageously volun- teered to nurse the cholera patients in Hamburg, have now returned home, a faet which may be accepted as an assurance that the epidemic is declining at its headquarters. In an interview which I have just had with them they tell me much surprise has been felt in Hamburg that no English doctors should have visited the town, especially in in view of a possible outbreak later in this coun- try.

The pathetic lament indulged in by Mr. Jerome over his alleged loss of ninety-nine out of every hundred ideas, and the stirring picture he draws of his hugging the hundredth—" invariably the weak- est," like the lamb that was lost and over whose return there was such rejoicing—will not hear the test of sober analysis. The statement, in chemists' phrase, betrays the presence of deleterious coloring matter—highly valued in journalistic circles—tor Mr. Jerome is in reality a copious notetaker. It is difficult to detect him, for apparently when he is about it his pencil lingers on the paper no more than a second. But the Idle Fellow is an expert in shorthand, and has jotted down an idle thought with two strokes and a flourish.

At last a Tory overseer hag been fined. it was about time to teach parish officials that they must not act as Tory agents. Registers in many consti- tuencies are fraudulently made up by the overseers, who work secretly in the interest of Toryism. The individual who was caught lives in the Spalding division of Lincolnshire. It was proved that he had attested a lie, and had acted in a partisan spirit by leaving off numbers of Liberals who were qualified to vote, and putting on Conservatives who had only commenced residence. The same system is practised with more or less stlecess in other places. This over- seer found guilty was fined .E 2. The Duke of Argyll, who has just received such an awful drilling at the bands of the Grand Old Man on the subject of Home Rule, will probably seek for consolation in the wild, weird music of his privste piper. Whether the latter will succeed in calming nis disordered mind as successfully as David did that of Saul of old is another matter. The Macal- I um More and his family are soothed by the execut- ant whilst they are dining, whether it be at the Castle of Inverary, or at Argyll Lodge., on Catnpden- hill. It is not generally known that a friendly rivalry exista between the Argyll piper and that of the Prince of Wales. The Macallum More's man is said to play with greater expression, but the Prince's piper is really the better operator.

Sir Arthur Sullivan, the composer, wee recently asked where be was able to compose best, and under what circumstances his ideas flowed most freely. Ile replied that there was no place in which he hail so many inspirations as in a railway carriage. There is something in the rapidity of the motion, in the clanging of the iron, and in the whirring of wheels, which seems to excite his imagination and supplies material for a host of harmonies. Unrh-r very different circumstances, however, was 'The Lost Chord " composed by the gifted musician. One night he was in the room next to that in vvhich his brother was dying. He had been watching at the bedside of the dying man and was thoroughly tired out. Sitting down before an organ that wa by chance in the room, he found the noble word* before him. He did not rise from his seat until he° had composed the music which has since thrilled the people.

div.head: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN SEALERS.
div.p: THE SEIZURE OF CANADIAN SEALERS.
PUBLIC RESENTMENT.

_ OTTAWA, TUESDAY.—Sir John Thompson, Minister of Justice, says that the British man-of-war now en route for Vladivostock, Siberia, will demand the release of any British sailors held prisoners by the Russians. The seizure of the Canadian sealers and the treatment to which their crews have been subjected by the Russian officials has evoked keen public resentment here.

div.head: CONVICT LA IiOR, BYiNDICAThS,
div.p: CONVICT LA IiOR, BYiNDICAThS,
BY H. WHITHAM. (Condoled.)

The trouble in' Tennessee is of old standing, and, so far as I am able to understand it, I cannot but think that the civil' authorities are carrying out a blundering, plundering policy, and if the American people as a whole would ive the question a like be righted. Theques- study, the wrong would soo, ij d m nut t crack. The on of prison labour is a ha' -t sentence of" hard labor" in Arne.'" simplyo means tidustrial labor. In Texas, Alab.B, sew "3 Carc4ina the convicts build railroads• ; they raise cotton in MisSissipui ; in the States of New ork and Tennessee they work in mines. Wire drawing Y and wire weaving in two States; shoe maki.lg "add tailoring in nearly all. At different prisons times convict labor has been employed in the 1. , I lowing systems :—l. Working the prisoners for the ' State in the manufacture of crude material fur- nished by the State. 2. The contract systems. 3. That of leasing the prison for a certain period ; the lessee assuming entire control of both discipline and industries, and furnishing food, clothing, &c. The first effect of the contract system is to place, for the whole working day, all the prisoners con- I traded for, to a great extent, under the control of men with no official responsibility, men who see in the convicts only so much material for making money; men whose only recommendation to the position they hold in the prison is that they were the highest bidders for the human beings hired by them. Convicts produce certain articles which are sold in the markets at less prices than the same goods produced by free labor. Convict labor is thus pitted against honest labor. The ho..lieSt workman must pay taxes, and them.:agln on prison-made goods goes into the I::;eirets of the contractors or prison lessees. This is the bed rock on which the whole trou4ie in Tennessee rests. That it could be solved there cannot be any doubt, but there is be- hind the throne a greater power than the throne it- self, power that makes and unmakes all officialism, in a word, corruption. Strikes are always in order in the States,but just new they are very unwelcome to the Republican,or Protectionist party. Workmen do not, as a rule,strike when the conditions of labor are satisfactory to them. That

div.head: PROTECTION DOES NOT SATISFY
div.p: PROTECTION DOES NOT SATISFY

is a self-evident fact, although strenuous torts are new being made by the Republicans to show that these labour troubles have nothing to do with politics. Possibly the tariff may have nothing to , do directly with the trouble in Tennessee, but, in- directly it must have. The Tennessee Coal, Iron, and Railroad Company is a rich and powerful company, well able to carry on any amount of log-rolling. The cOmpany owns all the mines and railroads of the district. It is also the lessee of the convict labour. Since 1891 it has employed convict labour working in the mines alongside with free labour. Of course, friction has always existed between the two classes of labour, and last October the fret miners drove out 460 convicts. A special session o the Tennessee legislature was called to consider the question of convict labour, but nothing was done. Of course, why nothing was done is easily understood. It paid someone that the wrong should continue. In January of this year, the miners attacked the State troops, the troops were outnumbered 100 to 1 ; and the miners swore to exterminate the troops and put an end to convict labour. But more troops were sent, and the miners had to submit. The cause of the present trouble has been a growing one, but seems to have cul- minated in the company's refusal to the free men's demand that they should have the same hours of work as the convicts. It must be borne in mind that the wages of free men average about 4s. 101. per day. About the middle of August the whole of the district around coal creek was

ABLAZE WITH RIOT. The miners captured the troops, and raided the convict stockade. Capturing over 300 convicts and disarming their guards, they were all sent off to Nashville, which was already crowded with re- turned convicts. 'nese successes nerved the miners on. Dynamite was laid under the rails to prevent the incoming of troops, and 2,000 miners, well armed and desperate, determined to take the war into other disaffected districts. Of course I cannot pretend to give in this letter the whole of the history of the coal creek trouble as gathered from the reading of several weeks' vipers,but quite big battles were fought, and numerous lives were lost. The upshot of the trouble came when Col. Anderson went out to talk with this miners, under the guise of a parley, he was made prisoner, and threatened with death did he not order the troops to surrender. He refused, and his bravery rather frightened the miners, who dare not kill him. An- other regiment was marched on the scene. The miners surrendered, and coal creek was again in the hands of the authorities, and under martial law. With Col. Anderson's release hostilities have, for a time, ceased. In New York State the rioting result- ing from the

div.head: RAILROAD sTRIIIRS AT BUFFALO
div.p: RAILROAD sTRIIIRS AT BUFFALO

have been of as determined a character as those elsewhere. Whole trains of cars have been burned. In one case a string of .50 cars was fired, and the flames raged unfought, the hose destroye4. even as it was run out. Several regiments of soldiers wore coon on the ground, and up to the time of the union going under desperate means were taken by the strikers to win. In one case as a train came along and was passing a body of soldiers, several of the men cried out that they were shot. On the surgeon examining the wounded men he found in the wounds pieces of tin such as is used in dyna- mite cartridges. The strikers had put the cartridges on the railroad track. The President of this union declared this strike off because of failure to induce other unions to declare sympathetic strikes. For doing this he was mobbed in the streets, and severely treated. Such is the miserable tale I set: out to tell toy friends in Warrington. Concerning ourselves with the strikes to which I have referred, , and leaving out altogether the one at the silver mines of Coeur D'Alene, where even more desperate methods were resorted to, there is •

div.head: MATTER FOR GRAVE THOUGHT
div.p: MATTER FOR GRAVE THOUGHT

for all trades unionists. -i-t-Th;;k iiii;;;7 -something of unionism. I ought to do. It has knocked me about pretty roughly, as it will do all who try to make it an intelligent study, and refuse to be led by an ignorant and undiscerning majority, and I am satisfied about the truth of several things con- cerning it. Of course Ido not expect that we shall ever make all men students of social questions, but we may make the wage earner a sober and intelligent man. Until he becomes this he should be debared from voting away his fellow workmens' wages. This can he done by the Federations of all Unions. Arbitration to be the first resource and to be enforced by the federated executive. In the case of refusal on the part of employers, the workers would have public opinion ' on tbeir side and could 'effectively use the boycott and the sympathetic strike. How many times have I been told, and read, that the extreme measures of ! English trade unions was driving capital out of England, and that if it was once driven out it would never return ! The question may be fairly asked now—Where can it be driven to ? I know of no place but India. There it will, for a time, find docile and cheap labour. What it will find in the , States I have tried in a brief way to sketch. America has three great troubles ahead, and the settlement of each may entail bloodshed.

div.head: RACE, RELIGION, AND LABOUR.
div.p: RACE, RELIGION, AND LABOUR.

, . Of the two former I may, in the future, have some- thing to say; of the latter, I may say it IS my chief study, as a recreation, and so long as permitted I shall be heard from. The lattsr sentence sounds like the finish, hut I have a few more words to say. In all my dealings with English employers, I found I had gentlemen to deal with. No unfair advantage was taken of me on account of my position in the union. This was all left toms' fellow workmen. In thi3 country the fair, and square employer is somewhat scarce, and now that war is declared, as it undoubtedly is, between labour and capital, the labour history of the future will be a very dark one. Not a doubt exists in my mind as to the result. Labour must win. So far it has been labour versus labour, or in other words organised labour against unorganised labour. Of course it is terribly up-hill work here to teach the hordes of labourers who arrive what is the inner principle of combination. but they love the dollar, and what cannot be done one way will be done another. Workmen mug educate and read, and they must not confine their reading to their own countries' literature. The happenings of one country affect all countries, alike. The doings of the English Parliament affect America, the doings of the Congress affect England, and so on all round. The time will come, and that shortly, when capital will be forced by stress of circumstances to take labour into its confidence, and then we shall see what co-operation means. The huge syndicates are paving the way to it. In the meantime

and when they are personified by such excrescences

THE REV. IL I. WADESON'S FAREWELL. The Rev. J. Carson having been tiducted to the living ot Wargrave, as rector, he will take up his , duties at the ChUICh 011 I.llldity,Morning next. The Rev. 11. 1. Wadeson, rector of &ft, who h°,B°ffici- ciated as curate in charge, since the (.I:.'"tti 41,41;19n Whitley, took his farewell on Sunday night, choos- ing for his text, Acts 20 c., 32 v. "And now brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up, and to give von an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.' After some reference to the words of the text,the rev. gentleman said her.c. waq a fittless la, the wardo /tet. dresse4 to them that evening. In all tprol;abillty that was the last time he should address them from that place, as having charge or responsibility over them. The time of his stay had been short, the changes had been many. Only a little more than three months ago, he came, comparatively a stranger, anticipating with the usual shortness of human calculation that his lot might be cast among them for several years to come, as the assistant of the late Rector. Those whe were present and heard the last words that Canon Whitley spoke from that place, knew better than himself how he spoke with almost prophetic earnestness. It has been said that the clergy were very much what their congregation made them, and there was truth in the saving. If there be one thing, which more than all others could strengthen a minister's heart and hand, it was the knowledge that behind him there was the confidence and support of is united people. Ministers were but men, with the usual share of human weakness and imperfection. Bat could they conceive anything mole likely to call forth their best efforts for their good, and rouse them to unweary- ing exertion, than the simple attitude on their part, which says in effect, if not in so many words. From the first they had shown unvarying kindness and his gratitude was due to them for oft expressed " good wishes." There was not one note in particular, of which little need be said, but which he thought claimed some acknowledgement on that the last opportunity. He felt, it his duty to offer them for the first and only time, his heartfelt thanks. Might they all, his friends, long he spared to raise up hearts and voices in holy thanksgiv- ing and prayer in their church. If at any time by tie' kind permission of his successor, he might address them, he should account it a privilege. TIIE REV. J. CARSON'S FAREWELL SERMON. . . .

At Winwick Church, on Suncitt—y--aft;;;;;,.the Rev. J. Carson preached for the last time as curate, to a large congregation, many of whom evinced much regret at losing cne who had been amongst them for over fifteen years. The text was taken from the second lesson, "On earth peace" sir. Carson acknowledgtd the friendly kindness of the parishioners toward him, expressing his gratitude to the Giver of all go)cl for the many blessings bestowed upon him and his during their sojourn in this place. Next he affectionately addressed all those young persons present whom he had baptized, urging to steadfastness in keeping their vows and constant prayers for the Divine grace 80 to do Those taught by him, and catechized were exhortkvi to continue the study of God's word; those still in the day or Sunday school should pay all attention to their teachers, of whose labours he had so long been an interested witness. Such as lie had !ire- pared for confirmatiol should beware of forgetting their Christian profession. The regular communi- cants of the Church were commended and earnestly advised to continue such ; whilst those of the con- gregation who neglected it were admonished to attend this Holy Sacrament, which too many of them had never once received at his bands. Neit those present whom he had joined together in holy matrimony were reminded of their solemn engage- ments, as set forth 80 plainly in the marriage ser- vice; they must remember they must hereafter give an account as to the discharge of their respective duties towards each other.

div.head: lONIE
div.p: lONIE
PRIDE OF THE MILL
THRILLING LOVE STORY. 3Y LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.
3FIAPTER XVII.
THE HOME-COMIN4 OP THE DISCARDED SON.

It so happened that business connected with the Iron mills took Arthur Rochester to New York for a day, which was quite contrary to his expectations; and the first person he met coming down the steps of the Stock Exchange was—his father!

John Rochester would have passed his handsome, noble son by in silence and without recognition, but Arthur suddenly stopped short. "Father, "he said, eagerly extending his hand, "have you not one kind thought left in your heart for me 7" Mr. Rochester's fine old face tuned a shade paler. He bowed stiffly as his eyes rested for one brief instant on the fair, debonair face and the happy expression on it. No one knew, save himself, how he had yearned for this son of his; but he was too proud to relent and recall him. And, although he received Arthur's overtures with coldness and lowering brow, that would have daunted any one less brave, at heart he was well pleased. "If yeu have anything to say to xoe you may come to the house," said Mr. Rochester, ungraciously, and only too pleased at the scant courtesy ex- tended.

Arthur took his place beside his father in his car- riage. 'How the old butler's face lighted up when he saw his genial young master! He hurried down , to the servants' han all in a flutter, exclaiming, thankfully: "The good Lora be; Praised! The old gentleman and Master Arthur ;IN§ ieconciled at last! He -3..aroeght nutig master home yvith him in his car- riage. They are in his study." Miss Rochester was almost crOCicome by the joyful intelligence, and Elaine Grangee,,Jhe heiress, old Mr. Rochester's ward, was, to use Vc- pression, " beside herself with delight."_. . ly for " 14116-fabg 7.tb4114"ti ffiaid. "PatriCe, ' ste said, excitedly, "I want you to bring my prettiest dress at once, and help me on with it quickly. Mr. Arthur Rochester is here." Patrice was becoming quite used to hearing her pretty young mistress bemoan Arthur's absence with every day that had passad. Aunt Hilda went down to the drawing-room at once, and she was most agreeably surprised to hear 1 the father and son talking upon the most amicable ef terms as she opened the door. Arthur had made a clean breast of it, telling his father all, arai how Rode was now not a poor working girl, hut Colonel Whitney's heiress; yes, heiress to the three millions of money which would be left her by the wealthy iron merchant of Pitts- burgh, who was her uncle, and whose only living , relative she was.

_ Arthur Rochester would have liked his proud old father rather better if be had not baid, eagerly: "As the case now stands. I am willing, of course, to withdraw my objections to the young lady. The heiress of Colonel Whitney of Pittsburgh, who is well and favourably known to me by reputa- tion, is quite a different personage from a girl who earned her bread in the mill." - - -

Arthur Rochester flushed to the roots of his !sir, curling hair. "My determination has never wavered, father," he said. "I would have won her had it lain in my power to do so when she was only a working girl. She refused me then—yes, that is the truth—she refused the millionaire's son, only to accept me when fate brought us together again, and I hadn't a dollar, but was making my own way in the world. She knew then that you had disinherited me, but she never knew why, God bless her." "I have repented of that, and have made a new will," said J.din R-tchester, huskily. "You are still my heir, Arthur, worth quite as much as the young lady herselt." "I am quite as much obliged, father, but I shall not accept it," said Arthur, decisively. "I have learned that I cad make my own way in the world, and life seems more acceptable to a man when he earns his own livelihood." The entrance of Aunt Hilda Rochester cut short any further conversation, and a few moments later Miss Ganger, the h-iress, joined them. All the old family sezvants gathered round the door, eager for one glimpse of "Master Arthur." It brought tears to John Rochester's eyes when he saw and realised how dearly his son was be- loved.

"I hope you hsve come to stay, Arthur," said Miss Granger, fluttering down into the velvet easy-chair opposite him, wondering the while if he did not hear' how her heart was throbbing, and if he notic+•.cl how the colour came and went in her cheeks.

_ Only for a day, Elaine," he said, smilingly. "I must return to Pittsburgh at once." He must hive been blind not to see how the colour faded from her far, and her lips trembled; but the fact is when a young man is in love with one wotnan he seldom observes the emotions of another.

"In that case it was cruel kindness to come near us at all," pouted the little heiress, striving to keep back her tears of vex4tion. "I have missed you so much, Arthur," she went on plaintively; "you know I always depended upon you as my cavalier on my rides and drives."

"I should have imagined you would have found many only too glad to fill my place at your side," he said, lightly. " Do you wish I had r she asked, quickly, and again he might have noticed the sudden whiteness of the girl's drooping face and the quick, spasmodic quiver of her lips. "Certainly," he responded, "you should have done so, Elaine. lam really surprised that you did Wt."

"He has not missed my society as I have missed his," thought the girl, bitterly, "or he could not say that." It had been a strict secret with Mr. Rochester and his sister as to why Arthur had left home se suddenly, and Elaine never thought of connecting pretty lonie Lawrence with the cause of it. It had been a dear wish of Mr. Rochester's that his lovely ward would one day be Arthur's wife, but he had long since abandoned all hope of it, having been brought to a full realisation of the old adage that:

"Love goes where it is sent." As the evening wore on Arthur pondered long and earnestly as to whether he should speak to the family of his betrothal to knie, and of their approaching nurriage, or whether he had beet leave that piece of news for his father to break to them.. He concluded upon the latter course.
"I shall have something important to write you very soon, Elaine," he said at parting, and those words dwelt for many a day in the girl's heart._
But the letter she looked for so long and so eagerly !evereame. . . . .

Arthur Rochester was all impatience to catch the western bound express the next morning. I It seemed to him the train fairly crept past the little villages, the green sloping hills and vales, yet he comforted himself by the thought that every step brought him nearer to his daitlng. "I ain one day late, but she will be all the more anxious to see me," he told himself, with a smile on his lips. How he planned on that long journey, just to fill In the time pleasantly, what their future would be like; how he should take lonie abroad, and how happy they should be, for the best part of all was, they were wedding for love alone. At the depot he took a coup 4 to drive him at once out to the villa, as be had written lonic he should do.

Would she be watching for his coming from one of the lace-draped windows ? Of course she would, and his handsome, bonny face glowed with expectancy as he neared the broad entrance gate. He scanned the windows eagerly, each one quickly in turn, but no lovely girlish face greeted him with answering smiles of welcome.

He ran up the stone steps, two steps at a time, ringing impatiently at the bell. • He was shown by the footman who answered the 81:111112101313 into the morning room, a petty little apartment which lonie favoured most. He looked eagerly around; no grateful form sprang from behind the velvet portiere to meet him with outstretched hands; no rosy, blushing face was tamed expectantly from the sunlit window; the room was quite empty. He touched the bell hurriedly. "Tell Miss lock I am here," he said to the servant who answered the summons.

A half hour passed, yet lonie did not make her appearance. She was trying to write him the letter In her boudoir which was to part them, but her hand trembled so she could not hold the pen. "Ire would demand to see her any how," she thougitt, "and see her he would, sooner or later.

It might as well be then as at any other time." With the desperation of utter despair, lonie brushed the tears from her eyes, and went slowly down to the morning room, with a prayer on her lips to Heaven for bravery. Arthur heard her footsteps, and he knew it wag ionie, for her approach was always heralded by the faint odour of heliotrope. Ile sprang from the sofa on which he had been seated, advancing to meet her with eager warmth and open arms, but she shrank from him with a pained, scared face.
"You , must not touch me, Arthur," she whis- pered, stding before him as white as a marble statue.

His asms fell motionless by his side, and an ex- clamation,of astonishment broke from his lips. Was hepad, or dreaming? Had he heard aright! " Arthur," she murmured, piteoutdy, raising those lovely dark, velvety eyes to his face, "I have that to tell you which must be told quickly; and you must. believe, too, that it is no jest; every word comes from the depth of my heart. It is this, Arthur—you and I must part. I give you back your betrothal ring—for your bride I can never be."
CHAPTER XVII/.
'1 HAVE I'AR.TgA FROM MY LOVER-I WISH THAT
X COULD DIE."

A thunderbolt from a clear sky could not have startled Arthur Rochester more than the words that fell from lonie's white lips. She sow the look a bewilderment on his face, and crept nearer to him, "It is quite true, Arthur," she said, bravely, "we must part." " lonie," cried Arthur Rochester, in the most Intense astonishment, "what on earth do you mean? You are trying to get up a sensation to frighten me, dear, and to test my love for you," and a merry laugh broke from his lips at his own cleverness in seeing through her little ruse at once.
"Hush, Arthur !" she cried. "It is quite true, oh, believe me."

He looked at her curiously. It wag no girlish jest, he was beginning to comprehend ; the sad, dark eyes, which had great circles under them, were t serious for that. Had she hewzi anything regarding him? No, it could not be that' ;:2.s life was as clear and open as the page of a book, ;:p "I think," said Arthur, " tkat ed ask Heaven for patience. You have promised to bio' '4,17 wife. and now you tell me some barrier has ansen— tween us to part us. You are cruel to me, lonie, Fate parted us once before; you Enlist noi take it Into your hands to try to make me miserable again." "Hush, Arthur I" cried the girl again. "I cannot /bear it."
" lonie," he asked, abruptly, "has the colonel espented giving you to me at the last moment ?"

"No," said lonie, faintly. "It is not that." "Then I will listen to nothing else," he declared, Impatiently. "I will not hear one word more. Nothing under heaven shall take you from me, I promise you, for I love you too well for that. Why, my darling, I cannot endure the thought, even, of life without you. You have agreed to be my wife, and trot for anything will I consent to release you —do, pray, plead, say what you will." She only looked at him sadly, tears falling like rain down her cheeks, answering that it could never be.

His anger overpowered him. "You have never loved me," he cried, "or you would say with me that nothing but death should ever part us. Remember, I am not asking you for the happiness of a few years—for the content of a few months. My whole life is at stake. If I lose you. I would be adrift for life. But you would not do that. You would not have encouraged and ac- cepted me if you had intended to throw me over." His voice died away in a whisper. He bent his fair, handsome bead and kissed the little white hands that were clutched so tightly together. "You must try to believe me, Arthur," she re- peated, piteously. "We must part; but all through your life you will know that you have my liking if not my love," she added, faintly. He dropped the little white hand and started back, as though she had struck him a heavy blow, and a laugh that was hardly human fell from his white lips. "Your liking 1" he repeated, with infinite scorn. "What word is that to give me? I ask for your love, and you ~peak of liking. Sun and moon, heat and cold, night and day are not more opposite than love and liking.. One is strong, the other weak. _

"lonic," he cried, "have you deceived me? Have you encouraged me with false hope, false smiles, false words you never meant ?" "You frighten me, Arthur," she cried, piteously. "You will be sorry in the time to come that you have spoken so angrily to mc," "I am sorry now," he answered with eager re- pentance. "Can you not see, lonie, that lam halt mad with wonder and dismay? But really, dear, you do not mean it. You cannot look at me and mean that we are to part." " I do mean it. Arthur," she said, with pitiful bravery. lie sprang forward and gazed into the pale, lovely face, his own darkening with bitter wrath. " Janie," he cried, "can you, whom I have be- lieved little removed from the angels, be that most detestable of all women—a coquette? Oh, surely," he went on, "you have not won my heart from me to hold it in the hollow of your hand, to cast it at your feet and walk over it? If you have done me such a cruel wrong as that you have killed me."

He stood looking at her, the great drops falling from his brow, the swollen veins standing out like whipcord on his forehead, his strong hands tremb- ling like leaves in the wind, his fair, handsome face convulsed by intense emotion. It was breaking her heart—thi'e terrible scene— but she could not tell why they must part. She clung to the nearest chair for support. How was he to know that she was offering up a wild prayer that she might die then and there at the feet of the man she loved

"I want an answer," he cried, "!have a right to demand it. Tell me the truth, lonic; I ask you a ptain qoastion. Great God that I should ask it and live I leave you purposely befooled me? Has It all been a farce, ar antual lie? "I have heard of won:HT ..zho have near] every gift that Heaven gave them to win a man's love, only to play with it, to amuse themselves with it, as long as suited their pleasure; then toss it aside. Did you think to do so with mine? Did you think I would submit tamely? It cannot be true!

"Oh, my beautiful love, my passionate anger bas led me away I See, lam kneeling at your feet, praying you to pardon me I I have been mad with fear." He was kneeling at her feet, his fair, handsome head nail buried in the soft, perfumed lace, cling- ing to her with kisses and tears. She was his idol, his darling, the one love of his noble life. "No man could live," he said, slowly, "with the knife of the guillotine touching his neck or the point of the pistol his heart. Save me or kill me, as you will. Tell me that you will keep your pledge —you will be my wife " She tried to answer him, but the words died on ker lips, making no sound save an inarticulate swam

"You have made yourself the sunshine of my life," he went on, eagerly. "You have won from me the strongest, deepest love that a man can give to woman. You have taken my whole heart from me. You have made yourself a necessary part of my existence. And now you would have me believe that I am nothing to you; that I am to live without you. And I tell you frankly I cannot. I cdn never give you up. "I cannot believe you have been duping and deceiving me for this one end and aim. It is too horrible to be true "I ask you once again, darling, take back the cruel words you have uttered. Look up into my face, and tell me you love me still; that our be- trothal shall be broken only by the stronger, more holy, more beautiful tie, the marriage bond, which will give you to me to love and to cherish until death parts us. What is your answer, dear I" She took off her betrothal ring slowly, and laid it into his hands. He would never know the happy tears that had been shed over it, the kisses that had been show- ered upon it, the bright, girlish day-dreams that clustered around it. It was better so. " There is an insurmountable barrier between us, Arthur," she repeated. "I can give you no other reason. My answer is, what it has been from the first—your path and mine He widely asundet through life. Try to realise it. " You are my betrothed bride, and now you tell me some mysterious reason prevents you from marrying me. You can have no such reason, Joule. Suoh an argument seems weak and foolish. It is all a pretence or subterfuge. I am speaking harshly to you, lonic. I cannot help it. I love you too well to think of losing you with calmness." A sudden idea came to him. He turned to her quickly. ..lonie," he cried., boarselyt_" answer me this:

Have you dismissed me to make way for anottier lover 1" She raised her beautiful face, white with the pallor of death upon it. It was best that he should part from her in anger. '1)1 am h to marry I—laonvoodthleorog ',' she said, gaspingly 0 Those were the words that slew the noblest heart that ever beat in a man's breast. Before he could reply a servant appeared at the door with a note for Mr. Rochester. He saw at a glance that it was in Colonel Whitney's well-known chirography. There were but a few words; the note ran as ' follows: "MR. ARTHUR ROCFIESTER—SIR : I have concluded to dispense with your services as superintendent of the mills at the close of the present week. Please con' eider this decision as final. Yours, etc., "COLONEL Wnrrscr." The note fairly struck him dumb with amaze- ment. He read it for the second time slowly aloud. "This cannot be true," he said, huskily. "I will go to the colonel at once and demand an expland: tion," he cried, hotly. "I have been too true and loyal to the colonel's interest to be dismissed with- out a word of warning in this way." "Stop!" cried lonie. "You must not go to bird-- I—l—asked him to write that letter to you."

- - _ "You I" he cried, recoiling with horror. "Yes," she answered, desperately, choking dovro a sob. and He turned from her without another word left her standing there, miserable enough to die. In hot bitter anger he strode away. The dist?: pointment was too great—to severe too bear. 07 took the little golden circlet she had Woo, aliv, which he still held clenched in his hand, and thre it far from him with a bitter laugh. ..r "Thus do I fling away her love," be cried. think lam brave of heart. It will blast my life, but it will not kill me. lam not the first u3:11:: whose live has been wrecked by a false, f woman," He would nover know that in that self-sargloei moment lonie lay in a deep swoon on the floor ~er the morning-reom, and that the bitter cry on " lips as she fell downward was: "I have sent away my lover I We are Part° forever 1 0, would that I could diet"

div.head: INTERESTS OF LABOUR
div.p: THE INTERESTS OF LABOUR

will acquire a primary importance amongst the subjects that receive consideration in Parliament and in the country. When we come to say how these things are to be dealt with, there is no doubt, there will he a diffe- rence of opinion ; there are these differences now. But we shall all of us agree that the life of a large proportion of the population, more especially that in our largest cities, but still the life of the working-classes,as a whole, is not what it ought to be, nor what I believe it will be. (Applause.) And the question that is pressing itself on the minds of so many people is how that con- dition can be altered. When we come to that there are, as I say at once, differences of *pinion ; there have been such already. It is a free country, gentlemen : we are entitled to our own opinions. (Hear, hear.) And if you would allow me to express mine, I should like to begin by saying how I think the interests of the wort"- ing classes are dot going to be served. I do not think the interests of the working classes will be served by socialism,

div.head: DITELOPSI3 SOCIALISM,
div.p: DITELOPSI3 SOCIALISM,

or the attempt to attaisi it. I won't attempt to define it. I don't know who can. No doubt we have a num- ber of laws and institutions of a so-called socialistic character, using the word in one sense. But that sense is so far opposed to the extreme form of Socialism which necessarily strikes at the root of individualismjhat the word becomes misleading. I am not able to see yet.— and I have read lately a good deal of socialis- tic literature—what it is the thorough-going Socialists propose to themselves. For instance, in an article written by a very able exponent ot the social democratic faith, it is said that it is not proposed to abolish private property, and yet in the very same article there is a sentenc,, which runs that the poor owe no duty to the rich, except that which an li..nest man owes to the thief who has robbed him. (Applause and laughter.) Well, ttuit is a very interesting point, gentlemen. Most points that touch our pockets so closely are, and I should like, therefore, just to take a very elementary and

div.p: A -VERT SIMPLE EXAMPLE.

to test that assertion. To begin at the beginning, sup- posing that a working man is in a position to save, and does save something,ny industry, and by exerrisiog very great thrift and self-denial, that by middle life that ina n has accumulated a certain amount of capital, a small amount, perhaps, but sufficient to enable him to enter into business on his own account. He becomes at once a small employer of labour. Is he an enemy to the men fur whom he finds employment ? Possibly he has a very hard struggle ; he may have an anxious time of it, and he may lose what little money he has saved, or he may succeed. He may, as many men have done, go on and accumulate more capital, and he may spend that in warehouses and in plant, and in generally developing his business, be- coming in a position to enaploy more labour. Possibly he lays out some of the money which he makes in that way, for the furtherance of other industries, and at any rate he now earns considerably more than he spends (if he is wise), and has become a rich man. When he is employing so much more labour, I want to know whether he is any more an enemy of the men for whom he finds emnloyment as a rich man than he was as a poor man. Then, supposing that the man is married and has a family, has not he an indisputable right to provide for his family by leaving them—l do not say all that he has made : that is quite another matter—hut beyond ques- tion the great bulk of it, and sufficient to enable them to carry on the work that he has been doing, and to maintain in a proper manner the position he has raised himself to. As I understand social democracy, the son who inherited that money would be dispossessed, even if the father were ever allowed to accumulate it. What are we to think of a doctrine like that ? Such men as I have instanced, who develop the resources, and the industries of their localities, have been during this century when England as a nation has made such enormous progress,

THE BACKBONE OF OUR COMMERCIAL SYSTEM, and, without them, I don't know where that great commercial position would have been. (Applause.) And, so gentlemen, I for one, must write myself down, what I daresay most of you write yourselves down, an individualist, in so far as one is opposed to a theory of the kind I have indicated. The ideal socialist says that instead of giving a man the incentive of accumulating wealth,honour would be found sufficient stimulus. Well, honour is a very good incentive,but you want something which is more potent and more vital than even honour to extract all you can get out of a man. The practical Socialist really admits this, when he says that men will be paid according to the positions which their abilities entitle them to hold ; and, as bearing on the point, I will just read you

div.head: WIIAT PROFESSOR HUXLEY SAYS
div.p: WIIAT PROFESSOR HUXLEY SAYS

on the incentive to getting on. lie says :—" Humanity is so constituted chat a vast number of us would never be impelled to those stretches of exertion which make us wiser and more capable men if it were not for the abso- lute necessity 4 putting on our faculties all the strain they will bear, for the purpose of getting on." The earliest historical records that we have show that man has always had a disposition to think of his own interest and those of his family first, and the interests of other people, if stall, second, and you cannot alter this. You cannot get rid of the inequalities of circumstances and capacity between man and man and nation and nation, and therefore I think that when social democracy would propose to do that, it is both a delusion and a snare. And I think, further, that those who advocate these extreme doctrines are really damaging the true interests of labour, just as some of us think that the interests of temperance have been and are prejudiced by some of the efforts that are made by out and out teetotallers. And so when labour questions come to the front,let us always try to get moderate men on our side, remembering John Bright's maxim, " Be moderate in your strength and strong in your moderation." (Applause.) I. do not think we shall. look in vain for that moderation. I think you had a most striking example only the other day, when Mr. Morley was returned for Newcastle, notwithstanding the tempting though questionable offors made and the advice given on tilt other side. I never felt prouder of being an Englishman than when, among the sunny mountains of the Pyrenees, I read in an English paper the account of that momentous and splendid contest, and in the French papers the remarkable majority by which "honest John" was returned; for even there they call him honest John. And so I do not fear any development whatever of communism, and I not only do not fear it, but I be- lieve the workmen would simply scout the notion, just in the same way as the ultra Socialist would shy at the logical conclusion of his theory if yet] came to him and said, `• Now, you have £5O a year ; divide it with the Elindoo, your brother man, whose income is £5. (Laughter.) One can be

div.head: AN INDIVIDUALIST,
div.p: AN INDIVIDUALIST,

gentlemen, -without being blind to its drawbacks. There would be drawbacks to whatever system we might live under, for life at the least can only be, as has been said of government, one long second best. The great drawback to the inevitable individualism of man, as we see all the world over, and especi- ally, perhaps, in the most highly civilized countries of the world, is the emarmous inequality in the con- ditions of life between the extrerxe rich and the extreme poor to which it leads. We ought not to be blind to these drawbacks ; all the more ought we to try to realise them, because it is possible to an almost limitless extent to reduce the unfair inequali- ties and the unfair want of opportunities which on the one band you have to deal with. You have free , education ; it is not entirely free, but the time will come when it will be entirely free. Why should you not follow that up by having, in all suit- , able localities and in all our large towns, free music ? (Hear, hear.) Why should you not have, in these congested centres of population, more free spaces, where people could get something like a breath of decent air ? (Applause.) Why should not there be more

OPPORTUNITIES FOR RATIONAL AMUSEMENT, and interest, and social intercourse. I dare say many of you have read the admirable proposal, made by Bishop Jayne, of Chester, the other day, with regard to the sale of intoxicating liquors. I have cut out a paragraph of his letter and will read it to you. •t He proposes that alcoholic beverages, though frankly recognised, should be deposed from their aggressive supremacy, and sup- plied under less attractive conditions. These conditions would, for example. be comfortable, spacious, well. ventilated accommodation, temperance drinks of every kind, brought well to the front, invested with prestige, and supplied in the most convenient, attractive,.and inexpensive way. The pecunialy interest of the managers, that is, in the form of bonus, ought to depend entirely on the sale of eatables and non-alcohelic beve- rages. Alcoholic liquors secured against adulteration, —(hear hear)—newspapers, indoor games, and, where practicable, outdoor games—(hear, hear)—and music provided." (Loud cries of " Hear, hear.") If all that could be done, I suppose that a change in that direction would be as great a step in advance as we could possibly make, and I should think that it is a change which must commend itself not only to artisans, but to those who have to sell liquor, and to live in squalid, badly- ventilated, unhealthy public-houses the whole of their lives. But great as that change would be, there are other things which will certainly in time have to fellow, I mentioned just now our

div.head: _ CONGESTED CENTRES OF POPUIATION.
div.p: _ CONGESTED CENTRES OF POPUIATION.

hy should not we try to relieve these centres? Why : should not peQple have more opportunity of living out- side someof these large towns, from which they could go to and from their work ? There would be a large num- ber of people who would not care to do so; there would be others who would very much care to do so. Then it

you say that the working. man cannot afford to FiI,TVI money on a railway journey night and morning to and from his work ; and if we say that he ought in tnne to sp-cial trams run for him night and mornin,, by which, if showing proof of regular employment, he should be aids to travel backward and forward at as nearly as may be a nominal charge—(hear, hear)—thatl suppose will he ca'led a socialistic proposal. Well, if that is to be called socialistic, all I can ',peat is that we have already got institutions which in that sense of the word are socialistic. Then, there are other matters in which your interests can be served, some of them without any demand for public expenditure; hut there are other things that cannot be done without public expense, and the question is where the money is to come from You cannot go on increasing the local rates. The more you do that the more you handicap your local trade, and that is, of course, dead against your interests, quite as mu,th as against, the large or the small capitalists' in- terests. But you can

TAX GROUND RENTS

(Applause.) You can deal with that most important matter of the unearned increment, which they have already tackled-20 years ago—in the States of America ; and you can advocate a system of fairly and thoroughly graduated taxation. (flear, hear.) It may be said that instead of providing for these things out of money so raised a much simpler plan would he to raise the rate of wages all round, and you may look to trades unions to do that. As for trades unions, whereas 25 years agn they were thought most terrible things, and denounced on dearly every hand, now, on the contrary. it is becoming the exception to find people who do not recognise the justice and the value of trades union;. (Loud applause.) In all the large industries of the country even if we do not all think them quite models of perfection. But still even trades unions cannot do impossibilities ; and in a great many trades, and a vast number of businesses in this country to-day

div.head: MARGIN OF PROFIT
div.p: THE MARGIN OF PROFIT

on the capital which is employed, is so small that it will admit of no advance whatever. Doubtedless some may do so, but there are a good many where, unfortunately, the reverse is the case, and where, if business is to go on, wages will probably have to be reduced. You see the condition of the main industry in Lancashire to-day. Iris in a most shocking state. Therefore, even if as time goes on there should be some advance in the aver- age wages paid for manual labour, still it seems to me that in the matters as to which I have just tenta- tively and suggestively made a few observations, we should begin by making the wages already earned go farther in the way of purchasing the necessities of life and the legitimate enjoyments which ought to be pos- sessed. (Hear, hear, and applause.) N I have spoken of the ways in which I think the money ought to be raised for such purposes. To consider how it may be best used is far beyond our province to-night. Mr. Morley reminded us the other day of the great Dutch- man's motto, Ago quo d ago—l do what lam doing ; an 4 perhaps you think I am rather forgetting that, because we know perfectly well, ther( are other questions that will take precedence of some of the things I have ven- tured to put before you. You have, for instance,

THE QUESTION OF THE CURRHNCY there is nothing at the present mo:nent which has affected trade nothing which has therefore, indirectly if not directly, affected wages more, than the condition of our currency. My Uncle George, I remember, when I asked him some questions about it once, told me that the man who tried to master the currency was only fit bra lunatic asylum. (Laughter.) I reflected at the time that he knew something about it himself, and eertainlY tis a question which cannot now be shelved. You see it has been pressed upon nearly every candidate in this part of the country who went to this Parliament ; and I was glad to see it received the attention of the Congress in Glasgow. Ido not know how this terrible fall in the price of silver, which is depressing Lanca- shire trade with India,China,aml the Straits Settlements, is to be checked. I do not know that it is possible or wise to attempt to fix a ratio between the two metals geld and silver at which all the most important Govern- ments would undertake to accept either metal brought in hulk. Such an arrangement, say the bimetalists, would have this result, that no one would consent to part with either metal below that ratio ; so that a per- manent stability would be obtained. Well, these are dangers, and I do not presume to expres any opinion. All I say is that the present state and prospect of silver currency is affecting Lancashire trade very serinusly.and that it will certainly have to be considered before very many months have gone over. Then you have the ques- tion of registration, which I think is of interest to all. Another question, which Dr. Houston laid much stress on, is the important question of the housing of the poor—(hear, hear)—which I see they are already tackl- ing in the London County Council. You have another question, that of

div.head: If INDIO ROYALTIES,
div.p: If INDIO ROYALTIES,

on which I read a most important ariicle in a number of the "Clarion," published in one of the early months of this year, giving a most trenchant exposition of the extent to which these excessive, iniquitous royalties can handicap trade, both against the interest of the manu- facturer and against the interest of labour. Yon have a great many other questions, but I am not going to try to Rive a review of the whole political situation; it would pass my wit to do so, and I know very well it would pass your patience too. I just want to make, before I sit down, some remarks on one or two things that concern us personally and more nearly. I believe it is your intention to hold at more regular intervala

SOCIAL EVENINGS at one of the rooms that my father has built at Bank Quay—(applaus()—and I am extremely glad to hear that. I hope that amongst the elements that will have a place in your gatherings music will not be entirely forgotten. (Applause.) Music is rath.r a hobby of my own, and lam bound to say that after a good day's work, I do not know of any more complete recreation, and rest, and amusement, than to listen for half-an-hour or an hour to some pleasant music. (Applause.) Tenny- son says of music:—

There is sweet music here that gentlier falls Than petals of blown roses on the grass, Or night dews on still waters between walls Of shadowy granite, in a gloomy pass; Music that gentlier on the spirit lies Than tired eyelids upon tired eyes. I find there is not a piano at your disposal at present. I am not a rich man, but, at any rate, I can run to that, and I shall be very glad when by a committee, drawn, I hope, from every quarter of our works—(loud applause) —just as I hope there will he men from every part of them, who will participate in the amusaments at your meetings—when ynu havesettled how they will he held and conslucted, should you then find that you want a piano, to supply one. (Renewed applause.) Gentlemen, Ido not expect impossibilities, that you are going to at once swallow Back or 13rahmm, or chamber music of that kind. (Laughter.) We do not want to improve humanity off the face of the earth, neither do we want as it were, force improvement. We want, like Bishop Jayne, to take human nature as it is, but to give it a bet- ter chance. We want the people to know more of the secret beauties of the glen,of the glory of the moor, of the spacious freedom of the upland and beyond every- thing else we hope to see them drink deeper at that greatest of all fountains of refined pleasure--nterature. Why not?
THP.SE THINOS Alin NOT IMPOSSIBLE ; on the contrary I think A was Sir John Lubbock who

said he shout I not he surprised if, in the generations t come, the liif readers of the people were to he found amongst the working classes. The working-class should read as much or more than any other class. It stands to reason that a 111111 who ha% been working with his hands all day should be more inclined to use his brains in the evening than the man who spends all his time at an office desk. And so, I say, let us all use the stuff of our lives to the best advaistag,e, and develop our faculties as far as we can; and do not let us he content with doing that only for ourselves, but let us extend as far as VIP can, opportunities to others, knowing, as you will know whenever you do so, that you are leaving less room for those pettifogging pettinesses and trivialities which have too large a place in all ranks of society, knowing to), that you are widen- ing the interests and the opportunities for happiness in life by so enriching the minds equally of those who are now dwelling amongst us, and of those others who have yet to make their sojourn in and fight their way , through this hard work•a-day world. (Loud applause.) Mr. CEOSFIELD subsequently gave in excellent style om the piano "Hinz des Vaches "; and "The bees' wed- ding," by Mendelssohn, which were much applauded. Mr. WILLRTT proposed the health of Mr. Crosfield, which was drunk with musical honours. Mr. CROSFIELD said he thanked them first of all for their hospitality, which he had thoroughly enjoyed, also for their toast, so heartily and kindly drunk, and once snore for their artistic testimonial. He dared say all of them knew that his brother was shortly going to enter upon the matrimonial career. (A Voice "That will be another 'jolly good fellow.' ") He had been fortunate enough to enter into an engagement with a young lady whom they had known for a long time, and whose per- sonal graces, he could asgure them were only exceeded by her grace of mind. (Applause.) They would have much better opportunity of drinking his health and her health later on. (Laughter.) Still he thought he should like to ask them to drink with him now both his brother's health and the health ot the young lady who was soon coming to reside amongst them. (Applause.) The invitation was heartily acceded to. Songs were afterwards given by Mr. .1. Allison and others, and a most enjoyabe evening was spent.

div.head: DOWN BY TIIE SEA.
div.p: DOWN BY TIIE SEA.
[WITHOITT TRIG BASSINETTB.] BY JOII4 PREM. (Continued.)

Here again in this lucious, bivalve—lucious, that 18,11 the past can be compared withithe present—in this estrea Liassiea we have another of nature's labels by whose presence we may tell the source, and, sometimes almost the locality of the contain- ing rock. In this place we may only expect to find them in the fallen blocks, which have come from the white has that caps the cliff, lying upon the black shales, which here form the Rhoetic series. Now, let us mark more particularly the bearing of this. If we stand with our face towards the South-Down channel—and look along the beach from our feet along the trend of the coast, we find that we are looking at the broken edges of the beds, these edges running, as I have said, from the cliff on our right down into the sea on our left. But from these terraced edges the beds slope away from us gradually until they dip under the ridge or broken edge of the succeeding and overlying bed. And this alteration of ridges and planes might be seen, as far as the eye would carry. Technically, the" dip" was about S.S.E. at a low angle, probably some 10 or 15 degrees. But, what I wish more particularly to impress upon the memory of the reader—the young reader especially—is, that if we walk trom where we have been making these observations, along the beach, southward, over this succession of ridges and slop- ing beds, we shall be passing from older to more recent beds. This will be very evident if we note the fact thet while here, at Lavernock Point the has is but a compantively thin capping to the Rhoetic beds ; further south they become the dom- inant formation beneath which the Rhoetics have entirely disappeared. Now, in this case the over- lying beds must be the younger, and 80, walking southward, we pass from the older to the younger formation. It is thus we find the shell oetroa Liossiea which before was only found in situ, on the top of Lavernock Cliff, here stands as the pavement like beds beneath our feet. To have fully grasped this fact will be for the young reader to have learned one of the fundamental principles of geology—viz. —each formation has, and is known by its charac- teristic fossils. For instance, where this old scallop Peden valoniensis is found, the Rketic oyster is always absent; and, vice versa, where the ostrea found in situ we need not look for the Pa/en. Of course there are other fossils characteristic of the two formations—as Ammonites Plansrbis—Maa'io!a minima and the to be mentioned Lima gigantea for the has ; while Avicula cantorta and the Rlicetic cockle are, with our old friend Paten, the distinc- tive medals of the Rhcetics. .

So now we can understand why, among the pebbles of this stone-strewn beach, we so often find fossils which are not to be found in the rocks under our feet. Here, for instance, is a pebble enclosing the large bivalve shell Lima gigantea. The sea has worn away the limestone in which the shell was embedded until the skive and structure of the fossil are distinctly visible. Now we may searth in vain for this shell in the beds we are treading on ; they come from the Lias, at the top of the cliff— being one of the characteristic fossils of that forma- tion. What to me was most interesting was the hone bed, or rather beds, for there are two—one in the black shales—which is the bone bed, and the other in the tea-green marls containing fish scales and lignite. A piece of the true bone bed is a marvel of minute,crowded,fossil fish remains. These are chiefly the teeth, scales, and bones of fish, mostly with high polish, and is synchromatic with the black shales in or on which they are found. For the proper understanding of the minute and highly interesting remains of an old—old world two things are absolutely needed—a good lens and a specialist to name and explain them. But with a lens, even without the aid of our learned expositor, we can admire the many beauties of form and struc- ture that meet our eye in the dense profusion of these fish remains. liere—in the middle distance of geological antiquity—we have beauty of form ere there was a human eye to see and appreciate it; forms of beauty and, doubtless, chromatic combina- tions which anteceded the appreciative eye of man by countless ages. In this may we not see evidence that man's idea of beauty of form is consonant with Nature's idea—so to speak—of the beauty of form resulting from the adaptability of a structure to its function? This, again, would seem to lead U 5 to the conclusion that our conception of the beautiful is an inherited quality—the result of our evolution

from beingA who had found that chiefly h'ititi fal or pleasing to them-vl%es4 which, 'mak:- weH adapted to its uses. Hence, neolithic mail found the rudely- chipped flint implement of his predece.sor of Paleo- lithic times to be both better for u4e, and more pleasing to his eye when smoothed and polished than when left in its Tattler state. So man—the lord of creation—who arrogates to, himself the sole conception of beauty, does but borrow it' from, the universal mother—Nature.

But to return to the Rhostics and our present business. Upon the surface ot the exposed ledges of lime stone we saw a series of impressed mark- ings like, at first glance, the tracks of some thick- toed tridayle. Their general sea-worn state, how- ever, prevented anything like a definite judgment being given as to what had caused them. My friend had noticed them before-time, but had never been able to get specimens definite enough to be of use. It was my good fortune to stumble upon a loose block, small enough to be portable--in which the longitudinal striae were very distinct.. This "find" we planted on a ledge of the cliff, from whence I next day transported it to the muQeum at Cardiff, where it now awaits, in calm indifference, the verdict of science on its case. . .

It was now time to wend homeward—that is Penarth-ward—to Cardiff. Over the footing of this pebble-strewn ',teach we struggled with eyes bent on the ground in search of any further treasures good fortune and ever bounteous nature might be willing to bestow. Beyond a few of our old acquaintances Lime and small Ammonites in the pebbles we bagged nothing of note. As we neared Penarth—or rather the esplanade— the features of the cliff altered very noticeably. The Liao capping gradually thinned out, its place as the topmost series of the cliff, being taken by the Black Shales, while the older and underlying Keuper marls rose correspondingly into greater prominence, their bright reds in high contrast to the overlying tea green marls forming the middle series. A band of white gypsum is very conspicu- ous, streaking the red Keupers and thickening as we near the esplanade. In one place it has been found thick enough to be worked profitably until it began to thin out, when the concern was floated as a limited company. Need I say that though the company was floated the capital was sunk. But see how beautifully this simple arrangement worked! For, if there is to be a loss sustained, the more there are to bear it the easier it is tG be borne—especially by the projector of the company. It says little for the sense of gratitude of our species under these circumstances that, when let in for so good a thing they should have raised such a bobbery. Some people don't know when they are well off! Now, as I, like an illustrious predecessor ot mine in the same line of business—a man of the name of Raleigh—some of you may have heard of him— who set himself the trifling task of writing a his- tory of the World—as I have set out with the de- termination to give you a description of the world, or at least a part of that part that lies between Penketh and Penarth,l should be much to blame and incur serious responsibility did I not attempt to give you some idea of Penarth esplanade. Besides, to it I owe a debt of gratitude for the relief its firm and comparatively level surface afforded after the rubble ot the beach. Here, on its long stone-faced sea-wall parade the fashionables of Penarth and neighbourhood take the air when the tide is in, and, when it is out survey the great extent of mud and shingle spread out for their delectation in all its vast expanse. Here, too, is the navy cut individual in blue with the ever present telescope, upon whose broad shoulders rests the responsibility of coast- guarding this esplanade and so preventing the catastrophe of its being carried by the board by the enemies of England, or, what is more probable, any- thingcontraband being landed thereon. Then there is the movable stage hauled in and out to suit the tide. But are not all these delights to be obtained by taking a Cook's ticket next year ? So, Excelsior ! Up the steep one in ten road we climbed until the Welcome 'bus was ready which whirled us into Car- diff—to hear again St. Mary's chimes. Soothed into peaceful meditation by their well-modulated tones, I readily gave way to the placid influences of the time. Very pleasant were the reveries they induced, as they called to living memory the fading recol- lections of the long long past. Au! the glamour of eld ! What a fascinating power it has over some natures. This feeling of reverence for what is old, merely is the dominating cause of one half of vests from the new to the older faiths. Some peo- ple like to take their religion as others do their port—with the cobwebs on—the fine old crusted sort, mellow with age. But if relative antiquity is to be the criterion of our faith, let us select one that in its hoar antiquity puts to shame all sects and denominations and dwarfs Christianity itself as a thing of yesterday. Let us go back upon the centuries—become Druids, follow the lead of our Celtic or British ancestors— and, beneath the spreading branches of an oak,per- form the sacred functions of the cult. But why draw the line at tlhe Druids ? Why not roll back the curtain of time until we have revealed the" old original" faith-sun-worship? For man seems to. have commenced this line of business by worship- ing the visible and partly known, and subsequently refined upon this by adoring the Unknown and _ _ .

There! the bells have ceased and I have come back to earth. The trance is over; and I think I will not be a Druid or yet a worshipper of the sun— though I dearly love the old fellow and am wishful for more of his acquaintance, especially at this time of the year. No ! I will be none of these ? Rather will I put trust in the moral, intellectual, and social evolution of my species. Let us learn to look forward with hope; for assuredly the man who is always looking backward, who has ever his face turned over his shoulder, will at last become so crippled as to be unable to look forward. And among all the dogmas let this be first and foremost —" Do unto others as ye would that others should do unto you." Instead of differing about non- essentials—whictl,being mere matters of opinionovill be ever in dispute, let us stick closer to this grand maxim, upon the practical importance and thoroughly workable nature of which we are all a,greed. So let us determine to trouble less about the airy unsubstantial nothings, the dreams of bigots,and more about the real interests of mankind. Let us in fact pay the full twenty shillings to the pouud—morally, socially, and pecuniarily. In this matter I am persuaded that we are very short of local preachers. I would have every man be. a local preacher of this doctrine, but precept must be

accompanied by exstnple—and every man must predict what he preacheB. But stop What would bechtne of the lawyers and the parsons, and even the doctors, if these things catne about? Every man his Own parson and practising what be preaches Why we should be healthier, wealthier, and wit,er ! Ah ! then we should require an emigration scheme to transport the members of these three professions to wore, or less, favoured climes.
(To be eontinued.)

The serious inroads that Dyspepsia has made amongst the community of late years are largely due, the doctors assert, to the indulgence in cheap and inferior teas, in which many harmful elements are contained. Why so many persons should con- tinue to be thus deluded is hard to understand, seeing that there is only the difference of a few pence per pound between the rubbish and the really good teas.

div.p: PRESCOT.

WESLEYAN HARVEST FESTIVAL—Harvest Festival Services were held in the above place of worship on the 22nd inst. and on Sunday morning, and evening. On Sunday afternoon a service of song wasgiven, entitled the " Children's Harvest Festival." Owing to the great number of people not able to get in on Sunday, the service of song was rendered again on Monday everting. FATAL COLLIERY ACCIbENT.—On Tuesday, a boy named Robert Roberts, aged 16 years, who resides at Whiston, met with a serious accident at the Wigan and Whison Colliery, where lie was employed as pony driver. The boy was seated on the front of the waggon when thepony kicked, hitting him in the face, breaking his jaw bone and knocking his teeth out. A furnace man came to his assistance, and Dr. Brindle being sent for, he ordered him to he sent to the Royal Infirmary, Liverpool, where he succuslbed to his injuries on Wed- nesday.

Wolter; BURNT lo DEATH —On Tuesday, an inquest was held, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the King's Arms Hote', on the body of Mary Londen, of Hulines Buildings, St. Helens-road, who it is supp ,sed, met her death by falling into the fire. From the evidence it appears, her husband (John Londen), had gone to bed about 10 p.m., taking the youngest child with him and leaving the wife preparing his food for the next day. He had fallen asleep, but, was awakened by the cries of the children, and found his wife's clothes in flames. She asked that someone might be sent for, and a neighbour soon came in. Dr. Barlow was sent for and was soon in attendance, and did all that could be done for her,. but the poor woman never recovered consciousness, and died on Monday afternoon. The deceased who has been subject to fits, is supinsed to to have been seized with one, and fallen into the fire. The verdict returned' was one of "Accidental Death."
"TUM 0' PEG'S FAREWEEL TO NYOWTON GOD BLESS 0'!"

Fareweel, owd Chums, a sad fareweel,— Aw've vanish'd fro yer view; Which on us, con yo tell me, lads, Will be i' th' bizgest stew? That aw shall miss sum on yo sore, Aw feel it in me n-aw ; An' tho' aw keep my sperrits up, Aw'm noan so fain, shuz heaw!

Fareweel, owd Nyovvton ! fare thee wed,— Thoose buzzes, an' that bell, That towls to wakken lung gone saints, An' frickens foak fro bell ! Fareweel, aw thoose Commissioners Wi' rai,iway-riddlet pates; Wo' botch up a three-corner't Hall An' welly tribble tit' rates ; Fareweel, owd Bashaw, lad, fareweel ! May theau earn lots o' quids, By lickin' aw theau meets at bows, An' breedin' Sammy Brids ! Fareweel, owd Skoller, may theau find Sum lovin' tender lass, To brush thi shoon, or, better still,

A widow wi' sum brass! Fareweel, owd George, ther's not a deaubt Aw'st miss noan moor then thee; For even wen theau grumble't, Theau woottsn't growl at me ! An' thee, my honest-hearted Ike, Befoor aw goo away, Aw'm fain to own I gie thee aw My sympathy to-day. Owd Birley Bill, thy quips an' cranks Aw never shall forgot; Fer grand lungworded drollery Ther's noan con touch thee yet! An thee, owd Roadie, duz ta think Theau'rt noan to hey one word? Perish the thowt I for aw shad then Desarve to be wee! pared! An' Cocker, aw shall miss thee too, That connot be denied; My Bing o' th' Kontridicterii, an' Eawr Kontinental Guide ! ! Wo travel'd mony a score o' times Alung a single line. Fro Joppo to Jeroosalum, Au' ne'er tuch'd Palestine!! Fareweel, owd Bob, my owdest chum, My pal r mony a spree; Wene'er my thowts revert to th' past, Aw'st allus peaunee on thee! To aw that live an' meet at th' "Bull," Aw'm like to say" Good bye"; An mony a time aw's think o' them, Wen far away, an' dry! Farewell to Cricket, Bcws, an' Golf, Th' owd Station Mester too; The very thowts o' leavin' him Brings wrinkles on my broo! But aw'll give o'er, aw'm feelin' quare, An' ditherin' i' my legs; So here's a warm Fareweel to aw— Yore sorrowin'
TUM 0' PEGS.
