RHYMES FOR THE PUOPLE.
NO. 5. THI; PUBLICIN,
I am.the man empowered by Law' To push the Liquor 1 racte ; And for my sign, behold wi h awe, A raving beast displayed !

In my Gin' Palace " here I' stand A licensee of Stete, To deal damna don o'er the land. Engulfing small arid great.. My drinks are poisons more or less By fiendish arts designed, To till the world with wretchedness, And ruin liminaukind.

My clients of all sizes are,. -And all degrees of men ; And here they come from near and far,, To wallow in my den. Like rats that brave the deadly snare To snatch a tempting meal ;- They gulp m' drinks, without a care Of what these drinks conceal. Then when their pockets well are drained, And they begin to fight, To turn thern•out I am constrained,. No matter what their plight. And when they get upon the street,. Policemen '''run them in," That Pilates on the judgment seat May fleece them for their sin. But though my gain comes through their lose,. My glory through their shame, No Pilate will my license cross, Or visit me with blame.

A safe and " roaring" trade I drive, Prompt cash its only rule ; And thus I vegetata and thrive, While elienta play the fool. My " finished products" are on view In paupers gaunt and grave; They crowd the prison dungeons too, And in asylums rave. Some fiq our alleys •dark and foul With every noisome thing ; While others through the country prowl, And some on gibbets awing. Nor in the land is there a home

Where drink has not defiled, And left its mark, for years to come, On husband, wife, or child. Accors'd of linen, accurs'd of God, Nly horrid trade I ply ; Nor reck that still at home, abroad, My slaves for vengeance cry. Mv God is Gold : for tnis I sell
Etch true and manly grace; For this I wage the war of hell Against the human race.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY STABBING AFFRAY
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY STABBING AFFRAY

AT WIDNES. On Saturday. at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, an elderly matt named Isaac Houghton, employed as a Waterman, was charged with wounding Walter Dyson, also a waterman, at present in charge of the flat Fanny, by stabbing him la the left side with a knife. Prosecutor stated that about 6.30 on Friday night he was near the locks on the canal bank. He saw the prisoner and asked him what flat had grounded in the Dee. The prisoner made no reply, so witness walked on. The prisoner followed and caught hold of him, when a scuffle ensued, and both fell to the ground. They were parted, and witness went on to his flat, when his mate discovered that he was bleeding. He took his shirt off, and found he had been stabbed. lie did not see a knife in prisoner's hand. Prisoner was the worse for drink, but witness was sober. —Frank Cookson, Oakland-st., said he was in a cabin on the canal bank on Friday evening, when he heard some- one quarrelling. On going out he saw the two men scuffling on the ground. Prisoner had a knife-similar to the one produced (which was a large double-bladed clasp knife) in his hand.—Dr. McCambridge said Dyson was brought to his surgery on Friday night, and on exam- ination he found a wound one inch and a half long over the seventh rib, penetrating to the bone. It was a bad cash, and must have bees caused by a heavy blow with a sharp instrument, which would have entered the lung but for the rib bone. He stitched the wound and it looked much better that morning, but the injured man was not vet out of danger, as erysipelas might set in. On the application of Superintendent Keighley the prisoner was remanded for a week.

An official communication was issued OR Tuesday, ;tating that the act of insubordination among the Ist Life Guards at Windsor had been exaggerated, but that it was caused, so far as could be judged, by the some- what injudicious conduct of one ot the officers.

WARRINGTON Made an excellent Science start last year with its Technical Au d Art. Institute, having some 600 pupils under instruction. There was a little delay in the beginning on the part of students, some of whom wished te see the classes in full swing before they joined, forgetting, apparently, that their holding back was calculated to defeat, to a bertain extent, the end they had in view. It is the same this year; some of the students are hanging back, and thus delaying their own and interfering with others' studies ; for it i 8 a matter of course to, say that the highest rate of progress can only be made • when a class moves as one body from beginning to end. It may be that there will be a falling off in numbers, now that the novelty of the institution has worn off; but we trust, that this will not be the case; for, with so many excellent elementary schools preparing the way, there Should be no lack of new students to take the place of the laggards who may fall out of the ranks. There can be no question of the value, of the Insti- tute in a town like Warrington, which is noted for the variety of its industries—a variety which affords the fullest scope for all the technical training that can be given the rising generation. Young men and young women who wish to make the most of their faculties with a view not only to " getting on in the world," bet to increasing their capacity for enjoy- ing all that is best in life, cannot do better than cling to the Institute as their sheet anchor. Parents who are conscious of their own defects— for there were no. such opportuunities of learning when they were young—should see to it that the advantages of joining these classes are laid before their children. Granted that youth is the season of enjoyment; it is the.season, too, of learning; and if it he neglected, it means that the after-crop, which might have been most valuable, will prove a very poor one. The State is doing its part in rendering pecuniary assistance ; and townsmen like Mr. Monks, the chairman, are giving a great deal of time and thought to the matter. It remains for the people to do their share, in their own interests, to make the Institute a powerful , instrum cut for good in the borough]. The School of Art, which has been an excellent training ground in Warrington for close on forty years, is now incorporated with the Technical Institute; and it is to be hoped that its growth and usefulness in the future will be even greater than in the past. Last year the number of students

in this school was 264. There ought to bemere this year; for the town is growing, and additienel advantages are offered. Previously, the fee for evening elementary classes was 2s. per naontb, which meant 18s. for the full session of nine months. The fee now is 10s. for the session, or ss. per term—a very considerable reduction. A simi- lar reduction has been made in the terms for the advanced classes. As a feature of moment to .students aiming to acquire some skill in drawing and painting as a part of general education, it may be pointed out that a Drawing Certificate will for the future be granted by the Science Pa Art Department to those who pass in—"l, kr"; tical Geometry (elementary stage). 2, FreelliteL drawing from the fiat. 3, Model drawing in °tit- line." Elementary teachers will find, too, that their needs have been specially considered, end it may be mentioned that there is a new class for "Decorative Needlework." Turning to the School of Science, we Pete:l class for Building Construction, with Mr. B. " Angel, gold medalist, as teacher. There will be two classes for Applied Mechanics, and two for Steam, all taught by Mr. B. DAVIE 3. Inorgmlie- Chemistry, Metallurgy, Shorthand, and Commer- cial Arithmetic, are being divided in a similar way, so that students who made considerable pro' gress last year will lose no time in gMail over old ground, whilst new-comers several new classes, including one find the way made easy for them, There sre, for Phri; graphy, another for Hygiene; and thirdzie English and Commercial Correspondence. ch class for Cookery has hardly as yet attracted eel ea a number of students as the importance ef subject merits. Good cooking. m ensures and comfort in the lions:31101d ; and that men that it will pay to dov"te time to it. ScheisrshiPly and prizes, it should be added, are offered iletm3_ Liwof by the Warrington Committee, but by the cashire County CoUncil, and the ,he Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes ; so that btr. co:ion:vs. lJniOfl capable and intelligent student has every /le co.ar_ agement to persevere in a task which wal grist to the mill, and make him a better citir`e and a better man.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

In view of the news which is to hand this week as to the legal proceedings against the American Coal Syndicates, Mr. Whitham's letter in our columns will be read with special interest. He has madoia study of the labour troubles in the 'United States; and places the issues in a remark- ably clear light.

The "Daily News" says a blind beggar has been discovered in Paris who is evidently a man of sterling business capacity. He exhibits a board with the inseriution: "Do not be ashamed to give me only one halfpenny. lam blind." That beggar knows his way about, and can "see his way" to Picking up coppers.

The Dean of Banger seems to have further dis- tinguished himself. It is reported, apparently Upon good authority, that he forbade the , Cathedral choristers to sing at the Rhyl Eistedd- fod. If this be so, it may be said to "bang Bangor" as a piece of petty spite. Happy thought: ' Can it be that the Dean is in favour of disestab- lishinent in Wales, and that he has a way of his own in helping on the movement?

Following on the death-blow to Coercion which Mr. Morley has administered as the new Chief gecretary for Ireland, there is an announcement of a Commission which will immediately inquire into the circumstances of the evicted tenants, with a view to early legislation. The Tories have been daring Mr. Morley to take action, and "honest John "in effect says : • I dare do all that may become a man; Who dares do more is none.

The Rev. C. S. Newham, Vicar of Prestolee, seems to have looked upon the wine when it was led; and had no small share of it, for at his examination in bankruptcy, on Monday, it was reported that he had expended kl2o in wines and , spirits, in four years. It was further stated that his liabilities amount to over 21,000, while his
only asset is his living ? Query : Ought not that living to be taken from him, seeing that lie has set had example by living beyond his living P

The Joint Cammittee of Lancashire and Cheshire mean business. Bury having turned a deaf ear to the entreaty to cease turning sewage into the Irwell and Itoach, the Town Clerk of that .town has been served with a summons at the instance of the Joint Committee. The case, if it Should be proceeded with, will become an impor- tant one. Bury would do well to take thought of the morrow, cease its funning, and give the fish a chance of visiting the Irwell—say, a hundred years hems.

The Tories,now that they have been driven from Power are desperately anxious to set Irishmen at, loggerheads, and raise a disturbance in Ireland. It is their idea of " patriotism" and" loyalty." But they might avoid making themselves glar- ingly ridiculous, by stating that which is stupidly untrue. Thus, a local Tory contemporary says : ',There is every probability that under Mr. . Gladstone. if he is in office, long enough, Ireland Nvlll revert to the terrible state she was in when Ur. Gladstone was last in office, and that the good . results attained under the late ' GovPrnment will be wasted for want of someone at, the head of Irish affairs who understands the Irish people and has the courage to do what he knows to be right."

The impudence of this statement will be in some degree realised by those who recollect, and who doesn't ? that when Mr. Gladstone was last in office, Ireland became so peaceful that the Tories, before they succeeded him, pledged themselves to the Parnellites to allow the Crimes Act to lapse ease they were returned to power. And they did allow the Act to lapse. It therefore comes to this that, if Ireland was not peaceful at that time, the Government were traitors to their Queen and 13ountry in taking srch a course; while, on the other band, if the country was peaceful, the credit is obviously due to Mr. Gladstone.

The Ameer of Afghanistan must he drawing the longbow when he proclaims that he has sent for two British brigades to assist him "to repel the Russians who are tyrannical Kaffirs." Lord Rose- will think twice before risking war with Rus- Pia by helping the Afghans. We have had trouble enough with that barbarous race—people who know nothing of "Perfection soap." The story goes that during our last campaign, a dirty Afghan 513 Y was caught, and orders were given to tub him lind make him clean. After a while, one of the two English soldiers who had the job in hand, Ported to his officer that they had been scrubbing for half an hour what they, thought • was the Afghan's skin, and had at last come to an old Shirt!

Bequests for public or benevolent purposes are conspicuous by their absence in the details of local Wills which have just been made public. The lack of interest in humanity on the part of many rich loeti is notable alike hi death us in life. A gradu- 4ted income tax dipping freely into largo incomes. Would to a certain extent check-mate this class of

fsen. The public would he all the letter for it; Ind their children in most cases would be pone the "me. It is not good for families to be brought kP in idleness...Besides,a life of luxury and laziness It fraud upon society. "If • any will not work, 'llBither shall he oat" ought to have the force of

There are of course lazy-bones amongst the poor 4ts well as the rich. They will beg, and they won't work, and yet some of them manage to fare sump- tuously every day; for there is a good deal of easy- going charity in the world which has always a ?_oPper to spare. The Poor-law Conference ,that uss hcen sitting at Chester is unanimous in urging - mischief of indiscriminate almsgiving. Work- Ibluuse authorities, seeing all this, are disposed to e hard upon tramps; and they can scarcely be too Luard upon the perennials. But what about the ,p„urtr(l-up who are honestly seeking emphyment P ,_'• ney should be treated tenderly. There ought to r 8 onao means of separating the good from the ad, 80 that the one may be encouraged and the tither discouraged.

t It is significant that the Conference passed a Leaolution, urging "Her Majesty's Government take such steps as may be necessary to check .heia influx of foreign emigrants, by establish- , such regulations at the ports of entry as may P,Z'vent the landing of such passengers as are 'elY to become chargeable to the ratepayers, rther through ill-health or want of means and Liends:' This is in harmony with resolutions ;•'ol3ted by the Trades Union Congress; and it ")oks as if the Government will be called upon to ftet. in the matter. It will be a new departure, ' it may prove to be a serious oue • for there 44 such a thing as retaliation. Still, self-preserve- -4121 6 the first law of nature.

The anniversary services were held on Sunday, when the Rev. S. H. Raveuscroft, of South Africa, preached two sermsms to large congregations. Mr. Ra.venscroft is a native of Runcorn, who has spent twelve years as a missionary, and his discourses were listened to with great interest. At each service the choir sang two an- thems in good style, solo parts being taken by Mrs. Temperley and Mr. Leithwood (Flalton). Mr. W. Tickle was the conductor, and Mr. LE Dutton the organist. The collections were in aid of the chapel funds. JOSF.PH PRITCHARD IS prepared to wind and keep in repair, private clocks from 10e. per annum.—Adrot. A WIDNES GROCER AND flis MARGARINE. . .

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday,itobert Hamil- ton, grocer, Dock-st., was summoned for exposing for sale margarine, which was not labelled a 8 such. Police Constable Thompson stated that on the 2nd inst. tut callei at defendant's shop and asked fora pound of butter. When he had been served the defendant's wife Said it was not butter bu; margarine. The defendant did not appear. The analyst certificate showed the article to be margarine, and contained 80 per cent,, of water and 8 per cent, of fat. A fine of 20s. and costs, in all £2 is. 6d., was imposed.

TRH DAVIES FUND AT RUNCORN.

A football match between Runcorn and Stockport for the benefit of the widow of T. Davies, the late popular three-quarter of Runcorn, took place on Tuesday after- noon at Stockport, before 2,000 spectators, in drenching rain. Stockport kicked off, and after even play, secured a try through a grand run by Saville, the kick at goal failing. Runcorn then pressed, and scored, the record at half-time being—Runcorn, one goal; Stockport one try. The game in the second half was very even, and it ended without further scoring, the result being : Runcorn. 1 goal ; Stockport, 1 try. Mr. Longshaw, the secretat y to the club, has received a cheque for £2O from the Cheshire County Football Committee. At Widnee Petty Sessions, on Thursday, seven boys, named Wm; Makin, Thomas Carroll, James Carroll, Thomas Hogan, James Devereaux, Daniel Murphy, and Partrick Sitinett, were charged with staling a cashbox containing £ll is. in money, and articles of the value of 9s. from the shop of Mrs. Bibby, Ann-street. It appears that on Sunday evening Mrs. Bibby left the shop locked up to go to church, and returned at half-past eight. Site then found the back door open, and the money anil articles missing. J. Carroll, Thomas Rogan. James Devereaux, Wm. Makin, and Patrick Sinnett were ordered to be birched, while the parents of the other boys were bound over to bring them up for judg- ment If called upon within three months.

On Wednesday evening a public demonstration to in- augurate the eleventh session, was held in Ellesmere-st. shoolroons. The Rev. J. Pu'ford Williams presided,and there was it large and appreciative audience. The chair- man expressed his pleasure at having that opportunity 'of showing his appreciation of Mr. Flolford, the teacher of the classes, and of rendering any help in carrying on the work of making musicpopular. Re expressed a firm cenviction that it the powers of song were more exten- sively cultivated and used by the fair sex that there would be less fear of their brothers, husbands, and fathers seoliing- pleasure and enjoyment in the public. houses. Mr. Skaife, of St. Helens, in addressing the meeting ,pointed out some of the advantages of the sol-fa method. He had known Mr. liolford for a long time, and hi‘d always found him to be most thorough and ear- nest both as a student and as a teacher. He pointed out that the fees were ridiculously low, and suggested that if they were doubled the people would think more both of the teacher and the lessons. During the evening, a choir, composed largely of last year's students, rendered several selections in good style, but achieved even more marked success in the tests of ear-training and sight- reading. The proceedings concluded by the singing of the National Anthem.

The first of a series of magic lantern entertainments for the winter months took place in this school, on Friday last week. Those children who had made 90 per cent, of attendances at school were permitted to be pre- sent free of charge, and there was an audience of about 400 bays and girls. The views were illustrative of a .tour from London to North Wales, and the youngsters evinced great interest in the " journey "as they were well acquainted with many of the places depicted. Afterwards a set oi slides of a humomous character, entitled'' The adventures of a flea," were put through the lantern, and created roars of laughter. The lantern was manipulated by Mr. Ednr Lea, and Mr. T. H. Annett, the headmaster, described the views' and at the conclusion of a most enjoyable evening, both these gentlemen were heartily thanked for their services.' 70111Frir PRITCMARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller. l, Nigh- at.. and 4, Bridge at.. imacern.—Advt. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE. _

The quarterly meeting of this society was held on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Heesom. A very interesting address was given by Mr. Daniel Bisbrown on "Temperance legislation." The speaker showed that the country was now ripe for legis- latim of an advanced kind, and • that the Govlartiment were pledged up to the hilt to give it in the immediate future. He referred to the recent declaration of Mr. John Morley, "that the volume of popular sentiment in favour of temperance legislation has had no para!l•l Anee that represented by the anti-slavery movement," Mr. Bisbrown proceeded to say that whatever the Government scheme might be he ventured to remark :that the three following alternatives should be pr4vided .for ;—(1) the inhabitants may either say, "No new licenses ;;' (2) a reduction of existing licenses; or (3) prohibition.—At the conclusion of the address there was a very interesting discussion, in which Messrs. E. Wynne Humphreys, Ed. Kay, S. M. Teniperley, and others joined. Von OF SANGER'S CIRCUS TO RUNCORN.

From an announcement in our advertising columns, it will be seen that Lord John Sangcr and Son's Roy at Circus, Hippodrome, and Menagerie, will ply a visit to Runcorn, on Friday next. The entertainment provided by this eminent firm of caterers for the pleasure of the public is known throughout the world. There is a suffi- cient variety to meet the tastes of all classes of society, there being a large collection of animals, m Inv of which go through wonderful performances ; and in addition a number of celebrated artistes submit programmes of n interesting and exciting character. Amongst the items of interest and performers are Messrs. Chivers }tad Verne, champion skaters of the universe; the Silvani troupe and lady bicyclists; Lieut. F. Taylor will have charge of the performing lions, and will put them through many daring feats. There will also be a vorl company of riders, clowns, acrobats, including rarro-san, the marvellous japanese artiste; and the Glineratta troop of trapezists. At one o'clock there will be a procession, which is well worth seeing. It may also be mentioned that this company had the honour recently of appearing before the Queen. It is a matter of course to say that each performasce will be witnessed by crowded audiences. FASIIIONAIILIt MARRIAGE' AT WIDNKS

On Monday afternoon at St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, the marriage of Miss Fannie Marie Agnes Leßert, only daughter of the Rev. N. B. Leßert, of Liverpool, and Mr. Thomas Edward Francis, on of Mr. Thotnas S. Francis, Sea View House, Castlebridge, Wexford, was solemnised, The sacred edifice was crowded. The bride who was given away by her father was attired in a gown of ivory bengaline silk, made with full train festooned with ribbon and lace. tier head was adorned with orange blossom, from which depended a fine Brus- sels net veil, fastened with a gold clasp the gift of the ' bridegroom. She carried a charming bouquet )f white lillies and maidenhair fern. The bridesmaids ware Miss Francis, sister of the bridegroom, and the Misses Ade- laide and May Horneck, cousins of the bride. They : wore dresses of cream crepon delaine, with vests, and trimmings of pale green, Marie Stuart caps, and em- broidered veils, and each cart.* a bouquet of beautifjl- white margueretes and maidenhair fern. Their throats were ornamented with gold shamrock brooches the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. J. Bidwell Leßert, brother of the bride, officiated as best man, and the Rev. 0. A. Leßert, M.A., Vicar of St. Ambrose, brother of the bride performed the marriage service. The service was full choral, Mr. E. M. Harrison, playing theorgan. Mr. and : Mrs. Francis left during the afternoon for Chester, en route to North Wales, where the honeymoon is to he spent. The presents were numerous and valuable.

NUISANCES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, William ; Statham, Trentham-street, was summoned for allowing ' a nuisance to exist, by his having the stench traps in , a defective state in connection with the piemises 24 and 52 inclusive in Portland-street, and 17 and 45 inclusive in Cawdor-street. The case was . proved by Mr. Percival, the nuisance inspector, and Dr. McDougall, medical officer. The traps, instead of being made of earthenware, simply consisted of bricks, the conse- quences being that the soil became saturated.—Dr. McDougall expressed the opinion that even earthenware pipes were not altogether perfect ; but they were superior to other arrangements. especially the one adopted by the defendant. An order was made that the nuisance be abated within 14 days, and defendant had to pay the costs, £1 14s. 6d. Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners. The following persons were summoned at the instance of Mr. Percival, nuisance inspector, for committing nuis- ances by overcrowing their houses, so as to be injurious to the health of the inmates :—John Charles Blower, Cholmondeley-plade, Runcorn,labourer ; John Flannigan, Back Mersey-street, labourer ; William Bonger, 2, Mill- street, labourer ; Phcebe Johnson, 4, Mill-street ; Christ, ophar Hagan, 2, Wilson's-row ' • Sarah Wright, 70, Lock- street ; and Peter Cr, n, 51. Nelson-street.—TNe cases showed t;:at the deferidalits raided in small cottages, as a rule containing two rooms, one upstairs and one downstairs. In some cases there were several persons in the house, more than could be allowed according to the air space. The defendants had been served with notices two months ago, but still the offences were going on.— In each case orders were made to reduce the Inmates to the qualified number, and the defendants had to pay the costs, with the exception of Mrs. Wright, who is in receipt of parish relief,

SHOCKING Cituntay TO PIGEONS. . Before Colonel W. W. Pilitington and Mr. J. C. Gamble, at the St. Helens County Police Court, on Tuesday, four Dialers named Samuel Ashley, John Litherland, James Litherland, and James Fnirlough Were charged with ill-treating pigeons by tying li witted fireworks to their Mlle.—Sergeant Smith said that, on Thursday afternoon, he saw the defendants at Windle Smithies with number of pigeons: Before throwing the pigeonsinto the air the defend- ante tied crackers to their tails and lighted these, with the result. that the cracker exploded three or .four times while the birds were in the air, each explosion jerking thein higher by two or three yards. After. each explosion a number of feathers fell.—Prisoners said they were doing it to make the pigeons fly better, as they were too slow.—Colonel W. W. Pilkington said it was very barbarous amuse- ment. —The two elder defendants were fined 10s. and costs, and as the other, two were youths they were discharged with a caution.

div.head: !SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: !SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WIDNES.

The Criunty Coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse, on Wed- nesday held an inquest at Widnes Accident Hospi- tal, respecting the death of Elizabeth Halliwell a single woman, 43 years of age who had resided at 51 Derby-road, Farnworth. The deceased lived with her sister, also a single woman, and together they earned their living by dressmaking. For some time past she had suffered from indigestion and a few weeks ago she went to Preston, her native town, and was treated there for this complaint by Dr. Moore. She returned home on Saturday the 24th September, and appeared in good health. On Mon- day night she retired to rest as usual, and on the following morning her sister heard a strange noise in the yard. on going there she found the deceased in the closet with her throat cut, a large carving knife lying besides her. Dr. O'Neil was siimmoned and that gentleman at once ordered her removal to the Accident Hospital, where she died on Tuesday at noon. A verdict of ". Suicide.whilat temporarily insane " Wee rlturtwd. STlOCifft4a BURNING PATILITir.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday afternoon, at the King's Arms, Prescot, touching the death of Alice Soden, twenty-nine years of age, wife of John Soden, of 1 Holmes-build- ings, limiest-en. The "evidence showed that on Sunday evening last Mr. Soden and the children retired to bed about ten o'clock,leaving the deceased downstit,rs preparing food for her husband to take with him on going to work the following taorn- ing. Nothing more was beard of her until midnight; when tbe eldest girl awakened her father, and he was shocked to see his wife standing undressed on the bedroom floor, her clothes lying on the floor outside burning. A neighbour named Stevens was called in, and Dr. ,Barlow was sent for, and found deceased was burned all over the body. The doc- tor attended her up to her death, which took place on Monday afternoon. The deceased was subject to epileptic fits, and she told her husband that she was winding up the clock, when she bad a fit and. fell in the fire.—The jury returned a verdibt of " Accidental death." UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. -4. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st..; Warriugton.-4v: TUE RIXTON Bin:UAL DIFFICULTY.

The question of tile provision of a cemetery for the township of Rixton with Giazebrook, which has I been the subject of prolonged correspondence and discussion, appears to have approached a solution, : as the Local Government Board have informed the clerk to the rural sanitary, authority (fr. S. Sutton) that they are prepared to sanction a loan of £1,660 for that purpose. They add, however, that they consider the Authority are not exempt from clause 25 of the Cemeterie4 Act of 1847, which requires theta to erect a mo toary chapel upon the consecrated portion of the ground. The parishioners have for some time been greatly inconvenienced through want of burial accommoda- tion. Difficulty was at first met in obtaining a site, and, after that, delay arose through the opposi- tion of a certain section of the inhabitants 'whose signatures were required as assentors,• and who for a long time refused to give their assent. This diffi- culty has, however, now been removed, and there is every probability that the work will soon be pro- ceeded with.

LIBERALISM AT EARLESTOWN. On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in the Old Primitive Methodist schoolroont Earlestown, for the purpose of further considering the advis- ability of forming an association of Liberals at Earlestown. Mr. W. Davies presided, and there was a fatr number present. The question has been under consideration for some weeks past, and a sub-com- mittee was formed to draw up and put into shape rules for the guidance of the members. The rules, as framed, were placed before the meeting and adopted. The objects of the ass-sciation are to pro- side for the Liberals of Earlestown apiece in which to meet for the purpose of discussing and furthering the principles of Liberalism. It is also intended to institute, during the winter months, debates on the leading political questions of the day. Newspapers and other literature, together with games, such as chess, draughts' dominoes, &c., will be provided. Mr. Peter Parr has been appointed secretary, and Mr. W. K. liaison, treasurer tro tem. A good num- Iser of members have already been enrolled, and the meeting was adjourned until next week, when a Committee will be appointed, ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

About two o'clock on Monday afternoon, a young man, named George Smethurst Orme, son of Mrs. Anne Orme, Lord-st., Runcorn, attempted to com- mit suicide. For some days he had been depressed in spirits, and, on Stuiday he complained of indis- position, which continued on Monday, and pre- vented him attending to his business at the office of Mr. Burton, solicitor, by whom he was employed at clerk, lie appeared greatly troubled in conse- quence. At the time stated his mother di-covered that he had left his bedroom, and, searching, found , him lying on the floor of a room occupied by a , young man staying in the house. He was bleeding from a wound in the neck. Dr. Mangan and Dr. Robinson were summoned, and attended to the wound which was very deep, the winapine being. severed. The untortunate man had used a razor belonging to the youth staying in the house, in his attempt to end his existence "Religious mania" has been stated as the, cause of the rash act. On inquiry yesterday it was ' stated that Orme was tniking satisfaetory .progress- towards recovery. Religious mania is supposed to be the cause of the rash act.

RUNCORN.• At the Runclrn Petty Sessions, on Monday,hefo^a Mr. James Handley and Mr. A. Thomas, Frederick Chell; Penketh-lane, hawker, was SUM inoned, at the instance of James Percival, nuisance inspector, for having on the 17th init. deposited in the public slaughter-house, prepared forsale and intended for the' food of Allan, a quantity of unsound meat, which by the order of a magistrate was destroyed. Mr. Lake, law clerk to the Runcorn Commissiooers, prosecuted, and Mr. Burton represented the defendant, who pleaded guilty.—Dr. McDougall said on examination he found that the beast had died from tuberculiiSi9 It was dan- gerous to the health of the people.—Mr. It•irton for the defence, argued that his client bought the cow about ix ago, when she was in good condition. flo inr.eivled t,.) keep her until Di . back end,but could not get a ley. De theiefore kept her in a coach-house near his premises. There was nothing to cause him to have suspicion that anything ..s wrong with her. On September 15711 the cow was killed in the pqblic slaughter-house, and was not cut up until next day. The moment he heard it was unfit for food it was destroyed. Defendant was not a butcher, and had acted as he had in total ignorance. During the time she gave milk it was used by the family, and defendant and his household,as well as a neighbour, I had some of the meat.—A fine of £5, including costs, I was imposed.

div.head: ST. cauitJa,
div.p: ST. cauitJa,
RUNCORN.
CONSECRATION BY BISIIOP JAYNE. DESCRIPTION OF TILE NEW CHANCEL.

The ceremony of consecrating the church of St. Michael and all Angels, at Runcorn, was performed on Thursday, by his Lordship the Bishop of Chester. The nave of the Church was built in 1885, and as since been used for divine wors'aipasbut the chancel has been added at a cost of £1,700. At some future time the tower ,and spire will be added, but in its present incomplete state the edifice is a noble pile nail is an'ornament to the town. The chatted is a very valuable and effective addition to the nave and aisles,and measures 41 feet by 21 feet from the step under the arch to the eastern wall of the apse. The ' floor is raised three feet above the level of the nave Adjoining the chancel on the north side ate vestries for the clergy and choir, divided by a moveable -partition, which, when removed, will throw the two rooms into ocie for meetings, and other purposes. Here are con- venient places for' surplices, and a. lavatory. The floors of the choir and sacrarium are of marble mosaic of ornamental patterns laid in cement, on a bed of con- crete. - The reading desk is placed on the south side of the chaueel, and the choir seats conaist of two rows of , benches on the north and south sides,with appropriately cut elbows and terminals. The walls are 24 feet high ,to the eaves. The roof is of pitch pine, framed in in- tersecting panels, following time octagonal lines from the oast end to the apex, and tiering gablets• over the heeds •of the windows with narrow - boerding the back. The chaneel is lighted by two elaborate and ornamental wrought iron gas standards, with numerous jets, snitably decorated in gold and colours, and two handsome wrought iron brackets, of corresponding pattern, and, decorated like time standard, are fixed in the piers of the chancel arch, to give further light. The whole of the wood work and fittings are of dressed pitchpine, varnished. A stone arch and jambs opening into the intended position of the tower, where the organ is hereafter to be placed, apron the south side of the chancel inside. • Externally the chancel is designed to group effectively with the. original butfing, as seen ! from the south east math.. et the intereection of the , roads, from which point the intended a over and spire will, when finished', pro,inne a very attractive feature, and complete the delign of ;he architect. For the stability of the portion now built, the soiral staircase to • the belfry of the tower has been carried up and left for ' future completion with the tower. The style of the 'chancel is of the " Decorat-d " period, as developed . about the year 1320. The work has been carried out from the designs, and under the superintendence of Mr. • Thomas D. Barry, architect, Liver)) sI. Natural light is • admitted te the chancel, by five poiotsd three liwht. windows, three of which are in the apse, filled with rail traeory of geometric patterns, in separate designs. Tile three windows in the apse ate tilled with tne finest stained glass, representing sacred subjects. The ceatro window has for its subject, " Our Lord's Ascension." " We understand, says the Octobar number of the "Parish Magazine," that It had long been the wish of thelete Mrs. Barclay to place such a window in memory of her husband, lately Vicar of Runcorn, in the new Church ot St. Michael ; a church in the erection of which he end his family had taken the great•est inte'rest, • end spared neither trouble nor expellee. It, was not, how- ever, permitted to her to wa uess the building of the chancel, but in her will she made ample provision for carrying her wish into effect, accordingly the east win- dow by Messrs. Clayton and Bell, of London, is now the principal ornement of the church. The subject, "The Ascension," was a favourite oue with Canon Barclay ; it has been, and it is one which also lends itself adinir- ' ably to the thought of Angelic Ministration, as suggested by the dedication of the church." The two stained glass windows to the right and left of the central window are from the manufactory of Messrs. Wailes and Strang, of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, and have been designed and executed in similar style to barnionise with each other in colouring and detail. In each win- dow the groups of figures are elevated from the sills be rich architectural bases of stained glass, and closed in above by rich canopied glass of similar design. The contractors for the building were Messrs. Hughes and Stirling, of Liverpool ; the masonic work has I been executed by Mr. McDermott; the elating and plas- tering by Mr. Rudd, and the plumbing and glazing by I Mr. Lea, all of Liverpool. The Mosaic floor o- the chancel was executed by Mr. Swift of the Temple. Liver- pool, the ornamental gas standards and brackets by , Messrs. Thomason and Co., of Manchester, and the heat- ing apparatus by Mr. Lea, of Runcorn. At the end of the chancel, occupying one bay of apse, is a very beautiful Reredos, refined and chaste in design and of excellent werkmanship. A base course of St. Ann's marble, and Ashlar of Caen stone carried to N height of the Super Altar, which is a slab of poliske,l Belgian rouge marble, support. a Caen stone super- structure of three gables, springing from shafts of clustered coloured marble columns. In the centre and largest gable is a panel containing a sculp- tured representation of the crucifixion. The arch mould 1 above this is richly cusped and carved and the beauty is further enhanced by tracery, Inlays of marble, and carv- ing. On either side are panels, having the vine and wheat carved In them. Between the junctions of the gables, and standing upon the capitals of the clustered column shafts, are statues of the four archangels-B.S. Michael, Raphael, Gabriel, and Ude!, with richly carved niche-like canopies above, finishing as gabled pinnacles. The altar rail, also, a beautiful piece of work, carried out in the same style as the reredos—extends across the channel, leaving an opening in the centre, and the two sides consist of a All(!.(:eS,ifin Of Cusped arches ef Caen stone supported by double columns of serpentine marble, and capped by a heavy Dore marble moulding in one piece. The inscription reads "Erected to the glory of God and in loving memory of John and Matilda Barclay by their daughter Edith. A.D. 1892." THE CONSECRATION SERVICE.

On "I hursday morning, at .lie time fixed fur Cone- ration service, rain descended in torrents, but neverthe- less a large congregation filled the church. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, presented a petition, praying his lordship to consecrate the church, and the petition hav- ing been read by Mr. R. Farmer, deputy registrar of the diocese of Chester. the Bishop attended by his chaplain, (the Rev. A. P. liolme), and the Rev. H. B. Blogg• bearer of the pastoral staff, walked along the centre aisle of the church, followed by the following clergy :

_ Revs. Canon Maitland Wood (Vicar of Runcorn), A. P. Holine, Canon Acheson, J. H. Wilcockson (Weston Point), G. D. Wray (Halton), E. P. Alex,inder (Alvanley); H. B. Blogg (Froisham), J. J. Bryant, W. T. Vale (Helsby), Jameson, J. Holden, G. H. King- ston, C. F. Montgomery, G. H. Seeley, G. W. Riley, and D. F. Ringway (Frodsharn.) On returning to the Chancel, the Bishop commanded the registrar to read the Seatence of . Consecration, which was done in solemn form. During this part of the ser- vice Messrs. J. E. Meredith and John Littler, Wardens %of the Parish Church, and Messrs. Thos. Speakman and W. Cropper, wardens of St. Michael's, stood reverently at the Communion rail. The service then proceeded. The Rev. Canon Wood read the prayer,Zr. Preston, the first lesson, and the Rev. A. P. /forme, the second lesson. The choirs of the. Parish Church • and St. Michael's Church were combined for the occasion, and both con- ductors, Mr. James Littler" and Mr. Goodwell were in i attendance, and the hymns and anthems were admirably rendered. Mr. C. Pownall was at the organ. The Bishop selected for his text, I Corinthians xi c.. 1.0 v. Because of the Angels." He remarked that St. Michaels' had been previously licensed but it had been raised to quite a higher level and status, by the cere- mony of consecrition, awl put on a saamger and more solid footing. It was not a new parish they had been forming. St: Michaels' would be a chapel of ease and, convenimice to the Old Mother 'Church—th'e Parish Church. His lordship then dwelt upon the le.ssons to be drawn from the text. _ TLIE LUNCHEON. .

After the service luncheon was served in the Scupen's Institute, by Messrs. Holland and 6;n, f Chester, and a large number of ladies alai gentlemen were present. The Vicar, the Rev. Canon IVood, presided, and he was supported by the bishop and most of tilb clergy who had been present at the service. The laymen present were Dr. McLennan, Messrs. Wis wall ,W. Hankinson, R. Abel, J. W. Lightburn, S. Taylor, W. Fisher, F. A. Lake, T. Speakman, E. Imison, W. Timmins, A. Salkeld, G. Moss, W. Sutton, I. Speakman, W. H. Rogerson, A. Buck, W. E. Lea, J. Poole, E. Gregory, J. Yates, James Liptler, John Littler, P. Davies, W. Mellor, J. E. M-exedith, W. Cropper. W. Whittaker, A. Linaker, T. Clegg, A.Jordan, and W. Shaw.

The Chairman submitted the toast of the health other Most Gracious Majesty the Queen, which was duly honoured.—Mr. B. Imison proposed "The bishop and clergy of the diocese," and in doing so referred to the i deep interest his lordship took n social matters. They saw that he was taking no small part in matters affecting the Working classes. His Lordship endeavoured to bring about a better state of feeling between the Salt Union and their workpeople, and showed that however their interests might be opposed, there was a proper way of conducting the matter. They knew that an early settlement was brought about, and therefore they found that the Bishop was useful outside the church as well as in it. Then they were aware that his Lordship had undertaken to prepare a Bill to deal with the liquor traffic. (Applause.) Everytate felt that the undue use of strong drink was an evil, and they must be thankful for any effort made by clsric or layman to .reduce the evils from which the country suffered. They hoped his Lordship'sservices in that direction might be auecessiul. Mr. Judson pointed out several Modes in which the clergy could increase their influence, cud in conclusion welcomed the Bishop amongst them, fcir he always brought with him happiness and cheerfulness. (Ap- plause.) The Bishop in responding expressed the pleasure it gave him to acknowledge the toast which kad been so wisely and weightily proposed by Mr. unison. When he came ' to Runcorn he always found the church people cheerful, happy, and hopeful ; thav were endowed with sincer- ity, as shown by the large congregation that morning, although it was so wet. There were peculiar difficul- tics facing church work in Runcorn, but he was sure these looked worse to those at a distance than to these at home. He hoped the proceedings that day would ' put a new heart in them, and inspire them to continue their efforts. He was cheered by the knowledge that some of the vrorkingtnen of Runcorn, at considerable cost to themselves, were present at the Consecration Service. He was thankful to them for their sell- sacrifice. Mr. Imison had referred to the strike in connec- tion with the salt trade in Cheshire. He would be a downright impostor if he allowed it to be supposed for a Moment that the work of Settlement was done by him alone. He only did a particular pottion, the way for which had been prepared by the co-operation and wisdom and tact and skill of others. .Ileference had been made to the idea—it was more than an idea, it was taking legislative form—about temperance reform, which was now before the country, and which he lamed was winning ground distinctly. It had received favourable treatment f ruin many quarters, and from one et the most eminent Non-conformist ministers in Liverpool, the Rev. Charles Garrett. Mr. Garrett, in the course of his remarks, said he would Ilk, the Duke of Westminster and the Bishop of Chester and others to get hold of all the puelie-houses in a certain district and work them ; he was quite satisfied if they failed they would acknowledge it was a failure. If they coold only get legislative facilities, and he was spared and Others were spared, there was not the, remotest possible danger of the thing not being practically worked in ellester and in Cheshire. They meant to be thorough- going, and to the last gasp he would see that it was carried out, and he spoke with full knowledge of what there was much stronger behind himself. (Applause.) Canon Acheson proposed!' Prosperity to St. Michael's Church," and in the course of his remarks said the pres- loerity of the clitireli meant tbe.4appinesi and ol all who lived in the parish. Mr. T. Speakman replied. He expressed the pleasure be derived by Ids connection with St. Michael's, and said no one was more delighted than lie to have the Bishop amongst them to consecrate the church. The Chairman proposed "The town and trade of Run- corn," and in hurnourous style referred to the antiquity of the town.

Mr. Wiswall, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, responded. He referred to the iinportant influence the Iliidgewater Canal had had in developing the trade of the town, and during the past twelve years that water, way had been so improved that traffic could be con- ducted along it at an advantage of 20 per cent, to traders. They could only hope and tract that by the completion of that vast undertaking, the Ship Canal, that Runcorn would become a more important place on the banks of the great waterway ; there was no doubt that the town and trade of Runcorn, would flourish in the future. (Applause.) _ .

- , Mr. G, Moss then gave' the Building Corrimittee," coupled with the name of Mr. W. Whittaker, who nar- rated the history of the movement for Ailding the church, upon which £6,060 had now been spent. The toast of the Ladies was given by the Rev. H. B. Blogg and responded to by the Rev. G. H. Seeley. The Bishop gave the " Chairman of the Dinner Committee," to which Canon Wood replied and Mr. W. Whittaker proposed the" Architects, Messrs. Barry and Son." In the evening a•service was held at St. Micuaels, and the Rev. J. F. Reeee, rector of Llanfwrog, preached to a large congre,gation.

div.head: ATTEMPTKD MURDER OF A
div.p: ATTEMPTKD MURDER OF A
BABE AT WIDNES.

A most shocking and pitiful case was heard by Mt:. P. U. Goosage, at the Widnes Pollee Court, yesterday. Sarah Ann Harrison, a single woman, 21 years of age, of Back Church Street, F'arnworth, wag charged with attempting to murder her newty born male child on the 11th September. The prisoner, who was in a very weak candition,was aeommodated with a seat. She was not defended. It appeared that on the day named, the mother of the prisoner, Mary Ann Ilarri son, heard a noise upstairs, and In the back bedroom she found her daughter, who said "Oh mother, let me die." In answer to an inquiry she said she had done nothing, but on going into the front bedroom the mother found a newly born baby covered with soot on the floor. There was a piece of string tied round its neck, and with the help of Mrs. Whitfield, a midwife who had came in, this was cut with a pair of scissors. Dr. O'Neil was sent for and quickly arrived. The child was brought to him and he observed a strong smell of soot. The hair on the child's head was strongly impregnated with soot, ,but its body had been washed. Ile found a slight impression on the neck, as a cord had been tied round it, and there were six little jagged cuts on both shoulders, caused no doubt by prisoner against stonework. The doctor considsred it likely that these marks had been caused by putting the child up the chimney of the room. The prisoner spoke incoherently, and said—" I wish it was , dead." Next day the mother aske prisoner " why she had done • "and she replied " I dont, know what I have done." The prisoner said she had concealed f rum her because she thoughts he would have !either had she known. The prisoner told Mrs. Whitfield she had dine it to keep it from her mother, and when asked if she attempt.' to put it up the chimney she laughed and said "Its either God's work or will, I don't know which." The prisoner had been keeping company with a s oung man but the mother had not seen him. The child is. new doing well. When formally charged, the prisoner said—" I have stothing to say," and she was committed to the Assizes for trial. She would be allowed out on bail, herself in £SC.I, and two sureties oi £25 each.
TRIENNIAL -ELECTION FOlt RUNCORN GUARDIANS. - •

The poll of the ratepayers of the Rnneern Union with respect to tile election of Guardians has resulted in a Large majority in favour of triennial elections instead ef annual, as at present. The numbers are for triennia! elections 3.375; for annual elections, 1030 ; majority in favour of the change, 2,345. Only atriut one4l the ratepayers have voted. Every township was favour- able to tile new scheme with the exception of Aston Grange, Dutton, Kingsley, and Newton-by-Daresbury. The new system will not come into force until the next election in the spring. Mr. Ashton conducted the poll.
It is announced that in consequence of the attick of rheumatic fever from which M. Paderewski, the great pianist, is suffering, all his engagements are cancelled for the present.

TRINITY WRSLILTAN CMAPEL.—These annual harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, on Sunday, when the Rev. Thomas Wilkes, of Runcorn, preached morning and evening to good congregations. The harvest hymns and the anthems " Fear not, 0 Land" (Berridge) and " What arm these r (Stainer) were very well rendered by the choir, Mr. T. Sant conducting, and Mr. W. H. Pickering presiding at the organ. The interior of the chapel was tastefully adorned with choice fruits and flowers. FARM FIRE AT ELELSBY. About ten o'clock on Sunday morning a fire was dia- -1 coved in the buildings of ' Mr. Thomas Littler, Junction Farm, Woodside, Helsby. A messenger was despatched on horseback to Runcorn, which was reached at 12.30. The bell was rung, and soon the fire brigade. with the engine, in charge of Deputy-Superintendent William Wright, were proceeding to the place They arrived on the scene about two O'clock, and then found that the cart house and bay, with the contents, a quan- tity of oats, were on fire. They discovered a good water supply at a distance of 200 yards, and were soon playing on the burning material. The flames, however, had got a firm hold, and it VMS found impossible to save any- thing, the remainder of the stacksunburned being totally injured by water. The roof of the building had collapsed before the fire brigade reached the. scene. The damage, which is covered by insurance, is estimated at £4.03. REVISION OF Vorsas.—The revision of voters' lists in the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire commenced on Wed- nesday, when Mr. E. Burke Wood, revising barrister, held courts at Dunliam-on-the-Hill and Frodsham. The Liberals were represented by Mr. W. Handley (North- wich), assisted by Mr. B. Kniveton, and the Conserva- tives by Mr. R. L. Owen (Chester) and Mr. They. At the Frodsham court, which was held at the Bear's Paw Inn, the name of James Kay appeared twice on the over- seers' list of ownership claims in respect of the Albert Inn, Church-st., Prodsharn, and adjoining property.— The Revising Barrister, on looking through the list, found that they were two different persons, one being of *Corporation-et., Manchester, and the other ef Timperley. —Mr. Owen said they were two distinct persons, but both were entitled to votes RS joint owners of the pro- perty.—The Assistant Overseer stated that when he received the claims he thought both names belonged to one person, and believing one was a duplicate, lie had only published one.—Mr. Handley considered that as the name of James Kay of Timperley was not published his vote could not be allowed.—The Revising Barrister said he should not allow a man to lose his rights through the negligence of an overseer. He had no alternative other than to put the name on the register, and let it be ob- jected to next year if necessary.

THE PRICE OF ORNAMENTS.—John Pemberton claimed from William Dowsey the sum of £1 125., for goods supplied and money lent.—Plaintiff said his wife received the order for the goods, and also lent the money.—Plaintiff's,wife said she kept a shop, and sold glass ware. She supplied the goods to the defendant's wife in November, 1888, and had sent in several bills. The goods included glass shades and other ornaments, and amounted to 17s. 101. The money lent to the defendant amounted to 153. After hearing evidence. , his Honour gave a verdict for . the plaintiff for the 15s. money lent, and costs. A MOLE CATCHER'S CLAIM.—ThORMLS Gascard, mole catcher, sued James Fairdough, farmer, for £2 10s., under an agreement.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. E. White for the defendant.— Mr. Davies stated that in 1880 the defendant was a farmer living at Burtonvrood, and he agreed with a number of other farmers to pay the plaintiff so much per acre for mole catching. The defendant had paid aver since 1880 up to last year, and no complaints were made by him as to defendant's work being done improperly. Defendant, however, told the plaintiff that there were no more moles on his farm. He had, how- ever, agreed to pay the plaintiff until 1894, and, he alo on with other farmers, numbering 40, signed a meme- rand'uni to that effect.—Mr. White produced a copy of the agreement, and it was pointed out that the docu- ment was not stamped.—Mr. Davies said he hardly ! thought it required a stamp. The defendant had I allowed him to do the work for eleven fears, and he had paid every year.—The Judge held that the document must have a proper stamp on it, and he nonsuited the plaintiff, withoutdeosts. CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.—AN ABRUPT CONCLUSION.—ICI this case, in which a jury was empanelled. George War- burton. cf fleatley, near Lymin, claimed damages fram Thomas Brooks, a cattle dealer, for injuries done to beds of willows, at Statham, near Lymm. Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Fletcher, ef North- wich, for the defendant. It was stated that the plaintiff, who is I. skip and hamper maker, rented some beds of osiers or willows at Statham. These willow beds adjoin land which is rested by Brooks and used by him for grazing horses and cattle upon. There being no proper fencing between the two lots,it was alleged that Brooks's cattle had been allowed to stray into the willow beds and destroy them very seriously. Brooks had declined to make any c:mipensation, hence the present action. Judging from what was disclosed the defence appeared to be that the plaintiff bad agreed _rm. sica...the fencing, -when he took thFland from the Ship Canal Company, the defendant having previously been the tenant of it. After toe plaintiff had been called, however, and had given some evidence in a confused manner, the two parties came to terms and the Case was withdrawn.

My nerves are quite shattered, my appetite's gone. I'm afraid I'm jut wasting away. let though double my years, your strength still appears, As though It would never decay. I am lonely and sad when I'm left by myself, Though wills friends I can never be gay ; -But you are quite lively and joyous and frea, Please tell me the reason, I pray. I can't get a psrtner to share my sad life— The ladies all answer me" •I'm always depressed when they're at their best,

Oh, tell melhe reason, I pray: I've swallowed vile nostrums and pills beyond conab, My vitals seem eaten away, But still I am mckly, while you are quite blythe. NON-PAYMENT OF ARREARS.—SaMIIii Brandwood was brought up to show cause why he should not be com- mitted to prison for non-payment of arrears, amounting to £3 us. Bd. due under a separation order with regard to his wife.—Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted and stated that in 1884 the prisoner was convicted of an aggravated assault upon his wife, and was committed to prison for six months with hard labour. There had been three children of the marriage. The defendant's wife was a most industrious woman, and had been employed at a factory, but she was no longer able to work owing to an affliction of her eyes, which necessitated frequent visits to the Eye Hospital at Manchester. An order was made upon the defendant to contribute a certain sum per week to the support of his wife. The money was at first received by the police, but owing to the irregularity with which it was afterwards paid, the police declined to continue acting as agents, and the defendant was instructed to pay the amounts into the office of Mr. Percy Davies. Mr. Davies added that the defendant had not paid a farthing since August sth, and that the defendant had been frequently brought before the magistrates with regard to the case.—The defendant was committed for a month. _ .
DRUNIZENNESS.—John Thomas and Martin O'Brien were fined.

THEFT BY A Sou:neg.—Patrick O'Connell, a soldier 46xtered at the Barracks, was charged with stealing from the stores at Orford Barracks a soldier's cap and badge. The prisoner admitted the offence, which was clearly proved by Sergeant Walsh, and the Bench sentenced the prisoner to 14 days' hard labour. As the prisonet was leaving the court he turned round, and, assuming a menacing attitude, said to Sergeant Walsh, " I will brain you when I come out."—The Bench hear- ing the exclamation, ordered the prisoner to be replaced in the dock, when Mr. Garnett said," You will have to go for a month now, and in future reserve your remarks to yourself ."—The prisoner was then removed.

Leathwood, in Winwick-road, the previous morning, was fined 103. and costs.—Turner for being drunk and disorderly in Bold- street, on Tuesday night, he having broken a window at 41, Sankey-street, was fined ss. and costs.—James Leary, drunk and disorderly in Peter-street, on Tuesday, ss. including Costs. OENTREPBEIOUS AT BANN QUAY STATION. Richard Coffey, bB, Tanner's-lane, was charged with traspassing on Bank Quay Station, also with assaulting there Railway-Detective Osborne and Ticket-Collector Bennett, the previous day. He was hanging about the station, and was twice requested to go by the complainants, and kicked Osborne on the grain and also kicked the collector. —He was fined ss. including costs. Margaret Francis, married woman, charged with unseemly conduct in Springfield- st., the previous night, was dismissed on promising to return to near Shrewsbury, from whence she came. WIFE DEISERTION.—Thornas Sheldon, hawker, 27, Heath Side, was brought up on remand from the previous day, charged with non-contribution to the maintenance of his wife and family. He had been £8 in arrears, and had now paid .£2, therefore the case was withdrawn.— James Appleton, 71, Haddon-street, Manchester; was charged with deserting his wife Elizabeth Appleton, 7, Baxter-street. Mr. Browne, appeared for the complain- ant, and said she had found him lodging with a woman in Manchester, having represented to her that he was a single man, and that his wife had been dead 6 months. The complainant corroborated this statement. She said he deserted her in March, saying he was going to meet a man on the railway platform, and never coming back. He took 14s. Bi. out of her son's box with him. In reply to the defendant, she denied having persecuted him and placed him in a lunatic asylum, and she did not admit she ordered him from the house or told him she hated the sight of him ever since the day of her marriatre.—ln reply to Mr. Browne she stated that Dr. Gornall had pronounced him perfectly safe.—The defend- ant said his wife sent him to prison on a charge of assault which he declared to his Maker he never did. He then made an accusation against her, which Mr. Browne , declared to be untrue. :4110 had given him a black eye. She told him all she wanted was for him to go away and did not want a halfpenny from him. She told him in Whit week that she would insure his life because she knew he would not last lon.—The case was adjourned a _month on account of the defendant's delicate health.

DEESE AND DISORDERLT.—Martin Connolly, drunk and disorderly in Butterrnarket-st., on Thursday night. P.C. Turner appeared against him. The prisoner con- ducted himself in court in a most violent and boisterous fashion, and said that a constable in the office hit him with a stick, and told the Bench that he would hit him unawares.—The Chief Constable told him to speak 0 the Bench,—The prisoner: Bench or no Bench they can do no more than they can.—The Chief Constable asked that the prisoner he remanded for a hours.—The prisoner, in a loud excited voice: You can remand me fifty times if you like; it will be just the same. lam not going to be knocked about. I will knock his brains out when I have a chance., Ths prisoner here referred to P.C. Turner, the constable who appeared against him.—He was remanded for N hours, shouting wildly. They were crossing the line in front of tie express. The defendants were fined the costs, 3a. 6d. each.

Complainant stated that she had occasion to sue the defendant in the County Court for a debt. Afterwards Southern came to her shop. charged her with being no woman,, and challenged her to come outside. Later defendant returned with• a female lodger, and abused her, striking her on the bead and shoulders.—Defendant said the commencement of the bother was that complainant made a serious accusa- tion against her. A Tneorrox ENGINE ()Am—Samuel Rumbie, employed by Messrs. Edward Box and Co., was charged with running, on September 10th, a traction engine in the Northwich-road, Appleton' at an hour, namely 7 30p.m., later than that prescribed by Act of Parliament. 10s. and costs.

CYCLING ON Tux FOOTPATH. —John Chadwick and Harry Buckley, for riding on a bicycle on the footpath on the 23rd of August, at Sevenoaks. Butler remarked that his clothes were wet,and he wanted to go home ;. he did not want to stop there,and was enjoined that he must behave himself respectfully in a court of law.—Chad- wick said he rode on the footpath to avoid the rough stones.—Mr. Long said an excuse like that was disgust- ing. These men must be taught that they had no right off the road any more than a horseman. ss. and costs. —William Bailey. of Northwich, for a like offence on September Ist, at Appleton, who had nearly knocked over the postman, as he complained, ss. including costs.

CRUELTY TO A DOMSFI.—James Simpson was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with cruelly torturing a horse at Grappenhall on the 12th September, by work- ing it while in an unfit state, and Sarah Lomas was charged with causing it to be so worked.—Mr. Dowty proved the case, and said the horse was in a very weak state. The animal had been destroyed, therefore he did not wish to press the case, and only asked for costs.— Lomas was fined the costs, and Simpson cras dismissed. DAMAGING FLovraes.—John Jameson was charged with damaging, on the 11th of September, four geraniums, the property of Peter Cliffe, of Whitley. The. complainant cut them while drunk in his garden, and on being told by the complainant that he wanted two or three fellows like him for the Daresbury Sessions' he- put them down.—The defendant said he offered to buy the flowers and was told to cut them for himself, and did so, being about to pay for thern.—He was fined the costs. •

POLCNlNG.—Sarnitel Rustage, Ship Canal worker was charged that on the 27th of August, he was found in New-rd..Latchford,about a quarter past 4 in the morning, coming frors land occupied by Isaac Turner, in posses- sion of .1 net and pegs and !di( rabbits. Frederick Shaw and Charles Forster were also similarly charged:--P.C. Millingon said at the time in question he saw the defen- dants coming out of the field. He met Shaw on the bridge, Wash-lane, but found nothing on him. Directly after the other defendants, with two other men, came up, and he found on Rustage the nets, six rabbit., and a peg, and Forster had a bag on his back. They all pleaded not guilty. Rustage and Forster were fined £5 and costs each, and Shaw 100. and costs,

- BREACH OF THE PERIM FIRALTH ACT.—Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Dutton Union Rural Sanitary Authority. made an application to the Bench for an order to close a cottage at Walton Inferior, owned by Mary Barlow, of that place. Mr. Farrington said the house was in an uninhabitable state, and had been condemned by the Authority.—Dr. Adams, medical officer to the Authority, said the cottage was in a filthy and dilapidated condition unfit for human habitation, and was open to the sky. It was overcrowded, and its condition was indescribable. —The defendant said she was anxious to get quit of the tenant, but could not,but these proceedings would enable her to get the tenant out.—Dr. Adams, in reply to the Bench, said the Authority could only deal with the owner, by compelling her to close the house. They could not enforce the putting of it into repair.—The magistrates' clerk said the Bench could only make an order closing the house nntil it was made habitable.—The defendant in reply to him said the tenant paid no rent. —The Magistrates' Clerk : Why do you let them stop if they neither pay rent, nor keep the house in repair? —The order was made, and the inspector was allowed costs.

div.head: FIRE AT AINTREE RACECOURSE.
div.p: FIRE AT AINTREE RACECOURSE.

Fire broke out on Thursday afternoon, about four o'clock, in the Grand Stand, at Aintree Racecourse. The Liverpool Salvage Corps and the Bootle Fire Brigade arrived shortly afterwards, but their efforts were frus- trated owing to insufficiency of water, and the Grand Stand was completely destroyed.
PUBLIC MEETINGS IN TRAFALGAR- SQUARE.

A official communication will shortly be published to the effect that meetings in times of political or social crisis will be permitted in lrafalgar-square. At the Home Office at the present moment a series of bye-laws and regulations is to be prepared to megt the new order of things at Trafalgar-square.
