div.head: RUGBY. WARRINGTON r SWINTON.-LANCASHIRE LEAGUE MATCH.
div.p: RUGBY. WARRINGTON r SWINTON.-LANCASHIRE LEAGUE MATCH.

, These teams met at Swinton on Saturday. Ordinary fix- tures have always been sufficient inducement for a large crowd to gather together,. but Saturday's engagement being the first meeting of the clubs in the above-named competition, there was no wonder at the "gate" numbering considerably over 5,000. Warrington had already won one match, and that decisively,. whilit the present occasion was the debts' of the Swintonians the tourney. Many took advantage of the special, train run by the Cheshire Lines Committee from Warrineon; and be it said to their credit,they were not found wanting in their enthusiasm when occasion required the necessary cheer. The homesters had a good team up, a like remark applying to Warrington. Some time was cut to waste in waiting for Swinton, who were being photo- graphed, but at 3.40 a start was made by Warrington lacking off towards the village goal, against both wind and sun.

The commencement was sensational, for Hall and' Ashton colliding, a delay occursed which lasted several minutes. On resuming, Ashton and Evans came away,. and reached Swinton quarter-flag, and then some neat passing by Bate and Heesom was spoiled by Potts failing to take a pass, Winterbottom and Valentine running the ball out of danger. Jolley, the Turners, and Donohue took the oval back to the Swinton quarters, but Valen- tine, with a lofty kick, eased his lines, and finally caused play to locate near the Warrington quarter-flag. Already the game had settled down to a vigorous ex- hibition, and little heed being taken of the unnecessarily , rough tackling by the referee, the players carried on ad libituse. The half-backs took particular notice of one ' another, and it was a rarity to see a direct pass, these individuals being compelled to adopt saving tactics.. A spell of scrambling scrimmages and line-outs was followed by Evans and Bate passing neatly, but, , Plumpton mulling a pass,Rothwell rushed up and punted to Boscow, who, in conjunction with Lewis, indulged in some exchanges, the ball eventually finding a resting- place at the Warrington quarters. Broekbank and Bumby passed well, but Pearson missed a glorious chance, and Bandies, Heesom, and Fair. Turner again cleared. Holmes and Berry shone with a short dribble, and Evans throwing over to Plumpton, the half-way was reached. Jolley was a conspicuous figure in some loose work, but another exhibition between Lewis and Boscow was followed by Bumby passing beautifully across to Pearson, who dodged his men in clever style, and scored a fine try amidst tumultuous applause, which I was renewed when Valentine placed a goal. Frank Turner again started, and Boscow and Pearson replying with kicks, the Warrington custodian had the better of the deal, play being at the home quarters. Bandies led up the visitors' forwards in a smart rush, whilst a fine opening was missed when Prank Turner passed forward ten yards from the line. Evans found a match in Brockbank, and then Valentineepoiled Heesom, and once more Swinton were the aggressors. A strong rush by the whole body of home forwards saw the ball being taken over, and a minor was forced. Another fine piece of play by Pearson placed his companions in the shade, and the Warrington defence was sorely taxed. Scrimmages and a monotony of lineouts, accompanied by vigorous tackling, were again an especial feature, and an attempt at passing by Bumby and Brockbank was negatived by the smart tackling of Holmes, Nevins, and Evans. By degrees the oval reached the half-way, a lofty kick by Bumby being returned by Boscow. Pearson now failed at a pass from Bumby, and Pair Turner, Jolley, and Nevins dribbling out of danger, play was on the half-way line when the signal was given for half-time, with the score as a goal and a minor in Swinton's favour. Bumby re-started, and no reply being forthcoming, play was at the War- rington quarter flag district. Jolley came away with the ball at his tees, and a sequence of passing by the visitors' backs was frustrated by Winterbottom. Bumby gave Valentine a chance, but he was soon floored, and then Bate looked all over a scorer, when Pearson and Valentine pounced upon him, and upset the Warrington calculations: Some time was now lost by Sharpies getting hurt, and on the game again being renewed, Warrington attacked in still greater earnest. Boscow was tested by Bumby, but the Warrington custodian was not found wanting, and a fine drop settled play danger- ously near the Swinton line. Pearson saved well, and, from a pack, Evans, Bate, Heesom, and Plumpton en- deavoured to improve the style by a series of exchanges. The pass to Plumpton was very low, and as a conse- quence he dribbled to Valentine, tackling that player before he could get away. Warrington were now play- ing a desperate game, attacking with renewed vigour, and it looked a certainty of their scoring when Pearson and Bothwell relieved, and Potts being badly charged by Valentine had to retire. With fourteen men War- rington stilt had the best of it, Ashton having a narrow shave for a try. 111-luck followed the visitors' efforts, but Swinton could not complain of being badly treated, for after some fluctuating play, during which time Plump- ' ton registered a minor from a free kick, a loose scrim- mage took place at neutral ground, and Winterbottom giving a chance to Pearson. another brilliant run by that player saw him landed a scorer, Valentine placing another goal amidst ringing cheers. From now to the call of time the play was of a give-and-take order, and although Holmes got in a splendid dribble opposite the grand stand, and looked to have a chance of scoring, Valentine upset the movement with a foul tacele, the Warrington element giving vent to their feelings in a marked manner. Beyond this item there was nothing else worth recording, and the final score read as—Swin- ton two goals and one minor to Warrington one minor. Teams z—Swinton : F. C. Twigs, back ; J. Valentine, W. Pearson and W. Winterbottom, throe-quarter backs Brockbank and W. Buinby, half backs; T. Bothwell, S. Hallam, A. Sharpies, G. Sharpies, S. Hall, G. H. Murray, N. cletchkiss, C. H. honey, and W. Chapman, forwards. Warrington: J. Boscow, back ;F. Plumpton F. Heesom, and C. Potts, three-quarter backs, John Bate and J. W. Evans, half backs ; H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, Frank Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, T. Donohue I Holmes, W. Bandies, and W. Berry, forwards. Referee Mr. J. W. Clegg, Wigan. WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT. The Virarringtonians journeyed on Monday, to Stock- port to fulfil their engagement with the leading club of that town. Being " Wakes Monday" there was a large attendance, the day being a general holiday. The visi- tors were represented by the same team, with two ex- ceptions, as that which received defeat at the hands of Swinton, Webster supplanting Potts at three-quarters, whilst Teare took the place of Berry, in the forwards. Stockport were represented by Haslam, back; Grange, Saville, Ashton, and Murray, three-quarters; Pickard and Norris, half hacks; Noble. Speet, Morton, Potts, Bailey, Abbey. Williams, and Downs, forwards. Win- ing the toss, Warrington had the assistance of the slight breeze, and although the Cheshiremen made a prominent show at the commencement, when play had thoroughly settled down, they were forced to defend, mainly through the kicking of Webster and the effective passing of Evans, Heesom, and Plumpton. A momentary inva- sion into the Warrington quarters was quickly neutra- lized by Boscow, and after Bate, Heesom, and Webster had passed well, the latter making a good bid for the try, Heesom with a strong run was knocked into touch a yard from the line. The threatened attack of War- rington stimulated the homesters to a united effort, and as a result of their perseverance they made a bold bid for a major point, the passing of the backs being loudly applauded. The defence was not to be penetrated and Plumpton essayed a shot at goal which proved to be a source of Warrington attacking. A beautiful dis- play by Evans, Heesom, and Plumpton terminated in a try, which proved to be the only score during this half. During the second stage, the visitors played a surprising game, and the forwards playing well to a man the game was rarely out of the Stockport quarters. From some accurate dribbling by Bate, Donohue, and Holines,Teare got in at the corner, and Plumpton again failing, the finish of a stubbornly contested game was a victory far Warrington by two tries to nil. RUNCORN T. BROUGHTON.

These teams met on the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, on Saturday, in beautiful weather, before 3,000 specta- tors. Runcorn were without Pendlebury at three-quar- ter, and D. 0. Hughes forward ; whilst the visitors lost the services of Whiteley, their half-back, who unfortu- nately missed the train, F. Gayter acting as substitute. The following teams faced each other, Runcorn Floughton, full back ; T. Robinson, J. H. Crompton, , and A. Limb, three-quarters ' • S. Abrams, and G. Robinson. half-backs ; W. Faulkner, P. Riley, A. Hemp- son, H. Williams, J. Davies, A. Taylor, S. Taylor, G. Moores, and .J. Langley, forwards. Broughton C. Tomlinson, full back; G. Piercey, S. Hassell. C. E. Craven, three-quarters; D. Roberts, and J. Shepherd, half-backs ; E. W. Broadbent, H. Hamilton, H. Hadwin, G. Ibbotsoa, J. Pickard, G. Skidmore, J. Skidmore, J. A. Squires, R. Tomkinson, and F. Gayter, forwards. Broughton having wen the toss, they elected to defend the town goal, Runcorn having to face a powerful sun. Faulkner started the'game, but Squires charged the kick down, and Broughton .rushed the ball over the line, a minor being forced. From the drop out, passing between Roberts, Shepherd, and Hassell again forced Runcorn to defend, and the visitors' fbrwards combining well, took play to the home lines where from a line out, Hadwin got over. Shepherd took the place, but failed to augment. Following this reverse, Crompton getting possession he made an effort to pet through, but was safely held by Hassell. Some pretty passing among the home backs saw Runcorn again attacking, and Limb was only pushed into touch by Tomkinson when close to the line. Abraras, E'. Robinson, and Crompton were prominent, and gave the Broughton backs an anxious time of it. Even play now followed for some time, until a strong rush by the visitors removed hostili- ties to the other end. and Roberts giving Hassell a good pass, the latter made an excellent attempt to drop a goal. Half time arrived with the score—Broughton, 0-1-3 :Runcorn, 0-0-0. Runcorn now had the advantage of sun and wind. Skidmore re-started, and Crompton replied, Tomlinson kicking to Faulkner, who sent the ball dead. Following the drop out, Crompton got a free kick, and the ball being placed for Faulkner, the latter

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 1, 1892. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 1, 1892. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

kicked a magnificent goal from inside his own quarter flag. This success seemed to stimulate the home players, who were quickly again at the other end, another minor being forced. Now Crompton, from a pass by Abra:ns, made a dash., but WAS safely held by Hassall, and Craven got a free kick, but the home for- wards were not to be denied, and upon Abrams getting hold, he threw to Crompton, who raced brilliantly over. 'Faulkner took the place, and made a good shot for goal. ; From the kick aut Broughton cou3dmake hut little head- way, the ball seldom being out el' their 25. Fau3kner, Abrams, and Crompton each made efforts to score,. and the latter had" hard lines 'from a good drop. Still the " Griffins "set up a stout defence,orrtil a grand passing, moVement between the home backs enabled T. RobinSera to store a meritorious try. Crompton this time tried the place, but with no better success. 'Vile kick out saw the grouF.,Mtoniana making a spurt, but Flbug,hton, with? a powerful kick, again sent them back,. Scrimmaging was now indulged irr for some minutes, until G. Robin- son secured, and passed wide to his brother,, who out- paced C:raven and Znniinson, thus Scorizg a fine try. Again the place was a failure. Runcorn still continued to have ranch the best of matters but failed tcraugment their score, A:good game ended in a win fhrßuncorn by 1-3-5 to 04-3:

WatinnvorON "A" ffWINTON " at Warrington, on Saturday. The home team wcnethe toss and very quickly attacked. Thornley charging liekick forced the Swintonians bacl4.and a clever piece'of play iby Lally, Barnes, and Lawfess forced a minor. Then Swinton dribblietto midfleld;. but Ashurst replied'splen- 'didly, and befbre Williams•eould clear his lines Ailey overhauled him: What advantage Warrington• had meteorologically was lost bytlie diajointed efforts off the forwards, and the Swinton men',. getting well together, quickly invaded the home territory, where several quick but not too correct passes, in which Lally, Buckley, Barnes, and Lawless were notablertransferred the com- bat to neutral ground. Then a capital piece of passing amongst Barnes, J! Lawless,• and Daniels was entirely, nullified by the final effort being missed, and Swinton once more breathed freely. A., most unfortunate ac& dent then occurred,. J. Lawless getting his shoulder badly &imaged, and had to leave the field. Some bad detence let in Evans, Chapman,. And Hotchkiss, but Ashurst at a critical moment cleared grandly. Davies, Bailey, and Glover materially increased this advantage, and although Swinton returned' to tbe attack, a vigorous run by Newey found the leather bobbing about the visitors' quarters. Here Warrington had a grand chance, which was mulled,. and Harris, Okell, and Holker quickly removed the dan- ger. Barnes intercepted a pass, and after running finely down the field, kicked across- to Daniels, who rushed over, whilst immediately afterwards,, from a kick across, the sameplayer secured possession and romped over. Buckley, Highanr,•Teare, . and Bailey were then prominent, but the best piece oh the day was witnessed when Buckley and Thornley passed' and re-passed splendidly, the last-named scoring, . half-time arriving with Warrington three tries to nothing.. Thesopening of the second half was sensational enough,. for after a brief raid by Warrington, Harris ran splendidly down the field, and the ball becoming loose, some bad defence saw the ball rushed over the line, and a try scored. The Warrington forwards led by Buckley, Mblyneaux Higham. and Glover, then had an innings, Barnes hav- ing a shy at goal, and Molyneaux, rushing up., scored but for some unaccountable reason the referee ordered a scrimmage. The game, which had been keenly con- tested, got most disagreeable through the referee's total incompetency, football being totally ignored. After this fortune again favoured the " Lions," the result of a bout of passing being the addition of a second try. For a long time the scrambling exhibition was fought near the Swinton hue, a try being disallowed, and when Barnes had a score at his mercy, a drop at goal lbst the opportunity. Nothing further was obtained, a most disagreeable and scrambling contest ending—Warring- ton, 0-3-2 to 0-2-0.

JUNIOR LRAOUR COMPRTITION.—WARRINOTON RLWORRS V. WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.—Tbe above teams played their first match in connection with the above competition, promoted by the Warrington P.C., on Sat- urday, on the ground of the former, before a fair atten- dance. 'rho Raners losing the toss, kicked off against a strong wind and sun, and after the usual exchanges play rested at centre, where Clerk got possession and made a good run to the line, but his pass was mulled and a good chance lost. Both teams now warmed to their work, and the Ckurch having the advantage of the wind forced the homesters on their lines, and good kicking by Garrety and Boleeworth forced a minor. Upon the drop out the game appeared to be evenly c,ontested,both sides attacking in turn, but eventivally the Parish held the upper hand, and rushing theball to the line, Makin scored the first point for the visitors, the kick at go al failing. The Rangers now played hard to equalize., but the effective tackling by the Churchmen prevented cer- tain scores, and half-time was called with the score— Parish Church, one try, one minor; Rangers nil. Upon the re-start, the home team, now having the wind, went off at a great pace and Massey almost got in. The ' Rangers had still the best of it, and from some loose play ' Savage got hold, and running strongly got ever in a good position, and Clark further augmented by landing a goal. The Churchmen, now being in a minority, strove hard to retrieve their position, but the homesters ,by combined forward play neutralized any advantage gained, and Bolt, smartly taking advantage of a mull'. I ran in between the posts, the kick at goal failing. Elated by this success, the Rangers still kept uptho ' pressure and severely tested the Parish Church defence, but with the exception of minors nothing tangible was scored when time was called, the Rangers retiring vic- tors by 1 goal, 1 try, 3 minors, to Parish Church, l'try, 1 minor. WIDNWS " A "V. WIDNES RANGERS.—The above local teams met on Saturday on the ground of the former. There was a fair num`ler of spectators. Final score, itangers, 2 points ; Widnes " A ' nil. Taylor scored I the try foe the Rangers.

WARRINSITOR ST. MARY'S V. WIDSRS MOSS BARRI— On Saturday, St. Mary's journeyed to Widnes to play the above fixture in fine weather. The homesters won the toss and played with the wind. Woods started the ball, for the visitors Abut the Saints could make no head- way, the wind being against -them, and having to play uphill. Several rushes were made by Widnes, but were brought up by the good play of the Saints' backs, who time after time kept saving, keeping their lines: out of danger, and Widnes could not succeed in scoring. When half-time was called the score was—Widnes Moss Bans., three minors; Warrington St. Mary's, nil. On changing ends, the visitors, having the wind and playing crown hill, had the best of the game. Hampson dribbled the ball over the line, Rutter grounding it, but the point was disallowed. The homesters dropped out, and the ball being well returned saw Bennett over, Hampson failing at goal. The oval being again started, Widnes tried to make the game even, but the ball was kept in their 25, where several scrimmages took place, and from a rush by the visito-s' forward, P. Hill picked up and rushed over. L inders failing at goal. Nothing more being scored, St. Mary's won by two tries, four minors, to three minors. WALICHR'S BRISWRRY v. FAIINWORTII.—This match VMS played on the Brewery ground in tine weather. The Brewery having lost the toss, had to play against the wind. Unsworth kicked off for the Brewery and the same player,after five minutes' play, got a splendid try. Jos. Warburton ran in another try,no goal being kioked. In the second half Farnworth kicked off,and the Bi•ewery soon had thein in their own 25.. 'this ended in a try be- ing got, which was improved upon, when the-whistle blew, the Brewery having won a fine game. Score— Brewery, 1 goal, 2 tries, 2 minors, to 1 minor.

RUNCOUN RAKOHRSI i. Wias RANGRIVI " AL." This match was played at Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon, in splendid weather. A splendidly contested are ended: —Runcorn Rangers, one try, three minors ; Widnes Ran- gers, one try, one minor. EARLESTOWN V. RUNCORN BFICREATION " A."—These teams met at the Vulcan on Saturday. The game in the first half was very fast and exciting, the visitors playing a splendid passing game. The back division of Earles- town did not show up well, their passing being of a poor description, and it was doubtless owing to this that the visitors won easily by 2 goals, 3 tries, to nil_
FOOTDALL.

As a result of the match --of—S—a—t.urclay, there are now any number of confident predictions, especially from the Manchester direction, that Swinton are going to be the first " champion of the League! These prophets for- got that it is never safe to prophesy untess you know. There is-no doubt that the Ssvintonians will play hard for the enveted honour, and we all know that they are a redoubtable teamr but then Warrington and some other clubs will play hard too. ohe swallow' does not make a summer, and one victory aloes not wln a League championship.

Besides, Warrington awintorz 14111,6, to meet again, •and the next time the fight will IN) cn the Warrington " midden " which we al f know sometimes makes- a mighty difference in football. Warrinton have before bsaten Swinton on the Wiftiersoool grnund,• and who sags they may not beat them again ? If they do they do the two clubs will be quits as far AS their intet,- enp,gements are concerned.

Irvine " crispy critiques " of the mateli-"*Pliilistine I in the " Athletic News," says; There is ;lot much to, say about this match. The football was of a very so-so order ;In fact there was so little of genuine Notball that few words would express all that' could be said. It may please seine people to call it a forcible game, .tsat'if such play is aitowed there will not be much pleasme in the pursuit, nor much enjoyment in the watching. It was altogether too roughtand the pity of it is that the referee did not stopsuch work on the first symptoms. The only items that made the match worth watching were the splendid effArts of Pearson when he scored the twO tries - gained in the contest. The referee most do his diity, ! and he must be firm. Strong clubs need a strdng • master.

S. Helens leave now got their team into good work- ing order. They have already placed big seores against Kendal, Dukinfield, and Lancaster, and on Saturday, after a grand game, they beat Ulverst.n by two goals' and three tries to nil. It is very evident that St. Helens are trying' to be in the first division of the Lan- cashire Cup competition.

The new members ot the first uivision of the League are finding, out that to oppose the very best clubs week after week is a vasttv different task from what outsiders are aware of. Sheffirid Wednesday went off with a rush, but they have since, the first few days fallen away. Notts Forest and Newton Heath can unfold a similar tale, neither having yet scored a League victory, al- though all the Saturdays in the first month have passed andf gone. Perhaps the new additions will profit by ex- perience.

Perhaps the :nost mystifying club in the country is Aston Villa. They showed such boundless and irresistible dash in the first few runtches that their friends were carried away in their enthusiasm. But what a trans- formation! Within eight days they have lost six points, and had thirteen goals • recorded against them. Form like this is all the more puzzling, when you see the team on the field. A finer set of players is not to be found anywhere,and it is a marvel bow they allow themselves to be so badly beaten.

Three of last Saturday's League fixtures which on paper promised to produce stubborn contests, turned out very one-sided, as represented by the goals recorded. Here they are : Everton EV Newton Heath Sunderland Bolton Wanderers Which was the greater victory it is not easy to decide, hut the very wide margin in each case is certainly most ramarkable, and we are hardly likely to have three similar results on the same day the season through.

To the North End belongs the credit of scoring theonly League victory on foreign soil. The nearest approach to it was the draw that West Bromwich Albion made at Derby. It was a smart performance, seeing that the .• Throstles " lost the services of clever little Geddes, coupled with the fact that the goal that was scored against them came from a penalty kick. The Albion are going much better than is their wont in the early part 9f the season, and we hope they will keep it up, as befits the holders of the English Cup.

div.head: FUNERAL OF A CRIMEAN B.ERO.
div.p: FUNERAL OF A CRIMEAN B.ERO.

On Monday afternoon the mortal remains of Chas. Roberts, aged sixty-one years, df Crab-st.,St.llelens, who for ten years had been employed as commis- sionaire at the offices of Messrs. Pilkington, glass manufacturers, St. Helens, were interred in the Windle Cemetery. Deceased, who was a native of Witney, near Oxford, enlisted in the 73rd Regiment of foot, at Reading, at theage of sixteen. He served with that regiment in the Kaffir war in 1847, 1850, 1851,1852, and 185. for which he was awarded a medal bearing i the inscription "South Africa, 1853; Sergeant C. Roberts, 73rd Reginvent." He also served in the Indian Mutiny of 1858-59, and in the Crimea, for which he re- ceived another medal inscribed "India, 1867-68 ; Sergt. C. Rnberts, 73rd Regiment, in the Crimea ; Corporal C. Roberts, 73rd Regiment, in the-Indian Mutiny." While serving in the Indian Mutiny he was shot thrmigh the right cheek, and the'ball passing through the lower part ; ci his head, cum out at the back of his neck. He was being carried off the field for dead, when the manner in ;which he gripped at the hand of a comrade who had • come to have a last farewell look at him convinced the carriers that he was still living, and he was then taken to the ambulance van. Four of his comrades were shot down while taking him off the field. He had also a sword cut on his left arm, inflicted by an enemy on horseback in the Crimea. Altogetherthe served twenty- two years in the 7.3 rd Regiment and fourteen years in the 4th Lancashire Militia,afterwards the 3rd V.B.South Lancashire Regiment. lie received his discharge on the 26th July, nal, since which time he has been in receipt of a life pension. Ile had excellent testimonials on leav- ing the service from the mayor, captain, and lieutenant of the regiment, and also from several comrades. The !deceased pensioner was well known to many members of the 2nd V.8.5.L.R., and being in the employ of Colonel W. M, Pilkington, the commanding officer readily gave permission • for members to attend the funeral. There was a large assemblage at the last obsequies,

div.head: MEETING OF CON G REGATIONALISTS IN IWA RR/N GTON.
div.p: MEETING OF CON G REGATIONALISTS IN IWA RR/N GTON.

On Tuesday afternoon a meeting of leading Con- gregationalists of the Liverpool district was held in Wycliffe Chapel. The circular convening the meet- ing was headed " Lancashire Congregational Union, in connection with the Church Aid and , Home Missionary Society <Liverpool District,") and stated that" at the annual meeting of this district, held in Crescent Chapel,. Liverpool, on February 2nd last, it was unanimously resolved to hold an I autumnal meeting of ministers and delegates, in order to discuss at greater leieure the necessities of Christmas work in this district, and any other topic of general spiritual interest that from time to , time raay arise." The Rev. a Lord, of Liverpool, , presided, and there was a fair attendance of minis- ters and prominent laymen-of the district, amongst whom was Mr. W. Crostielek ALF. ' I The CHAIRMAN gave an address upon aggressive work for Christ, in the district in, which they lived. They ; would all agree that such work needed to be done if they were to keep pace with the growth of the population. 1 There had he said, been a considerable increase in the pumber of their chapels, schools, and missions. He I remembered the time when they did not hold a brick from Liverpool to Southport, but to-day they had ; chapels and schools between; those two places worth ; some £40,000. (Applause.) The enterprise shown by 4 their Southport brethren had been most cheerful. Their ; work in St. Helens was also worthy of note ; indeed in the whole of the district, in which they might regard St. Helens as the centre, their work had gone forward with great spirit. At Newton a chapel had been erected of which they might be justly proud, while at Prescot. Htivton, and other places they had denominational nro- I perty that had been built at a cost of from £30,000 to £40,000. Even in the town in which they had assembled ; they had not been at a standstill, as the beautiful I church of Wycliffe had been erected in his day, as wall as the missi;an-room at Cocithedge. He had a strong ; conviction that neither in the erection of buildings for ' the preaching of the gospel, nor in the amount raised for the strengthening of their weaker churches, had they i reached the level of their duty. They had not been i sufficiently aggressive. If their churches had not rnen of; spiritand enthusiasm in which to go torward they were 1 certain to go back, hence the importance of good spirit- I ual leadership. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONHN said, there seemed to have been an I extraordinary combination of circumstances on that 4 occasion to hinder people, from attending: He had re- ceived a sheet of apologies, but at the same time he had I received a larger sheet or acceptances. The Rev. C. A. SINHLWIJON, of Leyland, then gave an address upon the rural congregationalism. In his open- ing remarks he said he was always hearing about the late Mr. Mcalinnies at Leyland. Referring to the work of the Church of England in the rural parishes, he con- tended that the body with which they were connected had done a great deal to stir up the Established parish churches they had corms into contact with, or, if they would allow him to do so, with which they had entered into competition. Instances of this were given. In one district, in which there was a population of 2,000 souls, there was no place of worship. There was a church tw miks away, but the district he had alluded to was not considered worth attention. The Congregationalists eventually built a chapel in the midst of the population,.4l and the result was that the Church of England erected a, ,4 mission church near to it. A noble work was beteg, done in the villages, and it was unwise on the part of; 4 Congregationalism to despise it. (Applause.) The Rev. G.. Vienee, of St. Helens, also gave are address upon rural congregationalism. He mentioned that music was-now very good in many country chapels,. owing to the tonic sol-fa system. He said that the sachet , evil existed in the country as well as in the town„, and sometimes even; in graver forms, but that was now pass- ing away, and this was largely due to the pure lives of their country pastors, and to their efforts in providing good and suitable entertainments, and the fttithful preaching ciqho gospel. With regard to the clergymen of the Church of England thereivrere now only few of the old fox-hunting clergymen left, but in some cases his place was taken by the ritualist priest. He believed that an alteration of their land laws was needed for the salva2ien.of the villages. Speaking of the' monotony of the enuntry, he suggested that it would be- a good plan if they imitated the Wesleyans by having-a three or fiv• years' system of changes. This plan, he thought, would act better for both pastor and people. In the course of some discussion which. followed, Mr. William Cmsfield, M.P., referred to thoestablishment of women's religious services. One of the- speakers had • Ireferred to a lack of sympathy in this direction, but ho 'declared that no lack of sympathy could compare with, that which the women's movement met in Liverpool,. when it was first mentioned to the ladies of the congin- gation. He did not believe there. was one lady engaged in women's work who was consulted as to the desir- ability of establishing a mission service who gave it the slightest encouragement. It was-considered to be doubt- ful whether anyone would attend. It was, however, determined to try the experknent. The first trial was a success, and there had not been a failure since. A week ago the, attendance. was aoo. (Applause.) He hoped no oce. would feel hesitation about starting such a movemeat. (Applause.) The Rev. Join,/ yoeue expressed his belief that the Liverpoet district had not been for many years as aggressive as it ought to have been. He had been look- ing over the minutes that morning for a period of nearly I 30ycors, and he was surprised to find that so few cases I of work had been initiated by the Union. People began I to work, and then applied to the Union. His idea was that the Lancashire Congregational Union 'should initiate

div.head: POACHING- AFFItA r AT GRAPPENHAT,L.
div.p: THE POACHING- AFFItA r AT GRAPPENHAT,L.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions,on Tuesday, be- fore Messrs. W. C. Jones (chairman), Chas. Alarson, W. Leing, and H. Neild, Taos Idarrop and Joseph Harrape brothers, were brought up on remantl charged with being found poaching on the night of the 13th of August, on lend occupied by Mr. Richard Barber, at Grappeahall. They were also charged with assaulting and beating Charles Chin- nock, gamekeeper, and Joseph, wae charged with wilfully and maliciously wonnding Charles Chin- nock with intent to do him grievaas bodily harm. Mr. R. Davies appeared for tbe prosecution, and Mr. A. Browne for the defence. Mr. Davies said about 1045 p.m. on the 13th of 'August, the defend- ants were in a field occupied by Mr. R. Barber, the shooting over which was taken by. Mr. Mclver, Mr. Mortimer, and others, and which belonged to Mr. Oswald Leigh, and the complainant was with Mr. Green, a watcher, near the field, and heard a noise pro- ceeding from it, and a hare screaming. They went quietly towards the place, and saw oneof the prisoners, they could not say which, them the other. Joseph Harrel-ewes seised by Green, and Thomas Harrop by Chinnock e After a slight strugg!i3 the prisoners agreed to go quietly, and did. so till they 1' got into the high road, when Joseph made a sudden rush upon Chinnock, and Chinnock was struck and wounded by him with, something, and said "-riu done." Then there- went on a severe fight until the prisoners were captured. Next day caps and some nets were discovered on, one of the prisoners. NO hare was found, but it might have got. away. It was at-first thought that Chinnocia had been wounded with a knife, but Thomas said the wound was caused by a stone. Chinnsck was taken to thehospital, his wound being ardangerous one, and remained there till September 3rd. The prisoners had been in Strangeways Jail eight days, and considering this fact and that the complainant had recovered, he obtained permission to reduce the charge cf wounding against Joseph to that of-common assault, as the prosecutor did not wish to preeehard on the prisoners, tut only de- sired protection for himself.—Charles Chiunock gave evidence. He said on his asking one of the pri- soners what they were doing in the field he re- plied they were looking for mushrooms. He asked him if they hail' brought two lurcher dogs they had with them to.finct mushrooms, and it wasoome time before he replied. He got hold of Thomas, and saw he had netting in his pocket, and tried to get it out when a struggle took place; and Thomas hit him co the head with a stick. HS took it from him and flung it over the fence, and told him, he would have to go to Lymm, He worked the nets out of his pocket, and witness, told him he had dropped them. Lie said "You know toomuch." I Witness described the assaults he charged the prisoners with committingeand said Joseph hit him with a stone I and wounded him severely about the head.—Me. Browne said he did not deny that Joseph struck him with the stone.—Witness in reply to Mr. Davies said Joseph struck him with the stone but did not throw it.—B&' Mr. Browne : Witness did not hit Thomas twice on the head with a stick and then. across the muscles of his arms to disable him, or push- him through a hedge, or compel him to walk through a brook. tie heard his brother say "if he doesmot keep his stick still I shall' are for him. He went to Lyinm, and to the police station, but Sergeant Boctte was on his holidays, then went to look for a constable,. and found P.C. Brevrineand gave the prisoners into custody. —Joseph Green, the watcher corioborated. Allred if he hit Joseph across the face and smashed some hones, he replied that he thought he only hit him once. Thomae told him that Joseph hit Chinnock with a stone that he pulled out of his pocket.—James Hankinson deposed to searching the field nest. morning and lindingethe stone„ the nets, and two hats. He washed a wound on the top of Thomas's head. Green gave witness a leaded stick. He did not see-Joseph with a black eye and' his nose broken.—P.G: Miliineton said Hankinson handed him in the field a stiek.the stone„ nets, and pegs, and -three hats. he had found there.—Mr, Browne asked where Ehe stick was, and Millin,gton said he believed Green had it.—Dr. Langdale, cfJthe Warrington Infirmary deposed to Chin- nock being admitted thereon the 14th of August, witk a wound over the left ear an inch and a half iting and a fracture of the skulle and remaining till September 3rdt 'The woundenight have been produced by a stone. There was also a contused wound over the left eye, which, almost went to the bone. Fatal consegeences were feared at fiest.—Mr. Browne said that his clients had some glas.nes after leaving Warrington, and went on the land with the intention possibly of taking, what they could getetherefore he had advised them treplead guilty so far asehat was concerned, but when they left Mir- ringtcn they could have had no such intention, because thev-tooknothine with them for the purpose. They had no ferrets, and it was. not proved that they had a net. The nets. might have belonged to Chinnock. There- could be no charge againtst prisoners for having dogs•on the land; they most have some implements for destray- ing game to be amenable to the law. The prosecutor and Green had given the defendants provocation, and both of them had been disfigured for life; one having a hrokenmose and the other a broken cheek,bone. Had his clients gone for a doctor they would' ref doubt have been sent to the- Tnfirmary too.—The, Bench, after a quarter of an hour'e paivate conversation, fined theeiri- soneraLland costs each, £5 each in all. They paid' 2.5 dowtabetween them, and gave security to pay there- snaiaule at the rate of £2 a month.

Dr. Heron, whose name has been, coupled w-t: 'Pa the strange death of the young actress,. Ruby Busaell,. has committed suicide at a private hotel Craven-st.,,Strand, London. He arrived at the hotel on,Saturday night. He was not seen up- to. Sunday afternoon, and the police were summoned to break open the door of the room which he had occupied. He was found lying dead on the flhor in a pool) of blood, and with is. terrible gash in his throat. A medical man who waa,called, and examined titie body, found deceased had taken- sufficient poison to ,cause death apart from the woondL Later incittiries tend to show that De Ileum went tothe-Craven Hotelyeraven- st., with the determined purpase-of committing suicide. Before leaving Brompton, on Saturday, he shaved off his moustache*, and presented a. very different appear- ance. The tragic end of the young:actress Marion, Sharp and Dr. Herart-still excites much attention. The Secretary of the Jubilee Hospital, Brampton, in an interview on Tuesday afternoon,expreseed, tbe opinion that there was no foundation for the suggestion that Dr. Heron poisoned the girl. Existence,, he said, would not be worth having if, through him, his pro- mised bride took her own life. Apart from this,, how- ever, owing to the unfortunats circumstances attending the death a his wife in Jamaica, suspicion must attach itself to him in this last terrible bereavement, and it was not worthwhile to stay andfight out the whole probable course a the affair. div.p: THE PIT-SHAFT ACCIDENT AT GARs- WooD. TERRIBLE DE.VtII OE' A FIREMAN.

Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Park Hotel; near Sr. I lelens, on Monday, on the body of Edward Grundy, aged 32. years, a fire- man employed by the Garswood Hall Colliery Co., who was killed on Friday night by failing down the pit shaft. Mr. M'Geever, certificated manager of the collieries, was present, and the Coroner said he had notified the death to Mr. Matthews, the assistant Government inspector of mines, but he did not appear, and he (the coroner) thought the proper course would be to goon, anl if they found any necessity for his presence, to adjourn the in- quiry. From the evidence of Thomas Bullen, enginewinder, Hobert Dean, and Richard Parkinson, fireman, it tran- spired that deceased went down the pit at four o'clock on Friday afternoon. At half-past eight he came up again for the purpose of lighting three lamps, it being an upcast shaft and contrary tu rules to unlock and relight the lamps in tile mine. He was seen by sullen to return with the lamps lighted, apparently with the in- tention of going down again. It is usual for the men to shout to Bullen that tney are ready to go down, but as no sign was given, the engmewinder became anxious, and went out in ,earch of Grundy. At eleven o'clock nothing had been seen of him, and Harrison, the surface manager, and Parkinson went down the pit. They found the dead body of the deceased at the bottom in the centre of the two shafts, and in the " dib " hole they found his " jack " lamp ; also a second lamp and a portion of another. One cage was at the bottom deck on the surface, and the other in the shaft. The deceased did not appear to have struck the cage in the shaft whilst falling. It was stated that a quantity of steam was coming up the pit at the time, but the theory was that deceased had gone through the gates, and had mistaken the shaft in which the cage was up, and, stepp- ing too far, had overbalanced himself. 'The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death, hut presented that in future the men should not use the bottom deck. The. Coroner : Mr. M'Geever has been telling me about this. This man was an official, and as a matter of fact did Use the bottom deck. He had no right to use it, but it was to save him the trouble of coming down and going up the steps to get on the top deck. The cage should have been brought to the top landing, and then he would have had the trouble to go down the steps. If one of,the, colliers had clone it he would have been fined, but here it, is one of the officials. Mr. M'Geever : It is a violation of the rules, for every one of the jurymen knows that they are suppGsed to get out at the top landing. This bottom deck is only used fer sending timber down the pit. There is no one to blame only himself. Bullen was then recalled, and, in answer to the coroner, said that Grundy had ordered him to stop there. He started working at that job four months ago, and Grundy told him the times that lie came up, so that he could stop at the bottom landing. He did not know that he was doing anything wrong. . The Coroner (to Bullen) : The jury have come to a verdict of " ACoidental death," but have added a pre- sentment ti:at the etlg should not be stopped at till bottom landing. It you do again you will perhaps get yourself into serious trouble. Bullen : I'll stop it there no more. A Juryman said it would not do to alwayS go to the top landing. He was a night fireman, and he had often to come up the pit for props, and they could not get props on the top landing. The Coroner said that it was understood. that they should always stop at the top landing unless there was good cause to do otherwise. The inquiry then terminated.
THE BOGUS LITEVARY AND ART SOCIETY. HEAVY SENTENCES.

The trial of Sir Gilbert Campbell and five other defen- dants for alleged conspiracy to defraud the public in connection with various bogus literary societies con- cluded on Tuesday, at the Old Bailey, after lasting seven days. The defendaat Montague Clarke, by permission of the Courtonade a long statement to the effect that he had been led astray by Morgan and never had any intention to defraud. Ile complained to the Common , Sergeant that he " had been handcuffed and chained to six other prisoners at Holloway prison, one of whom was subsequently sentenced to be hanged." Sir Forrest Fulton said he was shocked to hear it. Sir Gilbert Campbell spoke in his own defence, saying that he had had nothing to do with the Authors' Alliance, that when he allowed his name to appear on the prospec- tus he thought the Society was a genuine one, that he had served with distinction through the Indian Mutiny, and had always borne an unblemished reputation. In his summing up the Common Sergeant said the Author's Alliance was clearly a fraud. The jury, after nearly two hours' deliberation, found Morgan,"romkins, and Steadman guilty on all the counts, but found Sir Gilbert Campbell, Tolnde, and Clarke guilty of conspiracy only. The Common Sergeant said the tendancy- to float these bogus companies was a national danger. He sentenced Morgan to eight years' penal servitude. Tomkins to five years, Sir Campbell to eighteen months' imprison- ment, and the other defendants to terms of imprisonment ranging from fifteen to four months.

div.head: IRISH EVICTED TENANTS.
div.p: IRISH EVICTED TENANTS.
A COMMISSION TO BE APPOINTED.
The following letter from the Chief Secretary in reference to the evicted tenants has been sent for publication : " 28th September, 1892.

_ "Dear Mr. M'Carthy,—ln reply to your inquiry I am now ready to state the intention of the new Government in respect of the question of the evicted tenants. You will remember that in the discussion which took place in the House of Commons in the summer of last year upon this subject Mr. Balfour, Mr. Smith-Barry, and others fully admitted that a great evil existed to which It was most desirable in the interests of peace and good government that an effective remedy should be applied. An effort was made by Parliament to carry out this declared object of public policy by passing the 13th section of the Land Act of 1891. That provision has unfortunately proved not only inadequate but an entire failure. Out of the very large number of cases in which the settioa was intended to bring relief only 187 settle- ments have been effected, and of these 103 were on one single estate. The evil is wholly untouched. One figure supplies a sufficient test of its magnitude. It is estimated that the extra force of police required in connection with the evicted tenants and the consequent disquiet is not lee than 600 men, at a cost -tf some £45,000 per annum. I need not point out to you that the cost of police is only one item. We must add the charges of prosecution, counsel and witnesses, of the maintenance, custody,safe conduct, and removal of prisoners, and other miscel- laneous payments, which go to swell the aggregate of expense entailed under this head. The disturbed condi- tion of:one notorious estate alone has cost the country over £13,000 since 1881. Nor can we leave out of sight that at this moment no fewer than 753 persons in Ire- land are receiving special protection for the police. The necessity of the CA C, then, which was fully recognised but not met by Parliament and the Government in 1891, remains as urgent as ever, and the new Irish Govern- ment have lost no time in looking for other means of dealing with the question. In devising a inore effective remedy than section 13 we require fuller and more precise information than is now in our possession. We propose, thin; fore. by the Lord Lieutenant's warrant, to appoint & small Commission, to examine and report with strict impartiality, and as promptly as may be, the actual circumstances and practical equity of the case. We intend that the area of inquiry shall practically cover the estates within the scope of section 13, where disputes still exist between landlords and evicted tenants, but excluding all cases where the evicted tenants have quitted the country. The Commission will report on the number of tenants evicted since the date named in that section, with such of the particulars id the evictions as they may deem relevant, on the number of such holdings re-let or sold to other tenants, and on the circumstances of such new tenants or purchasers, on the cases in which evicted tenants have been reinstated, on the present circumstances of the tenants, ant..l on any specified offers of settlement that may from time to time have been made, on the estimated cost of lie- evictions to the Exchequer and to the local rates of any proceedings resulting from the evictions, including the cost of extra police and inciden- tal legal charges, and on such other facts and circum- stances connected with the evictions as the Commission may deem it expedient to report, and what means should be adapted for bringing about settlements and the rein- statement of evicted tenants. We institute this inquiry In good faith, in the hope that both landlords and tenants will assist in it, and in the belief that it is an indispensable preliminary to effectual measures for healing a deep social mischief in Ireland.—Yours faith- fully, " Jomq Monutv."
(Signed) "Justin M'Carthy, Esq. THE PROPOSED INQUIRY.

In an interview on Wednesday, the secretaries of the Irish Evicted Tenants' Association said while adhering to their belief that the object of the commission of inquiry into the evicted tenants' claims granted by Mr. Morley is principally for the purpose of gaining time, they are not disposed to offer any opposilion to it.

div.head: JOHN BRIGHT' RECREATIONS,
div.p: JOHN BRIGHT' RECREATIONS,

Poetry was an abiding pleasure with John Bright," writes Mr. C. B. Bright Maclaren in the " North American Review." " his favourite authors were Milton, Whittier, Longfellow, and Byron, and he loved to read their works aloud evet- ing after evening to his children. Ile explored the by-paths of literature for undiscovered poets. His memory was stored with poems, which he would repeat as he drove along in his quiet journeys with his sisters or children through Scotland or Italy," " There is nothing," he used to say," which gives so much pleasure as poetry, except little children.'' , Now and then be would jot down a verse or an epigram of his own in the album ot an hotel. In the visitors' book of a little Highland inn, near Inverness, he condensed his views on the land question in these words : In Highland glens 't Is tar too oft observed That men are chased away, and game preserved ; Glen Urquhart is to me a lovelier glen. Here grouse and deer have not supplanted men. Bright loved Ecotland, and, in a sort of way, the Scotch." He had a little family of Scotch terriers of whom he was very fond. But a dog rarely came near him that he did not caress. Salmon fishing became his favourite, and latterly, his only outdoor occupation, and be was a frequent and welcome guest on the best reaches of the Tweed and the 'Lily. " But I don't always like Scotch theology," he said once; " its too full of the gridiron." He had more sympathy with Robert Burns and the Scotch poets. His own religion was found in the Sermon on the Mount. Creeds and formularies were not to his liking. At a certain dinner he turned from a High- land minister of opposite political opinions and assertive tongue with the remark--" It's odd that, a , man who knows so little about this world can tell lus so much about the next." Mrs. Bright cared I little for London life, and so John Bright "always I lived during the Parliamentary session in bachelor quarters, and probably never gave a dinner party in his life." For many years before his death he occu- pied a set of rooms in Piccadilly facing the Green Park. Here he breakfasted and smoked his morning cigar, and at 10 o'clock he was accessible to everyone who chose to call. He received his visitors in a gray dressing gown. All were welcome; and it may be safely said that his kindest smile was for the struggling author, or for the American who sought him as a friend of America, often without other I introduction than his nationality. A large part of John Bright's idle hours in London were spent in the old club-house in Pall Mall so intimately associ- ated with the history of English Liberalism. Though he was an habitual diner-out,he made hut a pretence of the evening meal. After glancing over the day's papers at the club, ha liked, to make a dinner there in the afternoon, after which he would stroll from table to table in casual talk,and finally to the smok- ing-room or billiard-room, always surrounded by a knot of friends. Thus the day passed until it was time to go down to the House of Commons or out to dinner. Billiards was the only game he Cared for. and if he never made a good player it was not for want of practice. By an unwritten hut sacred law. the " little billiard-room " at the Reform Club was as absolutely at his disposal as was the corner seat on the third bench below the gangway in the House ot Commons.

div.head: STRANGE STORY OF THE SEA.
div.p: STRANGE STORY OF THE SEA.

The following strange story appears in the " Pun- gob," of Naples, of the 20th. About three years ago the " Secole XIX," of Genoa, published a notice saying that Captain Pirkson, on arriving in that port with that City of London, informed the captain of the port of the disappearance of a Mr. and Mrs. Hellbridge, first-class passengers from Bangkok, who, while the City of London was off the Lipari Isles, were suddenly missed after A tsmpest. The other day the Paraguay, of the Italian General Navigation Company, was steaming between Sar- dinia and Tunis, when early one morning an object was perceived floating on the sea. which, being picked up, proved to be a small barrel encrusted with marine animals. On being opened there was found within a champagne bottle corked and well protected by pitch, containing writing on apiece of parchment. It was perfectly clear, and ran as follows: " Saturday, sth September, 190. On board the City of London, from Hong Kong. The undersigned, John Iticirerlow, of Rangoon, and Miss Henrietta Hellbridge, both embarked on hoard the City of London, have decided to bury in the sea their last kiss. The Tiorreno (Meditertanean) is tempestuous, the sky is black, the infuriated elements desire their prey. Well, we will bury our infinite love. We confide this nocumant to the chances of the sea. Whose, r finds it will send word to the English Consul resid- ing in the place where it is fished up. God pardon ! Man will never curse two unfortunates, the victim of an ardent and desperate passion.—J. MacPerlow, Henrietta Hein-midge. This bottle will be thrown into the sea near Sicily." Some persons on board the Paraguay recollected the notice pub- lished three years ago in the " Secolo XIX." Later on the Paraguay cast anchor at Goletta.
