A PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY FOR RUNCORN.

Sir,—Now that the winter is approaching, may I sug- gest to the leading politicians of Runcorn the desirability of forming a Parliamentary Debating Society. The advantages of such a society are too apparent to need any enumeration. If the matter was taken up, say, by the Committee of the Liberal Club, no doubt a very good society could be formed in Runcorn, as great interest is always taken in matters political. The first step, of course, would be to call, by advertisement, a meeting of those interested.—Yours Sec WOUT Runcorn, 22nd Septenaber, 1892.

div.head: WOULD-BE-MEMBER.
div.p: WOULD-BE-MEMBER.
CHURCH AND STATE.

Sir,—Permit me very humbly a few remarks. England having taken the lead in her missionary work and the circulating of the Word of God in various languages, she is recognised as holding and defending the faith of the church catholic according to the creeds laid down in the Book of Common Prayer ; in which its followers are expected to be worshippers in accordance with its rubrics or rules. The laws of England are also in agreement with the Prayer Book, being a Christian State, in op- position to the Papal dogmas of the Roman Church which we threw off at the Reformation. This constitutes i us Protestants, or protesters against the authority of Rome in these realms ; therefore, it is absolutely neces- sari, that the Church of England should be an Estab- lished Church as a bulwark against Romish ascendency. Protestant dissenters should see the reason why they should be united with the church against any encroach- ment. Cromwell himself saw the necessity of the State being Christian by appointing his own preachers, after driving the clergy ; but his reign was short, being a usurper. We, therefore, sheiild hold fast'; to the Church in its connexion with the State, being Protestant, which has made this country what it is. We have of late wit- nessed what has followed the Disestablishment and rob- bery of the Irish Church—murders and crimes of all descriptions—a sufficient warning to Great Britain.— Yours, &c.,

div.head: WARRINGTON TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.
div.p: WARRINGTON TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.

Sir,—ln perusing the syllabus of the Technical Institute for the corning session, I notice that the class for Iron and Steel is ommitted. Last year a class was attempted, but fell through owing to lack of students, which fact is not very creditable to the young men engaged in the iron trade of Warrington. Bdt are the young men entirely to blame ? I think not. The'classes are held in the middle of the week when very few can attend, owing to the custom of night work in the iron trade. With due respect for the committee, I would suggest that if the class had been held on Saturday even- ing, between four and seven o'clock, it would not have been a failure, as all could attend at that hour. Owing to the failure of the Iron and Steel class, I joined the metallurgy class last year, at which we got a certain amount of instruction in iron and steel, but we had to devote a considerable amount of time to the study of other metals that had no interest for me, which I thought a waste of time so far as I was concerned. I sat for the examination in May and passed, but that fact is of little use when applying for a situation in the iron trade. What is wanted is a certificate for Iron and Steel. I should like to see an abler pen than mine take up the subject, and I hope the Committee will see their way to give a chance to the Ironworker, one of whom is— CROWN BEST. Warrington, September 28th, 1893.

SOME " SAGE " REMARKS ANENT A GOOSE. Sir,—l had thought to have treated " A Learner" with the silent contempt that anonymous scurrility de- serves. But Ido not see how I can better play the part of "sage" than in the stuffing of a goose. If the sea- soning is not quite to his liking—the pepper is of his own asking. It would be interesting to know in what department of human knowledge your correspondent is "A Learner." It cannot be English grammar, else he has learned so far to very little purpose. Perhaps he will tell us how one thing can be different to another? Is one may have a smattering of grammar and not be able to Write intelligibly, so a knowledge of some rules of logic does not constitute "A Learner " an adept at right reasoning. He is as the raw apprentice, who, hav- ing plenty of tools to work with, manages only to cut himself and spoil the work. See, for instance, how deep "A Learner" has got in ! natural history. Take one sentence :—" If the sage re- gards man as a distinct species, sui generis, then it is easy to see why moral laws should dominate the natural, but if man is linked on by evolution to the lower ani- mals, it becomes very difficult to see how a man can act differently to (sic) the animals." Here we have evidence that this anonymous blunderer either does not know what he is writing about,or lie does not know how to write ! about what he knows. For, neglecting one of "the lacunos in his scholarship" which I have italicised, even " A Learner" might, had he been really what his pen- name implies, have known that Homo sapiens is not only a distinct genus and is still "linked on by evolution to the lower animals." But does "A Learner" mean "a distin t species" or a distinct creation, which transposi- tion might make sense of an otherwise senseless para- graph. And now as to this logician's reasoning. Here is a sample. Because I am an Evolutionist, and as such, acknowledge kinship by descent from our fellow beings, I am thereby precluded from protesting against the maltreatment of our kindred in order to es- tablish a lucrative reputation for incipient sawbones ! Because a cat plays with a mouse ere devouring it—man may perpetrate without blame the most horrible and disabolical cruelties upon other animals. Has "A Lear- ner," among all his learning, never heard of mental and moral evolution ? I can easily acquaint him of any par- ticipation therein. The man who to the neglect of the central and essential principle—the denunciation of the barbarities which even now are filling the world with intense anguish—the man who from this can turn to indulge in mean and mindless quibbling, must be as as shallow in heart as he has proved himself to be in understanding. When "A Learner " hears of an animal making scienti- fic experiments he may then attain to a clearer idea of how moral responsibility is affected by the struggle for existence. In the meantime let him become in reality what he is now only in name. But I am afraid he, like the Bourbons, "learns nothing and forgets nothing"—not even the drubbing as a detected " fraud" which. if I mistake not, he has had before under another disguise, the sting of which seems to rankle. Small things affect small minds, and the meaner the man the longer he tears malice. When " A Learner " has sufficiently advanced in his studies to be able to think clearly and write intelligibly, let him godfather the vivisectionists in his own name. If he be a 'man, surely he ought not to be ashamed of either his cause or his opinions. Yours, Szu. JOHN PEERS. Penketh, Sept. 25th, 1892.

div.head: ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS.

Sir,—The 20th of September, 1892, will long be remembered by the people of Warrington for at least, four great evils. First, bartering brewers ; secondly, discredited magistrates ; thirdly, injured property owßers ; fourthly, endangered drink victims. The first two classes, are answerable to God and mankind for the wrongs they inflict upon the latter two classes and all concerned. Truly says Shakespeare :—" Devils sconest tempt, resembling spirits of light."

The brewers' counsel in vain tried to delude some of the thinking magistrates on the Bench, and readers whose minds can think without strong drink and whose conscience is not bartered away for some selfish interest will regard at its worth the statement that " public- houseswere not built for the sake of drinking facilities." Oh I no, but were always erected more for the purpose of supplying people with " meat and sleep, and have every other legitimate accommodation, the same as could be found if we went to Llandudno." What an impeach- ment of public-houses it must be, if any person should happen to say that public-houses are the places where the pitiable sot ever got anything to make his nose strongly pimpled, with colours proclaiming to all beholders a. grave lie about what had gone down his

throat in some so called" meat and sleep "apartments. Mr. Davies must know all about the mysterious painting I and beautifying, and ennobling influence of what is sold in such places,being a legal defender of them. Therefore he boldly affirmed that the two new houses " would be a benefit to the ton." Accordingly, some wondrous change may cQrne over all such grand moralising public- houses. People may not get drunk in them ? It is too wicked even to think that men, women, and young people, who go to such fine "eating and sleeping new houses " will never find " drinking facilities " there. Hence never get drunk, and always avoid crime, theft, insanity, idleness, murder, &c., of .which, if chaplains, judges, police, &c., as well as our own eyes, are to be believed, public-houses hitherto have been the most ruinous source under thewhole heavens. Who reaped last year the profits on the National drink Bill £141,220,675, causing about 300,000 persons to be apprehended for drunkenness, and helped over 1,000,000 paupers upon the books of the various parish Unions of this drink- cursed nation?

3,600,000 are estimated to have come upon the books of the parish Unions during the year 1887; and about a year or so before then 103,355 persons were confined as lunatics. 76,728,266 bushels of God-sent grain were destroyed tR manufacture the brewers' maddening liquor. . .

Alia voice of the vast majority of property owners and of the poor people in those districts concerned have again and again exclaimed—" Take up the stumbling block out of the way " ; reduce the alarming numbei ot dens of strong drink, poverty, woe, and crime in our midst ; and " Lead us not into temptation " by placing such places elsewhere, to pamper to the heartless greed of gold of one rich firm of brewers. Were Goethe here would he not scorn those who lent themselves to aid the Great Sheik who neglected the interest of this Borough during the late Government's time of office. But he was generous and true enough to himself not to omit to go and vote for the unjust Brewers' Compensation Bill.
" These, oye quacks 1 Are your remedies Alms for the rich ; gall of hell for the poor." And Webster would caution all concerned saying—

Accuse not Heaven's delay ; if loth to strike, Its judgments ; like the thunder-gathered storm Are but the greater." We know full well, that some like swine will trample such wise men's pearls beneath their feet, and laugh and still sin on. They would do well to ponder moro over such things as they are now the cause of, and ever remember as the poet wisely inculcates—
Justice, like lightning, ever should appear

To few men's ruifi, but ro all men's fear''' "Woe unto the-: that call evil good, and good evil ; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness ; that put bitter for sweet, aid sweet for bitter I"

Magistrates of the past and at the present are free,and therefore responsible for the number of drinking dens, that disgrace and curse our town and empire. So for no men can rule them. " But every dog has its day and licensing authorities have hitherto failed. A change is therefore signalised, and certainly for the better. All the moral forces of the universe are at work to effect it.

For right is the king of might, As darkness is slain by light ; And he conquers though he falls, Who nobly fights, for the right. Yours faithfully, R. STOREY. 160, Orford-lane, Warrington, Sept. 26;h, 1822.
THE EXAMINER, SATITIMAY, OCTOBER 1, 1892.

div.head: LEGAL EIGHT HOURS DAY.
div.p: A LEGAL EIGHT HOURS DAY.

Sir,—The much-talked of and more written of subject upon which much wind,ink,and paper have been wasted, is it a craze or a sober, practical, workable reality? In some oases and in some trades it may work very well, in others it will not work without much friction ;in fact so much friction that it will stop the wheels altogether and prevent any work being done at all. In the textile trades an eight hours day may work—but let us not forget that our neighbours and competitors over the water work twelve hours a day. Can we do as much, or a little more in eight hours than they do in twelve? If we can, we are right. Take the whole body of miners—would an Act of Par- liament restricting the miner to eight hours a day work well in all cases ? Let us see. He goes down the pit at six o'clock and comes out at two o'clock ; he may have a full mile from the pit bottom to his work. Taking in going and coming out, stripping and dressing, one hour, he has seven in which to work including meal time— quite long enough in semi-darkness and a foul atmos- phere. What can he earn in the seven or say six and a half hours, supposing he gets clearance for his stuff—no falls to clear away, no escape of gas from which he must get out of the way ? Can he make 40 hours week of profitable working? Will the demand for coal be so steady that full work can be done on each day ? 1 have known in South Wales weeks of had weather so that vessels could not go to sea, and every waggon full at the pit or port, waiting for shipment. ill this while the collier has been idle waiting for the weather to break. Would not a few extra hours—or two or three extra tons of coal in the week help a little towards making good, to some extent, the previous lost time. The legal eight hours day will not permit it ;it will be a mis- demeanour or a crime to be punished with "Treadmill and skilly "—pleasant exercise and nourishing diet for future hard work, though not by any means a cheerful prospect ; seven hours of hard work is quite enough and to follow it up anywhere. I could do with six. Under- ground it is more than enough, in a hot and dusty coal- laden atmosphere. As a colliery engine-wright, I have put several haul- ing engines and pumps underground, and know some- thing of coal-getting, its difficulties and dangers. I have , witnessed two explosions underground, with six men killed each time,and by a strange coincidence there were a father and two sons among the victims, and each explosion and each fatality occurred soon on Monday morning. The moan and the wail of the widow and fatherless, the bereaved mother and stricken sister, ring lin my ears, and bring the tear to my cheek, when I think ef it, although more than forty years have come and gone since then. I knew the men and their fami- lies and sympathised with them. Since then many a respected neighboer and friead has gone to his account from the °Dal pit. I would not have your readers suppose that lam opposed to the eight hours day for miners and other trades as well, but let us not have any Government tinkering in the business—no penal enactments. The question is surrounded with difficulties, variatioas, and exceptions—that make it next to impossible to legislate to meet, not every case, but the majority of cases. The miners know pretty well how to take care of themselves; , let them do their own legislation ; it will be more satis- factory to them and the public at large. , There are other trades too. Take the engineers ; they don't work 9 hours now 7 They knocked off one hour from the 54 per week less than two years since, without going to Parliament. An eight hours legal day in that trade would be very inconvenient, and in many cases would cause great loss to men and masters. Most establishments have about as much plant as the normal requirements of their business need, with not much spare shop room, employing generally the same numner of men ; so many fitters, so many turners, machine men, smiths, pattern makers, Zee. Sometimes the work is slack, and in the afternoon of a day, several are told they need not come in until breakfast to-morrow. The next day they are told—not to come in to-morrow ; give a look round,work may come in. Well, eventually work does come in, and is wanted out with all speed, and the shop is busy. As many hands are put on as the shop can accommodate, and overtime must be worked to get through. It may be a breakdown or two, with hundreds of hands idle—waiting for the work to be done, but the legal day says no overtime; let those people remain idle, whether they have anything to eat or not. The law must not he broken—while a few hours' overtime for a few men, would start those idle hands days sooner, to their benefit and their employers' profit. Masters do not want overtime; it means extra wages given to men, who are already jaded with the work of the ordinary busy day—hut it is a necessity demanded by the exigencies of the case. We all want more leisure, I have no doubt 7 and if shortened hours will answer financially, let us have them but we must not make cast iron rules. Is the world getting more lazy than formerly ? Jack wants to be as good as S's master, or a little better. He sees the moneyed classes going to business at 9or 10 o'clock in the morning, and going home to dinner at 5 in the evening, with an interval for an expensive lunch. They wear broadcloth and fare sumptuously, and Jack thinks, and often rightly too, that he does not get his share. The remedy is in com- bination, self-help, co-operation, strict temperance, and self-culture, industrial and thrifty habits—which will do more to ameliorate his condition than all the legislative enactments that Parliaments can pass. Let the working- man cultivate gentlemanly behaviour, and respectful speech, and he may become his own Parliament, and make his own legal day. I am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMHO. Sankey Bridges, September 22nd, 1892. -

[Our Correspondent makes some very pertinent observa- tions, as a workman who sees the difficulties in the way of a hard-and-fast enactment. As the subject is a most important one, we shall be glad to open our columns to other corresnondents.—En. Ex.]
THE CRISIS IN THE COTTON TRADE,
At a meeting of the Federation of cotton spinners held in Manchester yesterday, it was unanimously re,olved to give a months notice for five per cent, reduction La wages.

Mary Moseley, the passenger from America whose mysterious disappearance at New Brighton has heen reported, has turned up at Sheffield, where her peculiar behaviour resulted in her being conveyed to tk,e work- house on the strength of a naedicat certificate..

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.

ST. MARY'S MISSION, BANK QUAY, WARRINGTON. The harvest thanksgiving services were held in this Mission on Sunday. Tne decorations, which were pretty, had been carried out by Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Kent, Mrs. Ellison, and the Misses Jackson, Holly, Ashcroft, Leach, Hatton and Lloyd. In the morning the Rev. W. E. Glenn was the preacher, and in the evening the Rev. L. B. Radford, B.A. The Rev. W. E. Glenn also gave an address at a scholars' service in the afternoon. The ser- vices were well attended, the offertories being in aid of the day schools. LEGH-STREET PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WARRING PON. The harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above place of worship on Sunday. The Rev. 0. Lewis, of St. Helens, Auckland, preached morning and evening, and in the afternoon a sermon was preached by Mr. W. Tharme, Liverpool. Selections were rendered by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. John Pod more, and Mr. James presided at the organ. The chapel was suitably decorated for the occasion, and all the services were well attended. A fruit banquet was held on Monday evening, when the chair waa taken by Mi. James Dodd.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.

The annual harvest thanksgiving service was held at St. Paul's Church on Thursday evening. The service was choral, and the choir were assisted by Mr. Alfred Sutton's orchesaa, numbering 35 performers. An anthem "Oh clap your hands" by Sir Stainer was given. The preacher was the Rev. Hugh Hornby Birley, M.A., select- ing his text from James V, 7 and 8, "Behold the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it. until he receive the early and latter rain. 'rhe decorations were not very elobor- ate, but were executed with much taste. The church was crowded.

CHURCH MISSION ROOM, PENKETH. On Tuesday evening, the thanksgiving services were held in the Church Mission-roorn, Penketh, which was crowded. The decorations were very handsome. The work of decoration had been entrusted to the Misses Jeans (31 Miss and Miss M. Tinsley, Miss Daunt, Miss Ellison, Mr. W. Denton, and Mr. John Parkinson. Miss Bolton, Penketh House, lent the shrubs, ferns, &c., and the Misses Tinsley, Jeans, Ansdell, Moss, and other members of the congregation contributed vetetables, fruit, &a. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. R Jones. curate-in-charge, and the sermon preached by the Rev. James Davies, vicar of St. David's Church, Brownlow- hill, Liverpool. The offertory will be devoted to the gqineral church expenses. Mr. Ethelbert Foster was at the organ.

div.head: CAIRO-ST. CRAPEL.
div.p: CAIRO-ST. CRAPEL.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held in Cairo-st. Chapel, on Sunday, and were well attended, additional sitting accommodation having to be provided at the evening service. The decorations of the chapel had been carried out in a very pleasing and appropriate style, there having been contributed for the purpose a large quantity of flowers, fruit, plants, and vegetables. The work of decoration had been accomplished by Mrs. Freeston, Mrs. Winsar, Mrs. Rymer Young, and the Misses Monks, Long, and Houghton. The Rev. Dandy Agate, of Gorton, preached in the morning, the Rev.F.K. Freeston occupying the pulpit in the afternoon and evening. Special hymns were sung and an anthem was excellently rendered by the choir in the evening. Mr. Grey was at the organ. The fruit and flowers were afterwards sent to the Infirmary, the hospitals, and the Ragged Sanday School. PADGATE WESLEYAN CHAPEL. On Sunday the annual Wesleyan harvest festival was held in the chapel, which had been beautifully decor- ated for the occasion with corn, flowers, and veget- ables, by Miss and occasion, E. Bennett (Lyndhurst), Miss and MiSS H. Bennett (Pear Tree House), Misses Richard, son, Miss Eaglesfield, Miss E. Smith, and Miss E. Ward. At the morning service the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Alfred Frelman, who preached from St. Mark iv. 26-29. In the evening the preacher wr.s the Rev. John Kirtlan, the newly appointed superintendent of the Wes- leyan Circuit, who took ma his text the wu-ds " But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and goad heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience "—St. Luke vii., 15. Large congregations attended at each service, and at the evening service a solo was sung by Mr. Grounds, of Warrington. Miss H. Bennett (Lyndhurst) presided at the ruga.n. Collections were made towards clearing off the balance still owing for redecorating the chapel. ST. MARY'S GREAT SANKEY. -

The harvest thanksgiving, services were held in St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, on Sunday. There were three services, morning at 10.30 a.m., afternoon at 3.0: p.m., for die children, evening at 6.30 p.m. In the morning the preacher was the Rev. F. Millard. M.A., of the Warr;ngton Training College. In the afternoon a service was specially held for children.about 650 chilnren being present, the Rev. J. 11. Jones officiating. A great nnmber of children made offerings of flowers, which wore intended for the hospitals at Warrington. In the evening the preacher was the Rev. H. Gibson-Smith, M.A., vicar of Halewood. The church was packed at each service. lathe morning there was a congregation of 560 persons ; and in evening 850, and others could not gain admission. The sacred edifice had been adorned with taste and skill. The decorations, &c., were carried out by Miss Bolton, Miss and Miss Mary Tinsley, the Misses Jeans, Grange, Owen, and other members of the congregation. The collections for the day amounted to £l9 103. 5d., which will be devoted to the general church expenses. Miss M. Standish, of Penketh, was at the organ.

div.head: LOCAL WILLS.
div.p: LOCAL WILLS.
WILL OF THE LATE MR. EDWARD GREEN ALL

Probate of the will, dated 3rd March, 1890, of Mr. Edward Greenall (eldest son of the late Mr. T. Greenall, and nephew of Sir Gilbert Greenall,Bart.), late of Grappenhall Hall, Grappenhall, Cheshire, J.P., who died on the 17th May last, aged seventy- two years, has been granted to the acting executers, his sons, Mr. Edward Greenall, of Hill Top, Latch- ford ; Mr. Henry Greenall, of Beech House, Lymm ; and Mr. Alfred Greenall, of Grappeahall, power being reserved to grant probate to Mr. Frank Greenall, also named as an executor in the will. The net value of the late Mr. Greenall's personal estate has been sworn at £25,039 Hs. 2d., the gross value be- inc £35,038 Bs. 7d. The testator bequeaths to his wife, Mrs. Annie Greenall, daughter of the late Mr. Peter Greenall, M.P., the use and enjoyment for her life of Grappenhall Hall and its furniture, and the in- come for her life of the residue of his property. Subjact to Mrs. GreenalPs life interest therein, the Grappenhall estate and the effects at the hall are lett to the testator's son Edward, who is to pay £3.000 in respect thereof to the residuary estate. After the death of Mrs. Greenall, sums of £4,000 each are to be in trust for the testators's daughters, Annie Appleton and Helen Jones, and a sum of £3.000 Nr his son Peter. He leaves the ultimate residue of his property in equal shares to his sons Edward, Henry, Alfred, and Frank.

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE MR. JAMES MARSON, J.P.
div.p: WILL OF THE LATE MR. JAMES MARSON, J.P.

The will of the late Mr. James Marson, tlillt Cliffe, Appleton, Warrington, dated April 30th, 1891, was re- cently proved at the Probate Office, Chester. The testa- tor appoints his only son, Mr. Charles Marson, and his (testator's) wife, and Mr. Peter Stubbs, of Statham Lodge, executors and trustees. He bequeaths to his wife absolutely a legacy of £l,OOO (to be paid to her with- in one month of death) and all his household furniture and ornaments, plate, linen, china, glass, wines, liquors, books, pietares, paintings, prints, horses, carriages, greenhouse plants, greenhouses, and other glass-houses, and the fixtures belonging thereto,and the dead stock and all other property of any description (except money, securities; for money, and muniments of title) which, at his death, should be about the house at Hill Cliffe. All his estates known as the Lower Stretton Hall Farm,Fogg's Farm, and Steno's Farm, and all other lands of his situate at Antrobus, Whitley, and Stretton, in the County of Chester, with all appurtenances thereto, he devises to the use of his son Charles and his assigns during his life, and on the death of his son to the use of the first and every other son of the said son successively according to their seniority, with remainder to the use of the first and every other daughter of Charles succes- sively according to their seni • rity. From the determina- tion or failure of the several, estates he devises the said estates to the use of his trustees and their heirs and assigns to hold the Same upon the conditfions declared concerning his residuary trust estate. He bequeaths all the property, whether real, unmovable, personal or movable, and wheresoever situate (except that other- wise disposed of) to his trustees respectively, according to the piature and tenure thereof, upon trust, that they shall sell, call in, collect, and convert into money the said property at such time and in such manner as they shall think fit (hut as to reversionary property not until it falls into possession, unless it shall appear to his tills- tees that an earlier sale would be beneficial), and shall out of the moneys pay his funeral and testamentary expenses, debts, and the legacies bequeathed in his will, and the duty on any legacies bequeathed duty free. The residue is to be invested in one or more of the modes indicated. He empowers his trustees at their discretion to postpone the sale or conversion of the whole or any part of his estate., and par- ticutarly to postpone the conversion of, and retain in specie, any shares in Peter Stubs Limited which testator !night hold at the time o his death. Notwithstanding any such postponement regarding his real estate, the same should' l'or the purpose of transmission be considered as converted' from the time of his death. The testator provides that out of the pro- ceeds of the trust fund his trustees shalt pay to his wife an annuity of £2.000 clear of legacy duty during her his and to his sisters Sarah Marson and Ann Marson an annuity of £3OO clear of legacy duty during their joint lives and during the life of the survror (the last-mentioned annuity todan without power of anticipa- tion) IT quarterly payments. The trust fund is to held in trust or testator's said son Charles fcr his absointe use and benefit, provided that if he die in testator's life- 'time. nntlient leaving a child, whe shall attain the age et

21 years, the annuities provided for testator's wife and sisters to determine, the trustees standing possessed of all the residuary trust fund. If at the time of distribut- tng the fund his wife and one or both of his sisters should be living then, £30,000 and also one equal moiety of all the residuary trust to be held in trust for his said wife absolutely.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.
STILL SPREADING.

We regret to any that there are, as yet, no signs of an abatement of the smallpox epidemic in War rington. This may be seen from the fact that yesterday morning there were no fewer than twelve fresh cases notified. This makes a total of 115 r.uses since the 28th July. There have been alto- gether six deaths from the disease, five of these cases having been unvaccinated. Yesterda3r morn- ing there were 72 cases in the hospital, cud the need for additional accommodation was beginning to be severely felt. The pressure is all the greater because of the circanistance that most of the patients are women.. The new room at the front of the Haybridge works is being rapidly prepared, and it is expected that it will be • ready to-day. It will be used for convalescents and will give accommodation for another 100 patients. About seven or eight patients are left to be dealt with at their own homes, but these are cases in which there. are few persons in the houses where they are, and all these have been 'carefully vaccinated. Among the patients are four of the children of the late Mr. Lawless, one of whom has died. Another of the deaths is that of a man named Samuel Dumbell, aged 53 years, ,who continued at work until there were symptoms about his body showing the presence of the disease. This case was looked upon na precarious from the beginning, and he died on Sunday night, and .his body was interred at two &Clock the following ,morning. . .

Since 'the above was written there have, been three more cases of small-pox. In addition to the stnall?os there are over 80 cases of scarlet fever in the Aikin-st. hospital, It is proposed to use the newly-erected iron hospital for the treatment of typhoid fever patients. The following report was issued by Dr. Gornall yester- day morning : HOPE HOSPITAL—
Fresh cams of Snaall-pox notified l2 In Hospital
Total 84
AIKIN-STIMIT HOSPITAL— Fresh cases of Scarlet Fever nolified ... 3 In Hospital Other Diseases notified In Hospital
Total . . Room urgently required. 30th September, 1892. JOHN H. GORHAM., Medical Officer of Health.
THE COST OF THE OUTBREAK.

The cost of the outbreak to the town has been I estimated at as high a figure as .C 3,000 but the I actual cost as yet is not anything like so serious. It need hardly be said, however, that the outlay mast of necessity have been very considerable. , Nearly all the work that has been done has had to be done with the-utmost promptitude and almost regardless of expense; and in addition to this there is the rent of £2O a month that has to be paid for the use of the Haybridge ironworks. On the other band there is a quid pro quo for what has had to be spent on the new structure in Aikin-street, as that will always be available for use in any emergency that may arise in the future. With regard to the sum paid for tke additional land acquired in Aikin-street, that is an expenditure which woulcl, have been incurred by the Corporation in any event, though the purchase might not have been so rapidly carried out had not the epidemic broken out

div.head: NEW IRON HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE NEW IRON HOSPITAL.

The new hospital at the end of Aikin-st., is now ccm- pleted, though it is not yet in use. It is, .in fact, not now intended to use it for the purposo of isolating small- pox patients. The hospital is situaten about 100 yards from the existing infectious diseases. It is built upon land which has been acquired from, Mt. R. Pierpoint, M.P.. by the Corporation. The land is something over an acre in extent, and has been walled in to secure iso- lation. The building, as we have before explained, is 'built of corrugated iron lined with timber: With regard to its design, the two main apartments are the male and 'female wards, each of which is 37 feet by 20 feet, the 'height being 15 ft. The wards will each accommodate ten beds, and they are each provided with a bath room and lavatory at the ends. There is also an entrance hall, and near to this is the nurses' room 10 feet by 15 feet, and communicating with the kitchen. The roof is composed of corrugated iron, underlined with wood,and it will also be provided with a layer or felting for the purpose. of keeping the place warm in winter and cool in summer. All the interior woodwork will be stained and varnished. There is, of course, an adequate supply of gas and water. The building having been raised upon brick piers, there will be thorough ven- tilation underneath, and excellent ventilation has been provided for in the building itself. The wards, it should be added, are to be heated by circulating water pipes on a principle which has been patented by Messrs. Lea arid Son, of Runcorn. The work of erecting the hospital has 'been carried out by Messrs. Morton and Co., of Liver- pool. The brick foundations were • lad by Mr. Wm. Taylor, and the heating appliances were supplied by Mr. Caldwell. All the work has been done under the supervision of the borough surveyor. The cost of the building is estimated at £3OO. XDDMONAL ACCOMMODATION. AT ROPE HOSPITAL.

The additional accommodation which is being pro- vided in the Dallam-lane buildings will be completed on Tuesday. This has been obtained by converting the upper storey into two convalescent wards, and there will also be a dining and bath rooms for the patients on the same floor,for which purposes the offices will be utilised. There will be an easy staircase constrncted in place of the old ladder, and a corridor will be formed that will be used a a promenade for the convalescents. The rooms will be heated with Musg,ravela stoves, which are in use for the other parts of the hospital. The work is being carried out by Mr. William Taylor. The fencing off of a part of the ground surrounding the hospital is being rapidly proceeded with in order to pre- vent the public from approaching too near. The marked curiosity manifested by a large number of people cannot be too much reprehended. They even follow the ambulance conveying patients to the hospital, and the friends of the patients collect on the bank in the field adjoining the ground in which the building stands, and shout to the patients who are promenading about outside.

div.head: STRANGE SCENE AT TEIE " HOPE " HOSPITAL.-A DEMENTED PATIENT.
div.p: STRANGE SCENE AT TEIE " HOPE " HOSPITAL.-A DEMENTED PATIENT.

A scene of a remarkable and rattier sensational char- acter was enacted at tho Hope hospital, on last night week. One of the patients, a navw,developed an acute mania which is spmetimes caused by smallpox, and be- gan to act in a strange and alarming fashion. He went about the room on all fours and showed a strong desire to get under the beds of the other patients and attempt to overturn them. He also marched about the room with afire shovel. Dr. Gornall was at once sent for by the nurses, and he, accompanied by Mr. Bloomfield, came to the hospital it being then about midnight. They found the man to be. altogether unmanagable, and force had to be resorted to in order•to put upon him a pair of handcuffs. The patient is noW.,, we believe, doing well. DIFFERENCES ON: THE SAMTARY COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of'the Sanitary Committee was held on Saturday night, for the purpose of considering what additional accomodation it was necessary to make, in order to provide for the smallpox cases. Dnring the discussion which took place the Chairman of the Com- mittee (Alderman Bargess) was interrogated by two or three members of the Committee as to his reascns for ignoring the Hospital sub-Committee. It sh'iuld be stated that the duties of the Hospital Sub-committee as defined by the standing orders of the Town Council, are to visit the hospital from time to time and report thereon ; and it is generally considered by the members of the Council and the public, that the Committee has the general oversight of all that appertains to the management and conduct of the hospital. lit seemed, however, that this was not Alderman Burgess's idea of the functions to be performed by this Committee, and it was complained that, he being the convener of it, he has only thought it wmth his while to summon it together once since last November, and during the whole of the present crisis it hits not be encalled together oece. In reply to the interro- gatcories of various members of the committee as to what he considered to be the duty of the sub-committee„ AlAerman Burgess replied that he thought if there was_ aay whitewashing, or painting, or general repairs to he dime at the• hospital it might be called together for that'. purpose. As may be imagined, this expression ot opinion an Alderman Burgess's part roused considerable feeling, and a very indignant protest from Councillor H. Roberts,,who told the Alderman that, if his opinion were correzt, then the Hospital Sub-committee ought to be designated at once the"whitowashing ard painting sub- committee! This episode, we believe, is only one of many similar occasions which have happened of-late, in which more than half the members of the committee had expressed their strong disapproval from time to time of the conduct of the chairman. It is said that his assumption of the absolute control of everything which relates to sanitary. work has been strongly resented, and in the opinion of several members is largely frustrating the proper management of this impor- tant department ot the town's busities.ss As an example

of the rather circumlocutory way in which some of the business of the Sanitary Committee is transacted, it is stated that when the " Hope Hospital "was taken a sub- Committee of the general Committee was appointed for the purpose of preparing it for the reception of smallpox patients. This sub. Committee, with the assistance of the constructor,. prepared the two large wards, but when, last week, it was necessary to provide additional accom. °dation, although the sub-Committee appointed had only just ceased to do the work referred to the Chairman caused a meeting of the Committee to be called together again for the purpose of appointing 'another special Committee to see to further but comparatively small extension.

div.head: S'ANITARY COMM/TUE AND THE OUT-
div.p: THE S'ANITARY COMM/TUE AND THE OUT-
BREAK.

As might be expected the minutes which the Sanitary Committee aie^ to present to, the Town Council next Tuesday evening are largely taken up with the resolu- tion relating to the outkrealr of smallpox. The gist of inert of these have already been given in the "Examiner." A resolution adopted at a meeting on Wed- nesday was to the effect that theAogreement between the Corporation an& the Haybridge Company. Limited, for the tenancy of the Hopo hospital at £3O a month be approved. Other resolutions adopted at the earn. meet- ing were "That Mr. John Guest Oornall, MA., MB., M.R.C.S., L.R.C.P., b appointed to assist the Medical Officer of Health for a period of sir months, at a salary of £l5O for that period" ;and "That at the request of the Museum Committee, all booki belonging to the Public Library found in houses in which cases of infecti- ous disease exist be destroyed."

div.head: "THE REMEDY WORSE THAN THE :DISEASE."
div.p: "THE REMEDY WORSE THAN THE :DISEASE."

In apologizing for the absence of several gentlemen at the proceedings in connection with the presentation to the Rev. W. E. Glenn, in Holy Trinity ticheol, Museum- at., on Monday evening, the Chaitman (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) said a letter had been received from Mr. W. J. Forshaw. That gentleman had ben re-vaccinated, and was, therefore, unable to be present. It seemed to him (Mr. Carleton) that the remedy against small-pox which had broken out in the borough was worse than the disease. (Laughter.) Other gentlemen, whose names he had not got before him, had sent similar mes- sages of apology for their absence.

div.head: HEALTH AND WEATHER OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: HEALTH AND WEATHER OF WARRINGTON.

For week ending Saturday,Sept. 24th, 1892,whict was the 36th of the cutrent year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Birtlis : War- rington, 40; Latchford, 9; tntal 49: Deaths: War- rington. 17; Latchford, 2: total 19. The excess of births ovt,r deaths was 30. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 182 per 1.000 ogainst 23.7 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 196 the corresponding week of last year: The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 5.7 per 1,000, against 5.4, the average rate of the four previous weeks, arid against 3.9 the corresponding week of 1891. The ages of mortality, were— 0 to 1 5; 1 to 5,2; 5 to 15, 2; 15 to 25, 4; 25 to 60, 2; 60 upwards, 4; total 19. The deaths included-3 from enteric fever, 2 from diarrhoea, 1 from scarlet fever, 2 from heart disease,.3 from brain disease, 1 from liver disease, 1 from debility. The following cases- of infectious disease have been 'reported during the week: Smallpox 20, scarlet fever 16, enteric fever 1. AfeteorolOgy.—The mean temperature was 54.1 Fah., and therefore 1.4 degree colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 64 F., was recorded on the 19th inst., and the minim•im temperature 40 F., on the 18th inst. The rainfall measured 95in. The general direction of the wind was 8.W., the reading of the Anemometer denoting 820 miles.—Jourt H. Gonme.tx. Medical Officer of Health.

ANOTHER. CABINET COUNCIL,

A Cabinet Council was held at Downing-st. yesterday, all the members except Mr. Acland bsing present. Mr. Gladstone afterwards left London for Hawarden, where he will remain till the end of next month. THE RESULT OF BEDFORDSHIRE ' ELECTION. The result, was declared yesterday as follows : Whitbread (L) 4,e3a Duke 4,596
Majority
After the declaration of the poll, Mr. Whitbread ad- dressed the electors, stating that they had maintained intact the Liberalists of South Bedfordshire_
THE CHOLERA.

Despatches from Hamburg and St. Petersburg an- nounce a continued abatement in the cholera epidemic, but the disease is raging at Riga and other Russian towns. The captain and officers of the steamer Nor- mannia have beelrpresented with a testimonial by the cabin passengers in acknowledgment of their skill and judgment while the vessel was detained in quarantine at New York.

div.head: DECLINE AT HAMBURG..
div.p: DECLINE AT HAMBURG..

HAMBURG, TIIURSDAY.—To-day's official bulletin re- ports that seventy cases of cholera an.lo twenty-five deaths having been registered yesterday. These figures include twenty-six cases and nine deaths belonging to the previous day, thus leaving forty-four cases and six- teen deaths for yesterday, against forty-nine and thirty on the 27th. Sixty-six patients were removed to hospi- tal and twelve bodies to mortuaries, against fifty-eight and thirteen respectively on the preceding day. BUDAPEST, THURSDAY.—Up to this morning, five cases have been reported from the cholera hospital, four of the patients—namely, three women and one man—hav- ing, succumbed. Four fresh cases were taken to the hospital this morning. Sr. PETERSBURG, THURSDAY.—Thirty-five cases of cholera and seven deaths occurred in this city yester- day. HAVRE, THURSDAY.—Four cases c 9: cholera and two deaths occurred here to-day. VIENNA, THURSDAY NlGHT.—YeSteVthy at Cracow seven fresh cases of cholera were recorded and four deaths.

div.p: THE DOUGLAS TIUGEDI.

The inquiry into the death of Edith Anne Cooper, at the Regent Hotel, Douglas, said tc,have been caused by her husband was resumed on Wedaesday. Mr. Weldon,, manager, said he was told there - wasquarrelling in the Coopers' room, and went up with..-.the bead porter. The, room was quiet, but on knocking,,tltiedoor was unleolie.d. by prisoner, who remarked that, his wife was in a dead faint. Mrs. Cooper was lying on: the floor quite /naked. On the portermoving the body,.witness noticed a wound on the left breast, and large spots of blood on the bed.. Witness sent for the police. Gilbert Connock, porter,. stated that when he moved the body he saw 3, WOUndi two inches long on the left breast, and told Mr. Weldon the woman had been stabbed, to the heart. There was blood on the carpet, which appeared to have teen wiped, up. There was no blood about the wound. Police-Con- stable Whitfield said prisone.r stated that he 'tad beento Dumbell's Bank with Mr. Bradshaw, and on his return , he found his wife in bed " like this." Helot her out and poured water over hen. Dr. O'Malley stated that Mrs. Cooper had probably been an hour -when he was called. Death must have- ensued in five, minutesafter ' the wound. On further examination he found superfi- cial bruises on the right arm, produced by blows or pressure, also on the left breast. and foreheadt. and a small abrasion on the. right cheek. Be also noticed bruises Oa the legs, but these were uot recent. The wound on the breast could not have :teen self-inflicted. The inquiry was not-adjourned.. The inquiry respecting the death of Mrs. Cooper at Douglas was resumed on Thursday. Dr. Buxton stated that the deceased's black eyes SVC/0 not caused by sea- sickness, but by-violence, and it was possible, but not probable, that the wound was self-inflicted. There was no evidence that the decease was intemperate. Dr. Mackenzie concurred, and added that the prisoner was a man o excitable temyerament. Witness had prescribed sleeping draughts for him in prison. Deceased appeared to have been subjected to much vio, lence during life. Louisa Mary Cooper, sister of the deceased, said the prisoner and her sister wo- e publicly married on the 4th November- last - They sLid they had been privately married in the previous July. On New Year's rive witness res, red a telegram from the prisoner and went. to Manester, and found her sister with a black eye and lon,' ,ed forehead. Wit- ness gave evidence as to other acts of violence, William Cooper, brother of, the deceased, stated that on March I 2/3.th hogave priwner a thrashing for illtrestmeat of Lis

wife, and next morning prisoner thanked him and said he did quite right. Four days afterwards prisoner again struck his wife in the eye, and witness thrashed him ; with a riding whip, for which prisoner again thanked him. Afterwards he found prisoner standing over his wife, with a knife, which be took froM him. The in, quiry was adjourned until next day. ' THE PRISONER 'GIVES EVIDENCE. At therresumption of Cooper's trial,. before Demister' Drlukwater and a special jury,, yesterday morning, the expectation that Cooper himself would be the first to give evidence, drew an eager crowd of many hundreds of persons fo the vicinity, tied-besieged the Courthouse but not a tithe could gain admission. Mrs. Cooper's father, sister,. and brother were also present. The prisoner's arrival at court was attended with but slight. demonstration. The tension of the protracted trial is tellirig on him, and on taking his place in the dock he looked very ill and careworn. Prisoner in,giving an account of the scetle in the death chamber said, Having washed my hands I. took up' the knife and was panng my nails with it when sitting on the edge of the bed. It was a knife I gener- ally used for the purpose, and I took it from a dressieg case the first thing in the morning and used it after washing. The blow I got on the face was left handed. The knife was in rey right hand, and when I. got the blow I struck back forgetting the knife. When you found she was cut you merely thought it was. a surface cut ? That is so. I have heard the descrip- tion of the wound and I am not at all conszious of the knife having entered her body in the way spoken of. I was dazed and just knew enough to try and bring her round. When I struck at her she was lying half raised lon the pillows. She had her nightdress on and th&. knife if it cut her cut through the nightdress. After that I am in entire ignorance of what took place, except my efforts to bring her round. When the doctor told me she was dead I acted like a maniac. , The examination of the prisoner lasted three hours, and Cooper admitted having ill-used his wife when in liquor. Freak Whorral Friend, physician and surgeon, wa3. ealled for the defence. In the course of his evidence.. witness said that with a random blow of such a knife' the chances of a wound proving fatal were very small. Nothing could have saved her after such a wounr, but the prisoner had a right to assume that it was a desh woumi.—John Alfred Dearden, physician and surgeon. gave corroborative evidence.—Thomas Arthur Weed,' physician and surgeon, also gave corroborative evidence. —Case adjourned. DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS.

C OOP EFF, On Saturday evening Mr. Roberts, solicitor, ter, ace aecOmpanied by Mr. Arthur Earle Hunt, Manchester arrived in Dougla,s and proceeded to the Isle of Mn Gaol where, on stating their business, they were shown into the presence of George Barker James Cooper, who stands - committed for the wilful murder of Edith Annie Cooper. his wife: Mr. Roberts served Cooper with tormal notice, citing him to appear as co- vspondent in certain pr)ceel-- ings for divorce which Hunt has instituted against Mrs. Hunt. It is said that eight yearsago Mrs. Hunt elciped : with Cooperl leaving a note for her husband announcing her purpose of going to America " with George." The couple proceeded to Boston, Massachusetts, and are said to have lived together. In Boston, Mrs. Hunt had a child born, of which it is said that Cooper was the father. Cooper would appear to have deserted Mrs. Hunt, as two years later he returned to Manchester and resumed work at his father's warehouse. Mrs. Hant was left in America, but afterwards returned to England. On Cooper's return becoming known, Mr. Hunt proceeded to the warehouse, and in the presence of the empl.-164 adminis- tered to Cooper a sound horsewhipping. He is now tak- ing proceedings for divorce. At the time of her marriage' Mrs. Hunt was employed as saleswoman by Mefirs* Cooper. This fresh development has created a great sensation i Oouglas. n

T E MANCHESTER TRUST, LIMITED. Authorised Capital £1,000,000 • Sub.cribed Capital • £500.000 Paid up • Uncalled DEPOSITS RECEIVED IN THE FOLLOWING FUNDS. GENERAL SECURITIES FUND. A.—Certificates for sums of £5O or over will be issued, and interest allowed in this fund asunder. viz. For six months 3l per cent per annum. For twelve months 4 per cent per annum. For two years 4l per cent per annum. For three years 44 per cent per annum. For deposits withdrawable at the end of any six months on seven days' notice 3l per cent. per annum. E.—Pass Bo?ks For sums under 00 (or over that arnotint if desired for the convenience of the depositor) pass books will be issued, repayment being made either at fixed dates or I on one calendar month's notice. The rates of interest for fixed terms will be the same as above. For money with irawahla at ' any time on one calendar month's notice interest at the rate of 3i per cent, per annum will be allowed. THE MORTGAGE SECURITIES FUND. This fund will comprise mortgage securities only. For deposits fixed or one year and under three years the interest allowed will be 34 per cent, per annum, but if for three years and upwards the rate will be 34 per cent, per annum. The security thus obtained is of an absolute character, and constitutes for•the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment, both as to capital and income, free from all market fluctuations end vicissitudes. The depositors in each fund will be secured (Firstly).—By a first charge upon the securities lodged in the fund. (Secondly). —By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust Limited.
